articles.title_orig: European diplomats attacked in West Bank a day after beating of Post photographer
articles.title_zh: European diplomats attacked in West Bank a day after beating of Post photographer
articles.content_orig:
Masked settlers are accused of attacking the convoy
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".
It was also condemned by the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".
In Saturday's incident the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice.
"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
"As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice.
"Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."
Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.
But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux, the left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".
A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."
It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said a ‘serious incident’ caused the blaze at the facility in Wainwright
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Saturday that a “serious incident” caused a major fire at a military base in Alberta.
“A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta,” Carney said in a social media post.
“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” he said.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel.

articles.title_orig: Opinion | China’s ‘golden week’ holidays come at a cost
articles.title_zh: Opinion | China’s ‘golden week’ holidays come at a cost
articles.content_orig:
A week of uninterrupted leave might look generous on paper, but it can conceal the working days shifted elsewhere to make it possible
For iPhone users in China, the calendar has long presented a small but recurring problem. On a Sunday designated as a make-up workday, an alarm might remain silent. On a regular Friday converted into a day off, it might ring anyway.
Nearly 17 years after entering the Chinese market, Apple quietly updated its operating system in September to automatically recognise China’s official schedule of adjusted holidays and workdays. The fix is modest, but it points to a larger question: what happens when a society’s working week no longer matches the natural cadence of the days?

General Ron Clark, commander of US Army Pacific, said the “tyranny of distance” made it difficult to rely on air and naval forces during a panel discussion at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting this week.
The comments reflect mounting concerns among US commanders that China’s increasingly sophisticated air and naval forces could stop American forces operating freely in the region, leaving them in greater need of land-based support.
Clark commands more than 107,000 soldiers deployed in US Pacific territories and in allies such as South Korea and Japan, with rotational deployments in the Philippines.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia stirs bipartisan outrage
articles.title_zh: Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia stirs bipartisan outrage
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a midterm rally at Truist Arena on the Northern Kentucky University campus on Oct. 17, 2026 in Highland Heights, Kentucky.
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday that waives many of the sanctions in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Congress passed in the late senator’s name last month. The waiver, coming a week after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia, also underscores fraying relations between the U.S. and Ukraine.
The law, which was set to take effect Oct. 18, called for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and other entities, alongside tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported into the U.S. from major buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. Those measures were intended to restrict the financial resources supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Read More: Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
The U.K.’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office estimated in June 2025 that international sanctions had deprived the Russian state of at least $450 billion in war funds since February 2022, including through lost oil tax revenues and immobilized central-bank reserves.
While Trump’s waiver leaves existing sanctions in place, it blocks the additional pressure the new measures were intended to exert.
Trump has also pushed Ukraine to scale back its own campaign against Russia’s energy sector, repeatedly urging Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure and suggesting that those attacks are driving up U.S. fuel prices. But Ukrainian strikes are only one factor affecting fuel prices; disruptions linked to the war with Iran are largely responsible for constraining global supplies, while reduced Russian refinery activity has added pressure to diesel markets.
On Oct. 11, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “ energy ceasefire .” But Ukrainian officials reported Russian strikes on energy infrastructure hours after his announcement, and Zelensky said the purported agreement was news to him.
That same day, Trump called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky . Withdrawing sanctions within a week of those statements, and thereby improving Russia’s financial position,  points to an increasingly uneven display of support from the U.S.
Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, tells TIME that the decision is basically “is like trading [Ukrainian] democracy for diesel.”
A diesel deal with Russia, announced Oct. 9, is one of the many recent actions Trump has taken in an effort to reduce fuel prices for Americans ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. The deal came with an easing of sanctions as the Treasury Department issued a temporary license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel, including imports into the U.S., through April 7, 2027.
In his announcement of the deal on Truth Social, Trump said that Russia had agreed to supply global markets with more than 4.8 million tons of diesel, claiming  that it would bring diesel prices down “IN RECORD NUMBERS.”
But experts question whether the deal would actually have any material impact on the price of fuel for American consumers.
“There could be a modest short-term effect on wholesale prices, but only a small and delayed benefit, if any, would reach consumers at the pump,” says Tatiana Mitrova, a fellow at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy.
The waiver signed Friday, in comparison, could potentially prevent additional disruption to the global energy market . It allows Russian oil to continue flowing to importers like China and India, preventing further market volatility.
“The broader sanctions waiver may prevent additional market disruptions, but it does not itself create new supply,” Mitrova says. “The potential economic benefit to American consumers looks rather modest compared with the geopolitical cost of weakening sanctions pressure.”
Reducing that pressure—which has widely been interpreted as a component of the diesel deal, though it has not been explicitly identified as such—likely benefits Russia more than the monetary value of the diesel deal itself, Mitrova points out.
“The much bigger financial benefit for Moscow is avoiding additional sanctions that could have undermined its much larger crude oil export revenues,” she says.
And while Trump has touted the benefits of the deal, Colgan questions whether they will be tangible to any country other than Russia itself.
“Easing the sanctions probably won't move global prices very much (big market), but could mean substantial extra revenue for Russia,” he says.
But the potential consequences extend beyond Russia’s balance sheet. The waiver also raises questions about Washington’s commitment to Ukraine as relations between the two countries deteriorate.
Beyond its impact on global diesel prices, Trump’s sanctions waiver could deepen a growing rift between the U.S. and Ukraine—raising further questions about Washington’s support for Kyiv.
Konstantin Sonin, a Russian economist and a professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy, reads the move as a symbolic gesture of support for Russian President Vladimir Putin. He suggests that it could send a message to U.S. allies that extends beyond economic considerations.
“I think this will be read by Ukraine and Ukraine leadership—and European leadership—as another step in the United States withdrawing from being an active European player,” he tells TIME.
In addition to bolstering Russia’s finances and giving it latitude in its invasion of Ukraine,  Sonin says that the waiver of additional sanctions could also “boost morale” for Putin.
“It’s another bit of signaling that the United States is not as supportive of Ukraine as they were historically,” he adds. “You still cannot say that the United States is on Putin's side, but it is another bit of diminishing support for Ukraine.”
Mitrova agrees that the biggest benefit to Russia might be more strategic than financial.
“For Putin, the most valuable outcome may not be additional diesel revenues but the perception that Washington is increasingly prioritizing domestic energy prices over sustained pressure on Russia,” she says. “That could reinforce the Kremlin’s belief that it can outlast Western support rather than make meaningful concessions.”
Zelensky criticized the decision to block the new sanctions.
“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” the Ukrainian President wrote on X on Saturday. “And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people. This certainly does not stop the war.”
Mitrova argues that in easing sanctions, the U.S. also compromises its position with European leadership that has continued to align closely with Zelensky and Ukraine.
“Europe is still tightening sanctions against Russia, while Washington is now moving in the opposite direction,” she says. “By suspending sanctions that were designed to discourage major countries from buying Russian energy, Washington risks undermining a central pillar of the Western strategy toward Russia.”
Trump’s waiver earned a flood of criticism from both sides of the aisle, particularly since it undermined a widely supported act of Congress. The Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 cleared Congress on Sept. 16 with overwhelming bipartisan support: a vote of 86-11 in the Senate and a vote of 262-159 in the House.
North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is leaving office in January, called the decision “beyond irresponsible” on Saturday.
Suggesting that the Trump Administration is overtly snubbing the will of the legislative branch, Tillis wrote on X : “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.”

articles.content_orig:
Coverage for this event has ended.
Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged Saturday that his sister-in-law was involved in federal terrorist watchlist litigation during the Obama administration, days before former President Barack Obama is scheduled to campaign alongside him.
Fox News senior correspondent Mike Tobin asked El-Sayed pointedly about a 2016 lawsuit identifying Mariam Jukaku as a plaintiff challenging her reported placement on the Terrorism Screening Database.
"Yeah," El-Sayed responded.
"Basically, it's exactly the point. She did nothing wrong and was captured on that and then sued and got off," El-Sayed said, blaming Republican rival Mike Rogers.
Court filings allege Jukaku underwent extensive airport screening in 2012 and was believed to have been removed from the watchlist by 2016. The FBI declined to confirm or deny her status to Fox News in a statement.
The exchange followed Rogers' accusations about El-Sayed's alleged family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which the Democrat denies.
Fox News' Mike Tobin and Patrick McGovern contributed to this reporting.
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., fired back at President Donald Trump on Saturday, mocking the president's rally in Dalton, Georgia, a day earlier as the two traded personal attacks ahead of November's closely watched Senate election.
"Maybe you saw Donald Trump was in Dalton yesterday. Oblivious to the collapse of his presidency. A crowd smaller than this one endured two hours of senile babbling while the price of oil hit its five month high," Ossoff told supporters at a Cobb County rally alongside Democrat gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms.
Trump had taken aim at Ossoff's campaign spending on makeup during Friday's rally for Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins, joking about his own television-ready appearance.
"And by the way, I wear very little, and I do it myself," Trump told supporters, before accusing Ossoff of spending a fortune on professional makeup.
The Washington Free Beacon previously reported that Ossoff's campaign spent $2,887 on makeup services between February and July 2026, citing federal campaign finance records.
Ossoff's Saturday remarks did not directly address the makeup criticism, instead targeting Trump's handling of the Iran conflict and accusing his administration of corruption.
Sen. Bernie Sanders , I-Vt., took a playful jab at Florida's Republican reputation Saturday night as he rallied supporters of Democrat Senate candidate Angie Nixon in Melbourne.
"You know, I was I was told that Florida is a red state. Doesn't look too red tonight," Sanders told the crowd.
The Vermont independent argued that working-class voters in traditionally Republican and Democratic states face many of the same economic pressures.
"So I don't believe in red state, blue state nonsense. I believe that we are all in it together," Sanders declared.
Sanders also praised Nixon's upset victory in the Democratic primary, saying she had overcome a massive fundraising disadvantage and skepticism from political insiders.
"She pulled off one of the great upsets in modern political history," Sanders said, predicting Nixon would defeat Republican Sen. Ashley Moody in November.
Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers delivered a fiery warning about the future of the Great Lakes State on Saturday, taking aim at Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed during a campaign rally in Birch Run.
"We are not going to let Michigan be the first Democrat Socialists of America state in the union, to have somebody in the United States Senate. We're not going to do it," Rogers told supporters at Birch Run Speedway.
Rogers also accused El-Sayed of misrepresenting his family's alleged connections to the Muslim Brotherhood, calling the purported dishonesty "disqualifying."
"He looked at the camera and lied to America when he said, my family or me had no connections to the Muslim brotherhood," Rogers charged.
The Republican also attacked El-Sayed's energy agenda, claiming it would increase household utility bills and gasoline prices.
"Money in your pocket. Hell, you won't even have pants when he's done with it," Rogers joked.
"This is the election where we will stand up for the freedom and future and everything that we have fought for in this country for the last 250 years. This is that election," he declared.
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., is fighting to hold onto one of the nation's most competitive congressional seats as Democrats target his suburban New York district in their bid to retake the House majority.
Lawler faces Democrat challenger Cait Conley in New York's 17th Congressional District, a race Fox News Power Rankings currently rates as leaning Democratic.
During a Saturday appearance on "Fox News Live," Lawler took aim at Conley's position on New York's sanctuary policies, accusing his opponent of supporting laws that shield criminal illegal immigrants from federal immigration enforcement.
"The idea that anybody would support policies like that, that Kathy Hochul has prohibited local law enforcement from cooperating, from turning over these criminal aliens, from honoring detainer requests is outrageous," Lawler told anchor Aishah Hasnie .
"And sadly, my opponent, Cait Conley, supports it, and we called her out on it," he added.
The race could prove pivotal as Republicans fight to defend their narrow House majority in November.
California Democrat Gov. Gavin Newsom fueled speculation about a potential 2028 presidential bid Saturday during a visit to New Hampshire, telling Fox News Digital that the Granite State's storied presidential primary history stirs a sense of emotion.
"New Hampshire is New Hampshire. It's part of the spirit," Newsom said to Fox News Digital on the sidelines of his visit.
"I was at an event this morning. There was the bust of JFK's first campaign stop. So you can't talk to me about New Hampshire and primaries without getting filled up with kind of a sense of emotion," he said.
Newsom, who visited the first-in-the-nation primary state to campaign alongside fellow Democrats, left the door open to another visit.
"If I'm invited, I hope to come back. If nothing else, come back this time of year. This place is off the charts," he said.
President Donald Trump announced plans for a $100 million federal investment in a Kentucky pharmaceutical manufacturing facility during his Saturday rally in Highland Heights, tying the project to Republican victories in November.
"If the Republicans win, the Department of War will be investing $100 million in the pharmaceutical company and there to revitalize a gigantic drug manufacturing facility in Winchester, Kentucky," Trump told supporters.
"That's a big revitalization project," he added, warning that the investment would not move forward under Democrat leadership.
Trump, who traveled to Kentucky to campaign for Republican Senate candidate Andy Barr, also hailed his administration's efforts to bring pharmaceutical manufacturing back to American soil.
"Pharmaceutical companies are building $600 billion. We're going to make all our drugs here," the president said.
Rep. Barr reinforced the economic message, showcasing investments at GE Appliances and Ford alongside the Winchester pharmaceutical project.
"Mr. President, in addition to all of those announcements and those jobs you've brought to Kentucky at GE appliances, at Ford, at the pharmaceutical investment in Winchester," Barr said, before praising the administration's support for Kentucky coal miners.
Barr also touted a $100 billion private investment in a western Kentucky energy hub, framing the projects as evidence of Trump's commitment to American manufacturing and energy dominance.

articles.title_orig: The AI bubble is about to burst — and a big market correction is coming
articles.title_zh: The AI bubble is about to burst — and a big market correction is coming
articles.content_orig:
On Jan. 1, 2000, the world got a reprieve from a much-hyped technological Armageddon when it turned out the Y2K crisis wasn’t a crisis after all.
Still, a real threat was looming if anyone paid attention to the stock market.
A new and life-changing business known as the internet, you will recall, was going to make us all rich, and not just the oligarchs behind the technology.
Dot-com stocks — even those of companies that weren’t making money, and that means most of them — were also supposed to defy common sense and gravity.
We were in a “new paradigm” — the code word for the era’s irrational exuberance in which emotion rather than metrics pushed stock valuations.
At the time, few people heeded warnings that not every business with that “new economy” suffix was destined for greatness.
It didn’t matter to masses of new investors who flooded the markets armed with the opinions of financial TV touts and newly invented discount brokerages as they kept buying with clicks on a computer screen.
People with no real knowledge of Wall Street suddenly rivaled Warren Buffett for their acumen picking these no-lose stocks.
It was all the rage in financial media at the time, overwhelming the occasional Cassandras who just didn’t get it.
That is, until reality set in.
In March of that year, the historic stock run-up was exposed as one of history’s great investment bubbles.
Many of the business models of the companies in the middle of the frenzy and the subsequent collapse were outright insane; most just overvalued by the market.
A precious few held real and tangible promise, but they too needed to survive the correction.
The losses were staggering.
A generation of investors were burned.
The tech market took years to recover from the fallout.
History, I’m afraid to say, does repeat itself when it comes to market manias.
That’s why our current mania involving all things AI will almost certainly follow the same trajectory with investor losses to follow.
Exactly what prompted the internet mood shift back in the day — and what will spark the coming artificial intelligence 180 — is hard to pinpoint.
Sign up to receive On The Money by Charlie Gasparino in your inbox every Thursday.
The most likely culprit: the collective instincts of the smart money of hedge funds and institutions that do their own research and filter out TV touts as opposed to the faux Buffetts who don’t.
As they did back during the dot-com mania, these investors are now sensing that something isn’t quite right with AI, the data and the Wall Street sales machine.
Then as now, big investors began to take profits and then more.
When the market crashed back in 2000 it was not just speculative stuff like promises of a Pets.com becoming the next Microsoft.
The aforementioned tech giant got swept up in the mood shift as well, as did just about any public company that was tied to this revolutionary business.
Scary stuff for small investors who dived into the market and never looked back until they lost everything — and many did.
What’s even scarier is that most investors either don’t remember those crazy days or are blissfully ignorant of the past as they weigh what’s up with AI and want to be part of the hype.
The AI hype is so similar to the dot-com hype it’s almost breathtaking.
The sales pitch is nearly the same: groundbreaking stuff (which is true) that all investors, not just the oligarchs, will get rich from (which really isn’t). It may be true someday, though if history is any guide, that day is far off and getting there will be messy.
I can’t tell you whether last week’s market ructions — spiking rates after a bad inflation report then a selloff in AI stocks — is the herd making its final statement on AI by rearing its ugly head as it did back in 2000.
There might be more froth to come; IPOs by hyperscalers like Anthropic and possibly OpenAI could hit in the coming weeks and months.
But common sense and history teaches us it won’t last.
Interest rates will increase because AI is in competition with the massive borrowing needs of the federal government.
The correction is coming to AI and all the companies tapping into its technology through big spending, much of it using debt, the main ingredient of any crash.
If history is any guide, it’s time to take your profits and not get greedy — or pray that whichever AI you’re betting on will be a survivor of the crash that’s coming.

articles.title_orig: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Gets a Warm Steam Welcome With 90% Positive Reviews
articles.title_zh: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Gets a Warm Steam Welcome With 90% Positive Reviews
articles.content_orig:
These are our impressions of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s campaign. Reviews of DMZ and multiplayer will follow.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's campaign has been set an unenviable task: tie the bow on a seven-year-long series of stories I’d politely describe as “uneven.” To its credit, it handles this challenge well, delivering a genuinely exciting string of missions that are great when they focus on what is new, rather than getting bogged down in the past. It’s the best Modern Warfare has been since its 2019 reboot by quite some distance, and a reminder of how good Call of Duty can be when the people making it are given time to cook.
This collection of blockbuster sequences that has clearly been built from the ground up as a single-player experience is in stark contrast when compared to 2023’s woeful Modern Warfare 3 campaign, arguably the low point of the entire series. A mishmash of multiplayer maps mixed with slivers of near-incomprehensible story, I don’t envy Infinity Ward having to pick up from where it left off. The studio has done about as good a job as it could, though, thanks to a smart structure which splits the two halves of this story until they inevitably collide, providing both variety in mission design and tone.
Captain Price has been at the centre of the Modern Warfare plot, and that doesn’t change too much here. Following the disastrous finale of MW3, he’s now on the run, acting as a lone wolf, wanted by the very people he used to work for. His half of the story is initially tied up in knots so twisted even Alfred Borden would have trouble with them. Infinity Ward’s answer? Take a machete to much of it and kill off any characters introduced in the past two games that it deems superfluous. It’s almost an admission of guilt over how poorly these people were handled in the past, but it does give a sense of finality to this seemingly saga-ending chapter.
A tale of string-pullers and warmongers, Price’s story takes place over the course of five days in the run-up to the North Korean invasion of South Korea (plenty more on that in a moment). The former SAS captain has the blinkers on for his nemesis Makarov and whoever his boss may be. It’s fair to say that the Russian terrorist is not close to being the well-developed threat from the original Modern Warfare 2, which feels like a wasted opportunity to revive a famous villain. In his place steps Mads Mikkelsen’s The Archer.
For the most part, Price’s chapters of the story play like a Bond movie, packed full of parkour escapes, car chases, and stealthy infiltrations. Mikkelsen’s casting only reinforces this feeling, and while he’s classically unsettling in his performance, his character was never given quite enough screen time for me to grow a connection with him. As such, while the missions that make up Price’s side of the story are fun, it comes across as the weaker half. Infinity Ward clearly wants Price to be the strongest emotional bond to the player and for his personal vendettas to feel like our own, but, in truth, many more of the missions are dedicated to the Korean conflict. Incidentally, this is also where I found a lot more of the engaging storytelling to be found.
MW4’s 16 missions took me around the world as well as back and forth in time. The Korean invasion takes place in the “present day” as I followed a squad of soldiers from the moment war is sparked to its conclusion, while we switch back to Price every now and then as he hunts for whoever is behind the plot in the preceding week. These time shifts also allow for a clever mixture between traditional military missions and behind-enemy-lines ingenuity. For example, an early level has you fistfighting and gun-fu-ing your way through a New York nightclub as Price puts on his best John Wick impression. The next, you’ll be holding off paratroopers on the streets of Seoul armed with a mortar. While the Korean sections are generally louder and more traditional boots-on-the-ground “Call of Duty” in their approach, it came somewhat as a surprise to me that it managed to build such a strong connection to its playable character.
There’s an endearing nature to Young Mazino's Park Hyun Jun. Just as Farah did in 2019’s reboot, he gives an emotional anchor to the story that offsets the gruff military types nicely. The same can be said for his whole squad, a mixture of Korean and US soldiers who maintain a well-balanced mixture of levity and seriousness. Their bonds rooted me in its events well, and I actually cared what happened to them by the end. In general, I found the Korean side of things much more compelling and ended up caring about the likes of Park, his friend Jae, and their northern counterpart, Ko, a lot more. While Mikkelsen’s The Archer can come across as a moustache-twirling, nuclear weapon-wielding caricature at times, MW4 actually does a good job of bringing depth to the North Korean threat instead of painting each and every one of its leaders and people following their orders in one shade of evil.
The general direction of the story may not surprise you, but there are some engaging character moments that the past couple of Modern Warfare installments have desperately lacked. One such moment happens during one of the campaign’s standout missions: Stranded. As is the way these days, Call of Duty is now an interconnected beast, so this particular mission actually gives you a taste of MW4’s DMZ extraction mode as it takes you deep behind enemy lines. Due to your stranded nature, you have to go out into the wild and forage for ways to rebuild your arsenal by raiding outposts or heading to mystery markers on the map, then head back to the safety of your basement hideout to craft new equipment. What could so easily come across as a glorified, crowbarred tutorial does actually fit in and play around with the larger story in interesting ways.
Tasked with three main objectives to complete in any order you choose across a large snowy map, Stranded embraces freedom of approach as few other missions do. You could fast travel between the three key locations and move on with the story quickly if you’d like, or spend a couple of hours unlocking each of its snow-covered secrets, ranging from exotic weaponry to keypad-based puzzles to solve. It’s an evolution of Black Ops 6’s Phantom Pain-inspired open zone mission, trading in the sand for a much cooler climate that I enjoyed skulking around with my thermal-scoped sniper rifle. It’s elegantly folded into the campaign, too, making each of its chosen mechanics make narrative sense while also being very fun to play through.
This expansive chapter was the standout mission across the roughly seven hours it took me to complete the campaign, alongside Korea’s answer to D-Day – opening with a beach landing from hell where Infinity Ward’s phenomenal sound design gets to shine – and an airfield escape in which you can dynamically switch characters at will to hold off your attackers. The latter contains a great sense of spectacle that felt like pure Call of Duty at its core. These huge-scale operations are often the highlight, with the amount of moving parts at times simply astonishing. It’s a full-blown campaign crafted to be played like one, not a hodgepodge of other modes where the story feels held together with sticky tape. A sweet relief when compared to what preceded it three years prior. That being said, while the quality of the missions is consistently very good, there isn’t a genuine all-timer here to rival the likes of All Ghillied Up or Clean House, either.
That consistency only stumbles once or twice, usually when forcing you into some unforgiving stealth segments or asking you to engage in its imprecise counter-based melee system. First-person thumping can be disorienting at the best of times, and it's not done particularly well here. This is made even more frustrating by the fact that it often rears its head during some of the story’s key moments, meaning having to retry these

articles.title_orig: New Round of ‘No Kings’ Rallies Focuses on Getting Out the Vote
articles.title_zh: New Round of ‘No Kings’ Rallies Focuses on Getting Out the Vote
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrators take part in a "No Kings: Vote Early" rally near Memorial Circle in Arlington, Va., on Oct. 17. The national day of action is taking place in cities across the country focusing on voter turnout, early voting and election protection, ahead of the midterm elections. Amid Farahi/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
At the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington D.C. on Saturday, a large inflatable donkey bounced around next to a paper-mache replica of Donald Trump's head. Next to both of them: a sign reading "VOTE EARLY."
Athena Haresign wears an inflatable donkey costume at the No Kings rally in Washington, D.C. Ava Berger/NPR hide caption
The donkey, the floating head and the voting sign were all part of the "No Kings: Vote Early" day of action. Thousands of gatherings across the country drew protestors, voters and grassroots organizers to the streets and to voting centers.
Organizers said the events were a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting in the midterm elections . The nationwide push to vote marks a pivot for the No Kings coalition, which comprises hundreds of partner organizations , including the American Civil Liberties Union and Black Voters Matter.
Demonstrators take part in a "No Kings: Vote Early" rally near the Lincoln Memorial in Washington D.C., on Oct. 17, 2026. The national day of action is taking place in cities across the country focusing on voter turnout, early voting and election protection, ahead of the midterm elections. Amid Farahi/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
"The first three No Kings were designed to send a message," said Ezra Levin, the co-founder of Indivisible — one of the major organizations within the No Kings network. "We're done sending a message."
Now, he said, they want people to vote.
The events looked different across the country. Some were larger marches or rallies, but many were smaller community gatherings such as block parties and cookouts. While some protests, like the one on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, were reminiscent of the first three No Kings rallies — with signs blasting Trump and his administration's actions — other events focused on spreading information to community members on how to vote.
People gather during a "No Kings: Vote Early" demonstration in Portland, Maine on Oct. 17. Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Saturday's events all shared similar restrictions, Levin said, including a rule against political endorsements and inviting current candidates to speak.
In Golden, Colo., a "Paws to the Polls" event invited people to bring their dogs on a march. Organizers in Everett, Wash., planned a "concert for democracy," featuring an environmental troubadour .
Thousands gathered in The Commons park in downtown Minneapolis as part of the No Kings early vote rally on Saturday, Oct. 17. Speakers including Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and former Minneapolis Mayor R.T. Rybak encouraged attendees to vote early and push their neighbors to do the same. Matt Mikus/MPR News hide caption
Superhero capes and masks were the staple of Cammy Dunford's event in Frisco, Texas. Dunford, a co-leader of Indivisible Frisco, planned a "voting is your superpower" gathering.
"I don't care if you're an independent, first-time voter, Democrat, Republican," Dunford said. "If you are eligible to vote, you need to get out there and vote. Because without everybody voting, we don't have a democracy."
Early voting in Texas does not start until Oct. 19, but Dunford and a group of her neighbors put together 500 goody bags to hand out — filled with QR codes linking to voting information and voting resources.
Alan Watkins, from Overland Park, Kan., dressed as Uncle Sam for a No Kings rally on Saturday, Oct. 17, at Mill Creek Park in Kansas City, Mo. The event was part of a nationwide day of action, with several gatherings planned across the metro. Julie Denesha/KCUR hide caption
In Washington D.C., under the shadow of the Capitol, about two dozen people huddled around an official ballot drop box, where voters can send off their mail-in ballots.
Members of the grassroots community group Free DC, which advocates for statehood in the nation's capital, organized Saturday's gathering, flanked by fluffy dogs and giggling young kids. The group cheered as each person slid their ballot into the early voting box.
Chris Salm, a union organizer and informal leader of the group, led a chant: "What are we here to do? Vote! When we vote together? We win!"
"Let's get it done!" Salm shouted as he banged on a makeshift drum: An old metal umbrella stand fastened around his shoulder by a worn-out belt.
Chris Salm, a member of the Free DC group, puts his mail-in ballot in an official ballot drop box in Washington, D.C. hide caption
Across the city at the Lincoln Memorial, protestors young and old held signs echoing that early voting message: "YOUR VOTE IS YOUR VOICE" and "VOTERS OVER VANITY!"
Celia Zanni attended the rally with her sister and mom. The 16-year-old held a sign that read "I studied checks and balances in school for this." She said Trump "needs to have his power checked."
"I'm here because I want to make my voice heard and do something about this because I'm too young to vote," Zanni said. Still, she pre-registered to vote two years early out of excitement.
Nearby, wearing the inflatable donkey costume, Athena Haresign, a horse trainer from Maryland, said she was voting in the midterm elections for the first time.
The front of her costume read: "Donkeys against Tyranny."
Before the protestors marched over to the memorial, organizers set up tables with voting information and ways to protect the election. Another focus for No Kings groups was getting volunteers trained as poll watchers.
Paul Hinojosa holds a "Vote Early" sign at a No Kings rally in Ogden, Utah, about 40 miles north of Salt Lake City, on Oct. 17. Macy Lipkin/KUER hide caption
"We want people not to just vote. I mean, that's the baseline," said Lisa Finn, one of the organizers of Saturday's D.C. rally with the advocacy group Third Act Virginia . "We want people to do more than that. We want people to be ready for anything in case something bad happens."
Levin, the Indivisible leader, said it's a response to actions by the Trump administration that he views as threats to election integrity. Levin pointed to the failed SAVE America Act that would have required voters to show a document proving their U.S. citizenship, such as a passport or a birth certificate, when registering to vote. He also raised concerns that federal immigration officers will be sent to the polls , as well as President Trump's attempts to restrict voting by mail.
At a rally in Fort Myers, Fla., Diane Scire dressed as the Statue of Liberty holding a sparkling flame. The 59-year-old construction company owner, who's a Democrat, said she urged everyone to vote.
In Fort Myers, Fla., Diane Scire dressed as Lady Liberty held a sparkling flame and waved as vehicles honked. The 59-year-old construction company owner said she urged everyone to vote. Amanda Inscore Whittamore/WGCU hide caption
"I'm hoping to see a lot of these corrupt politicians come to justice," Scire said.
Debra Marin, left, dressed as a suffragist (down to the bloomers), and Carolyn Quinn at a No Kings rally in Ogden, Utah, Oct. 17. Macy Lipkin/KUER hide caption
Both Cheryl Singleton and Sandy Hill at a No Kings rally in Ogden, Utah voiced concerns about corruption, data centers and public lands.
Cheryl Singleton and Sandy Hill of West Point, Utah, hold signs at the No Kings rally outside the Ogden Municipal Building in Ogden, Utah, on Oct. 17. Macy Lipkin/KUER hide caption
"I have a lot of grievances, and I was raised Republican," Hill said. "This is not a Republican administration. I am obviously now a Democrat, but I would vote for anyone who oppose these present policies"

articles.title_orig: Former MIT Scientist Wins Defamation Case Over Sexual-Harassment Accusations
articles.title_zh: Former MIT Scientist Wins Defamation Case Over Sexual-Harassment Accusations
articles.content_orig:
A Suffolk County jury on Friday awarded $6 million in damages to ousted star scientist and former MIT professor David Sabatini, whose career imploded after he was accused by a much younger colleague of inappropriate sexual conduct in his Cambridge research lab.
The verdict was a stark rejection of a high-profile #MeToo claim from Kristin Knouse , a fellow scientist who said Sabatini had subjected her to a coercive relationship and fostered a hostile and sexualized workplace environment in his lab at the world-renowned Whitehead Institute .
The jury of seven women and six men directed Knouse — who had brought her own suit against Sabatini — to pay the $6 million verdict, plus interest, finding she had defamed him and interfered with his ability to make a living.
“We are so happy that we got David Sabatini’s good name back,” his lawyer, Lisa Arrowood, told the Globe. “Now he can be regarded as the brilliant scientist he is.”
A 2021 internal investigation revealed that Sabatini’s relationship with Knouse had violated a strict workplace relationship policy at Whitehead. Sabatini had been a rising star in the biology world: His discovery of mTOR — a protein regulating cell growth — offered key insights into aging and cancer and also stirred talk of a Nobel Prize.
Sabatini said he and Knouse , then a Whitehead fellow, had begun a consensual sexual relationship in 2018 that ended when he began pursuing another woman. But Knouse told investigators their relationship was coercive in nature, and that Sabatini was in a position of influence and had fostered a toxic and sexually charged work environment.
Sabatini sued the institute after he was removed from his lab. Knouse countersued, asserting Sabatini abused his position of power . The institute was eventually dropped from the case, leaving Sabatini and Knouse as the lone remaining litigants.
The scene in the courtroom on Friday afternoon was tense. Minutes after the verdict was read in Suffolk Superior Court, Knouse and members of her legal team sat in the empty courtroom crying and embracing one another.
Arrowood, Sabatini’s lawyer, said a longtime member of Knouse’s lab who testified on her behalf, grew visibly angry and “body checked” a member of Arrowood’s legal team after the verdict was read aloud.
“I’ve been doing this for 44 years and I’ve never seen anyone react like this,” she said. “It was incredible.”
Knouse’s attorney, Ellen Zucker, denied that account.
“That is completely ludicrous,” she said. “Dr. Knouse was fortunate to have have friends and colleagues in the courtroom supporting her …They were standing with her and none of them body-checked anybody.”
Zucker said in a brief interview with the Globe her client intends to appeal. She said she regrets the verdict, but not the decision to pursue the case.
She and her client “engaged in this particular legal battle” because it was the right thing to do, Zucker said. “So, we’re not going to stop.”
“Multiple women came into court to speak about David Sabatini’s conduct towards them,” said Zucker. “This is unfortunate, not only for Dr. Knouse, but for a lot of people ... the good women and men who investigated this, who came to court to speak of their experiences and have tried to help move this culture forward. This is a sad day for all of them.”
Zucker said the verdict is symptomatic of a culture that fails to believe women and fails to hold men accountable, similar to the situation at Cornell University, where law enforcement officials initially did not pursue criminal charges after a former student accused several fraternity members of gang rape.
“We as a country have often excused conduct that objectifies, harms women,” Zucker said. “It does seem to be a symptom of a time where calling individuals to account for their violation of the rules and their failure in basic human decency, it’s still tough to do that.”
Being forced out at MIT and Whitehead knocked Sabatini’s once-promising career off track. About 200 graduate students, faculty, and alumni from New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine staged a walkout in early 2022 after learning Sabatini might be hired there.
In 2023, New York hedge fund billionaire Bill Ackman and an anonymous donor pledged $25 million over five years to help Sabatini get back into science. Sabatini took a position at a laboratory in the Czech Republic .
Knouse is currently an assistant professor of biology at MIT and a faculty member of its Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research.
The case is an unusual example of a high-profile #MeToo case in which the alleged perpetrator — in this case Sabatini — wound up with a large judgment. Perhaps the most widely known example of such a case involved actor Johnny Depp, who sued his ex-wife, actress Amber Heard, for defamation over an op-ed she wrote that suggested Depp had physically abused her.
A jury awarded $10 million to Depp, but also found he had defamed Heard and awarded her $2 million.
Chris Serres of the Globe staff contributed to this report.
Madyline Swearing can be reached at madyline.swearing@globe.com . Bryan Hecht can be reached at bryan.hecht@globe.com . Follow him on Instagram @bhechtjournalism . Tonya Alanez can be reached at tonya.alanez@globe.com . Follow her @talanez .

articles.title_orig: US wants Israel to 'crack down' on settler violence in West Bank, Rubio says
articles.title_zh: US wants Israel to 'crack down' on settler violence in West Bank, Rubio says
articles.content_orig:
United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has demanded Israel prosecute and jail those responsible for the attack on Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine in the occupied West Bank.
“Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Huckabee wrote on X on Saturday.
“Those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison,” he added. “We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.”
Levine was covering Palestinians’ annual harvest of olives on Friday in the occupied West Bank when Israeli settlers brutally attacked her and several Palestinians.
Israeli settlers stormed the area, beat her and stole her passport, telephone, wallet and equipment, according to witnesses.
The perpetrators, armed with bottles and slingshots, “were kicking me for like 10 minutes, and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag”, Levine said.
Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera that Levine “was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground.”
Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah.
The American photojournalist underwent surgery on her finger, which was nearly detached from her hand, and was left with a broken rib and multiple broken vertebrae, as well as lacerations, her daughter told The Associated Press news agency.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who wants to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base ahead of closely fought October 27 elections, claimed on Friday that Palestinians or “far-left” activists may have been responsible for the attack on Levine and other Palestinians.
Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has sharply criticised Israeli settler attacks against Americans, did not identify the culprits as settlers after Netanyahu tried to sow doubt as to their identity.
The ambassador, appointed by US President Donald Trump, met Palestinian-Americans in the occupied West Bank town of Turmus Aya in September to hear locals’ testimony about their experiences with pogroms. In August, Huckabee called a days-long Israeli settler siege an “act of terror”.
The US State Department criticised Friday’s attack using a cautious tone on Levine’s beating, stating condemnation of “criminal violence by any party”.

articles.title_orig: Trump Offers Putin Economic Relief in Hopes That Russia Will Return the Favor
articles.title_zh: Trump Offers Putin Economic Relief in Hopes That Russia Will Return the Favor
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy expects Trump to lift more sanctions against Russia. What we know on day 1,698
US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said that US President Donald Trump’s waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy. Rubio said also no one at the White House ordered the slow down of the speed of Ukraine’s access to Starlink to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph, referring to Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet network.
“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia. Pointing to high energy prices and the Iran war, “we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is,” he said.
Trump’s abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress , which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation. Republican Senator Rick Scott said it was clear Russia was the aggressor, and said the US had “to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia”. On social media, fellow Republican Thom Tillis described the move as “beyond irresponsible” and a capitulation “to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine”.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy expects the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and has called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin. “Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, had met Friday with US presidential envoy Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law . Zelenskyy said the US was working to arrange a three-way meeting involving him, Trump and Putin, potentially in the Middle East, Europe or the US.
Russian air defence ⁠units intercepted and destroyed nearly ⁠200 Ukrainian ⁠drones ​headed for Moscow on Saturday, ⁠Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. Sobyanin, ⁠in a long ​series ‌of ‌online posts, noted ‌that 195 drones had been destroyed since midnight, with emergency crews examining debris on ‌the ground. Russia’s civil aviation authority, ​Rosaviatsia, said two Moscow airports – Domodedovo and Vnukovo – had ⁠suspended flight operations.
Romania said Saturday it shot down two Russian drones over the Black Sea, the latest in a spate of incidents believed to be spillover from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine . Ships have been attacked in recent days by drones in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania and Bulgaria.

articles.title_orig: Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
articles.title_zh: Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
articles.content_orig:
The demonstrations began at high schools, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities morphed into a nationwide movement
Rioting erupted in cities across France on ⁠Saturday as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze, in Marseille black-clad protesters broke into City Hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti and in Lyon protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be “intimidated” by violence and blamed the unrest on the “far-left” and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.

articles.title_orig: Huckabee condemns Israeli settlers’ attack on Washington Post photojournalist
articles.title_zh: Huckabee condemns Israeli settlers’ attack on Washington Post photojournalist
articles.content_orig:
Prominent Israeli Rabbi Dov Lior issued a Jewish religious ruling on Friday permitting settlers to steal olives from Palestinian orchards in the occupied West Bank.
Lior’s ruling claims that Palestinian landowners who could not access their olives during the harvest season due to Israeli restrictions have been sufficiently compensated in the years they had access to the fruit. According to the ruling, Jews are permitted to pick these olives to claim ownership of the Palestinian land.
Lior, born in Poland in 1933, went as far as classifying the theft of olives from Palestinian farms as an “additional virtue”, as settler pogroms and Israeli occupation continue in the West Bank.
He added that settlers should “conquer the land” far from Jewish communities in order to publicly “demonstrate our ownership” and follow biblical commandment.
“The Jewish people have never given up on the Land of Israel, as we express in our prayers every single day,” the ruling continues. “The Arabs never purchased the land from the Jewish people or from any individual Jew, and therefore it is stolen land in their hands… They never bought it in any way and it remained under the ownership of the Jewish people.”
The ruling coincides with another wave of settler pogroms against Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest season. On Friday. at least 19 people were injured in 34 attacks by the Israeli military and settlers on Palestinians harvesting their crops across the West Bank.
An American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was assaulted by settlers while covering the daily violence, and five vehicles were torched.
Many Palestinian farmers have been unable to access their crops due to Israeli restrictions and the dangers from the settlers.
While settler pogroms are not exceptional, they come weeks before Israeli elections, with a push by far-right parties to gain the support of settlers and their supporters. But not all Jewish religious leaders backed the call to steal Palestinian olives.
Rabbis from the religious council of the Gush Etzion settlements published a letter calling the illegal harvesting of Palestinian crops theft, blasphemy, and a moral defect.
Tzohar, an organisation of 800 orthodox rabbis, said in a statement that only the state has the authority to confiscate property. As long as the state recognises Arab ownership of the olives, they belong to them, it added.
Mamoun Abu Amer, an analyst on Israeli politics, told Al Jazeera that there could be political reasons behind the religious groups’ rejection of Rabbi Dov Lior’s comments.
“The position of the other rabbis who rejected this call might be a move driven by political motive and pressure from entities within the government to give the impression that these are anomalous voices that do not represent the general opinion of the settlers.
“The Israeli government is trying to portray that those who carry out these riots are a limited-number group that does not represent public opinion in the settlements, and that the settlers are peaceful, good, and law-abiding, and that the issue is confined to the ‘ Hilltop Youth ‘ boys who commit these crimes,” he explained.
Rabbi Dov Lior holds immense influence among hardline settler groups, such as the Hilltop Youth, who fiercely back his hardline religious decrees that oppose any territorial compromise with Palestinians.
He is also a prominent figure within Israel’s Religious Zionist movement and serves as the spiritual guide for the far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
“Ben-Gvir relies on the religious rulings of Rabbi Dov Lior, which rely on biblical texts and the Book of Deuteronomy,” Abu Amer noted. He claimed that Rabbi Lior adopts the most extreme interpretations in the Jewish religion.
“There is an important matter, which is that Ben-Gvir competes via the TikTok platform, propaganda, and populist rhetoric, and this is a rhetoric that serves him and brings him votes, given the environment and general atmosphere in Israel after the events of October 7, as there is a ‘market for extremism’ in the Israeli society,” Abu Amer added.
Knesset member Gilad Kariv of the left-wing Democrats Party criticised Lior, accusing him and his followers of dragging Israel into a flood of moral vice.
“Whoever stands on the sidelines in this issue joins the camp of Rabbi Dov Lior and his criminals,” Kariv said.

articles.title_orig: Unrest Mars Day of Protest in France, as Student Movement Turns National
articles.title_zh: Unrest Mars Day of Protest in France, as Student Movement Turns National
articles.content_orig:
Riots broke out across major French cities on Saturday night as unrest spread beyond the capital, with government buildings torched and more than 1,000 people detained by police.
In the central city of Limoges, the historic town hall was set ablaze, with video showing its roof collapsing. In Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into city hall and defaced the building, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office, the Reuters news agency reported.
As night fell in Paris, groups of young people looted and started fires as protests ended, prompting police to respond with tear gas and baton charges in the narrow streets.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been detained nationwide in the unrest, and condemned the “unacceptable levels of violence.”
The destruction followed what had been largely peaceful protests, which have grown out of sweeping student-led rallies that gripped parts of France last month, sparking a broader movement against crumbling schools, the spiking cost of living, and perceived government inaction. The rallies have become emblematic of long-simmering, intergenerational anger among people who say their calls for social and political change are going unmet by negligent governments.
Some 550,000 protesters hit the streets across France, including 110,000 in Paris, interior minister Laurent Nunez said. Organizers estimated an even higher turnout.
“There’s an accumulation of wealth and power that’s completely out of control,” one protester, who gave her name as Pauline, told CNN in Paris on Saturday.
“We’re also here to support the youth. There are victories, but if we look at the bigger picture, it’s not going in the right direction,” the 36-year-old added.
Another demonstrator complained of “less democracy” and a “concentration of power” under President Emmanuel Macron’s leadership. “There are billionaires who control the media,” Louise, 38, told CNN. “We are fighting to change things.”
Macron slammed “sowers of chaos” for interfering with peaceful protests, and warned late on Saturday that “those who have broken, attacked (police) prefectures, as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished.”
“We do not back down in the face of rioters and those who’ve come to attack law enforcement,” said the Paris Police Prefecture – the body that oversees the Paris Police Force, emergency services and various other administrative departments – adding that its staffers stood “their ground with courage and professionalism.”
The police response to the weeks of protest has come under scrutiny. Earlier in the week, that response had left a 14-year-old boy with a fractured jaw. Another police officer was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in the northwestern area of Alençon, an action now prohibited by law.
A protester in the city of Saint-Étienne, about 40 miles southwest of Lyon, lost his hand during a march there on Saturday, a police source told CNN affiliate BFMTV. This is the second reported instance of a demonstrator losing their hand in the current wave of student protests.
A student in the northeastern city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade earlier this month, prompting the temporary suspension of one type of stun grenade by police. That ban, which still allowed police to use several different grenades, has now been rescinded.
Overall, authorities said that the “vast majority of individuals” had demonstrated peacefully on Saturday, according to BFMTV.
Posting on X, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left La France Insoumise Party, emphasized that the majority of demonstrators on Sunday had made their point peacefully. “While news channels are flooded with images of violence in dozens of cities, everything is unfolding peacefully with tens of thousands of people calmly mobilized. Two worlds, two realities.”
Youth activists led solidarity protests in Belgium, Albania and Italy on Saturday as well.
Earlier this fall, high school students in France organized scattered protests demanding reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investments in infrastructure designed to withstand the climate crisis and end to police violence against young people.
In the past decade and a half, a rise in fertility coupled with funding cuts has led to more students, but fewer teachers in classrooms. The French Education Minister Edouard Geffray has met with student protesters multiple times in recent weeks, although an agreement is yet to be made.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: VEDS Took Center Stage as the Marfan Foundation Convened the World’s Best Scientists in Barcelona
articles.title_zh: VEDS Took Center Stage as the Marfan Foundation Convened the World’s Best Scientists in Barcelona
articles.content_orig:
Scientists around the globe are working tirelessly on behalf of the VEDS community to advance research progress. And, they’re being convened by the Marfan Foundation and its division: the VEDS Movement.
From October 4–7, 2026, thanks to the generosity of our community, The Marfan Foundation – the umbrella organization of the VEDS Movement division – convened the world’s best scientists and clinicians in Barcelona for Science in Spain. Close to 300 registrants from 23 countries took part, making it the largest global scientific gathering in the Foundation’s 45-year history. And vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (VEDS) was a major topic of study and discussion throughout.
VEDS opened the meeting. The first scientific session of the 12th International Symposium on Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, Vascular Ehlers-Danlos and Related Syndromes was dedicated entirely to VEDS, with researchers from the United States, Switzerland and Hungary presenting their work. The Symposium was part of the Science in Spain event. VEDS came up again across the poster sessions and in the joint meeting of the Genetic Aortic Network and the European Society of Cardiology that followed.
Many folks with a focus on VEDS helped shape the agenda, too. VEDS expert Peter Byers of the University of Washington co-chaired the symposium’s planning committee, joined by community leaders Jared Griffin of Annabelle’s Challenge and Tony Yasick of the DEFY Foundation.
Why convening matters No single lab or hospital can answer every question about VEDS on its own. By bringing together the world’s best scientists, clinicians and community advocates in one place, the Foundation creates the collaborations that may lead to the next breakthroughs: a deeper understanding of VEDS, safer care, earlier diagnosis and, one day, better treatments and cures.
“The meeting in Barcelona was fantastic! So many young scientists and researchers in attendance presenting their latest work that has been supported by established investigators,” said Marfan Foundation and VEDS Movement Board Chair-Elect Dr. Alan Braveramn. This meeting has provided new insights in disease, potential advances in imaging, and the hope of genetic manipulation in managing disease. And, great networking and sharing ideas with colleagues from around the globe is one of my favorite things about these gatherings.”
Here is a VEDS-related research recap. Please note: the research below is early, and some of it has not yet been published or peer reviewed. It is not medical advice and does not change current standards of care. People living with VEDS should not start, stop or change any medication, treatment or other part of their care based on it. Always talk with your expert healthcare providers about your individual care.
Safer care, from the emergency room to the operating room Procedures through the leg artery: Some people with VEDS need procedures done through an artery in the leg. Tiffany Lian of Oregon Health & Science University led this research, which Sherene Shalhub presented. Drawing on more than 30 years of patient data, it found no major complications at the entry site when doctors used smaller tools. Complications were more common with larger tools. This work aims to guide how care teams approach these procedures.
Closing gaps in care: Maura Boerio of Boston University led a survey of 165 people with VEDS. Emergency room doctors were the providers most often seen as lacking VEDS knowledge. Many respondents also described trauma related to their care. The researchers recommend VEDS education for providers and trauma-informed care.
Sharing what every doctor should know: At the joint meeting of the Genetic Aortic Network and the European Society of Cardiology, Marfan Foundation Professional Advisory Board member Dr. Sherene Shalhub gave two talks: one covered emergency department care for people with VEDS, and the other covered what every surgeon should know about VEDS.
Helping people find answers sooner David Murdock of The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston presented a phone app that uses AI to look at facial photos for features linked to VEDS, Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. In testing, it identified these conditions with high accuracy. The goal is to help people get referred for genetic testing sooner, including by doctors unfamiliar with these conditions.
Understanding VEDS more deeply Several studies looked at why VEDS can look so different from one person to the next.
Differences between men and women: Tiffany Lian of Oregon Health & Science University shared findings from 557 people in the VEDS Collaborative Natural History Study. Men had aortic and certain arterial issues earlier and more often. Women had higher rates of other vascular events, such as tears in the arteries of the heart. The goal of this research is to help doctors tailor monitoring for each person.
Gene changes and timing: A UK team including Fleur van Dijk of the National EDS Service London reviewed 260 people with VEDS. Those with one type of gene change (called haploinsufficiency) had their first major event at a median age of about 42, compared with about 30 for another type. This work aims to improve care planning and genetic counseling for families.
It’s not just how much collagen, but how it’s built: VEDS is caused by changes in the COL3A1 gene, which makes type III collagen. Using skin samples from people with VEDS, Apoorva Bhandari and colleagues at Oregon Health & Science University found that different gene changes affect how collagen is built and organized, not only how much of it there is. A related study suggests skin tissue may offer a window into a person’s arterial risk. This work aims to support more personalized risk assessment in the future.
Moving toward treatment through mice studies Researchers from Switzerland, Hungary and the United States shared early laboratory work on how medicines affect the arteries in VEDS. All of these studies were done in mice.
A closer look: Janine Meienberg of the Swiss Foundation for People with Rare Diseases found that results in VEDS mice varied depending on which manufacturer made a particular medicine. This work aims to explain why earlier studies reached different conclusions about a single drug.
Testing a newer medicine: Máté Csonka of Semmelweis University in Hungary studied liraglutide, a GLP-1 medicine, in VEDS mice.
Building tools to test future therapies: Roland Stengl, also of Semmelweis University, developed ways to measure how much pressure the aorta can handle in VEDS mice. The goal is an objective way to evaluate new treatment approaches.
How some medicines may affect the arteries. Scott LeMaire of Geisinger College of Health Sciences presented work that aims to build insight into how certain medicines may affect the arteries in VEDS.
Investing in the next generation of VEDS researchers The VEDS session closed with the Trainee Awards for Scientific Excellence in VEDS, presented by Tony Yasick of the DEFY Foundation. Two early-career VEDS researchers, Apoorva Bhandari and Tiffany Lian of Oregon Health & Science University, were also among the 20 top-ranked abstracts selected for Science in Spain scholarships.
Honoring a VEDS champion Jared Griffin of Annabelle’s Challenge, a member of the symposium’s planning committee, received the Charging Forward Together Award from The VEDS Movement, a division of The Marfan Foundation, for his outstanding commitment to the VEDS community.
Your support makes this landmark convening of scientists studying VEDS possible.
