articles.title_orig: Alberta, home to the world’s 4th-largest oil reserves, will vote on a first step to leaving Canada
articles.title_zh: Alberta, home to the world’s 4th-largest oil reserves, will vote on a first step to leaving Canada
articles.content_orig:
For decades, Alberta separatism was a fringe cause. On Monday, voters in Canada’s oil heartland will decide whether to take the first step toward a referendum on leaving the country.
Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is not voting to leave Canada on Oct. 19. Instead, voters will decide whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation .
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith , who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, has said that support for starting the separation process, which was around 23% in a recent poll, is “still too high for my liking.”
Alberta has long feuded with the federal government over oil and federal power. Liberal prime ministers Pierre Trudeau and, decades later, his son Justin became deeply unpopular in the province over energy policy.
Justin Trudeau’s government imposed a national carbon tax and other climate measures that Alberta leaders said hurt its oil industry. Yet separatist parties typically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney said.
Then came the pandemic and the Freedom Convoy , which paralyzed parts of Ottawa, the Canadian capital, and blocked major Canada-U.S. border crossings.
“They needed a new cause,” Kenney told The Associated Press. “And it naturally morphed into separatism.”
Jeff Rath, a leader of the independence movement, said federal vaccine rules preventing unvaccinated Canadians from flying were his breaking point.
“If Trudeau won’t let me leave Alberta, I’m just going to pick up my whole province and go,” Rath recalled telling a friend. “COVID was really the straw that broke the camel’s back.”
“A lot of people were radicalized by the convoy,” he said.
The 2022 Freedom Convoy began over vaccine requirements for cross-border truckers but grew into a broader revolt against pandemic restrictions .
Kenney said people mobilized over anger at globalization, vaccines and pandemic restrictions, while social media allowed previously isolated activists to find one another and organize.
“They found each other and they found a cause,” Kenney said.
Kenney said the movement also became more professional, building organizations, raising money and drawing in political operatives with campaign and fundraising experience.
He also sees substantial overlap between separatist activists and people who support Russian President Vladimir Putin or believe conspiracy theories about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Kenney stressed he was describing activists, not typical separation voters, whom he characterized as frustrated Albertans sending Ottawa a message.
Kenney said the MAGA movement has been “inspirational” for some separatist activists. He said they “tried to infiltrate with at least some success” the United Conservative Party he founded. Smith replaced Kenney in 2022 after appealing to United Conservative Party members angry over COVID-19 restrictions.
“Literally, you can look at the players,” Kenney said of the convoy and separatist movements. “It’s the same people.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney has made getting Alberta oil to new markets a national priority and backs a proposed pipeline to the West Coast. His more business- and energy-friendly policies, along with his opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and 51st-state rhetoric, have made the federal Liberal leader unusually popular in conservative Alberta.
Kenney, one of the most prominent conservative critics of Trudeau’s approach to Alberta, said Carney “speaks as an Albertan,” understands the province’s grievances and aspirations, and is moving in the right direction on energy.
Rath called Carney a “formidable opponent,” saying “every major politician” in Alberta and Canada is against the separatists and acknowledged an uphill battle. He said he would be “thrilled” with more than 30% of the vote — well short of a majority.
“Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life,” Carney said. “We have to be strong and we are stronger together.”
Alberta sends roughly 90% of its crude oil exports to the United States, and separatists have taken their campaign directly to Washington.
Rath confirmed he and other independence advocates met with U.S. State Department officials three times and presented a document outlining what an independent Alberta could offer the United States.
Rath claimed people involved in the meetings were going directly to the White House and that a possible oil pipeline through the U.S. to the Pacific was “literally a topic of our last meeting with the U.S. State Department.”
The State Department said that “The Department regularly meets with a wide range of representatives. The vote is a decision for the people of Alberta.”
Kenney called the outreach “bonkers,” saying people with “zero democratic mandate” were discussing with a foreign government “the status of a separate state that does not exist.”
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta “a natural partner.”
Keith Wilson, another Alberta independence leader who was lead counsel for the 2022 convoy organizers, said separatists see the vote as a way to give Alberta more leverage in dealing with Ottawa, even short of independence.
“That’s right, because it’s called leverage. It’s called negotiation,” Wilson said. He said he would accept substantial structural changes to Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa short of independence.
“I don’t think it will recede,” Kenney said of the separatist movement in Alberta. Even 10% to 20% support, he noted, would far exceed separatists’ historic vote share. If low turnout pushed them toward 30%, “they’re going to be even more emboldened.”
“That’s not a threat to Canada,” Kenney said. “But it is a threat to the conservative movement.”
Alberta is not Canada’s only national-unity challenge. Quebec voters returned the separatist Parti Quebecois to power Oct. 5, although support for independence remains around 30% and its leader has said he will not hold a referendum while Trump is U.S. president.
Quebec voters have twice rejected independence, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum.

articles.title_orig: US debt interest costs hit $3 billion a day and jumped 8% in 2026—faster than spending, revenue, GDP
articles.title_zh: US debt interest costs hit $3 billion a day and jumped 8% in 2026—faster than spending, revenue, GDP
articles.content_orig:
The federal government’s fiscal year ended last month, and the final tally offered another stark warning about the trajectory of U.S. debt.
According to Treasury Department data released on Friday, the federal budget deficit widened to $1.99 trillion, 12% worse than the $1.78 trillion gap in fiscal 2025.
That came as revenue increased 3% to $5.4 trillion, lagging behind the 6% bump in spending to $7.4 trillion. Social Security and Medicare were the biggest line items, but in third place was interest payments on the national debt, topping defense spending and Medicaid.
Gross interest costs for fiscal 2026 came in at $1.36 trillion, Treasury data show, with an average interest rate of 3.53%. That’s more than double the rate in 2021, just before the Federal Reserve embarked on an aggressive tightening cycle to rein in inflation.
Net interest payments rose 8% to $1.05 trillion, outpacing increases in total spending, revenue and GDP. In fact, it exceeds real GDP growth of about 2% as well as nominal GDP growth of about 6%.
Fiscal 2026’s net interest costs translate to about $2.9 billion a day, and the Peter G. Peterson Foundation estimated they represent 3.2% of GDP, breaking the previous record set in 1991.
With gross U.S. debt at $40 trillion, publicly held debt at 100% of GDP, and borrowing costs up, interest payments are projected to be the fastest growing portion of the federal budget in the coming years.
At the same time, the debt burden is being increasingly exposed to market volatility that threatens to make interest costs even steeper.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been issuing more short-term debt to finance the deficit and is retiring long-term obligations.
Now, about one-third of publicly held debt, or more than $10 trillion, is due to mature within the next 12 months, meaning the federal government must roll it over at today’s higher rates.
In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected annual debt interest expenses will reach $2.1 trillion by 2036. But then President Donald Trump launched the Iran war, which sent oil prices and bond yields soaring.
The 10-year Treasury yield is now above 5%, blowing past the CBO’s forecasts for 4.1% this year, 4.2% in 2027, 4.3% from 2028 to 2031, and 4.4% from 2032 to 2036.
If bond yields remain about 1 percentage point above the CBO’s estimates, interest costs will surge to $2.8 trillion, or 5.9% of GDP, by the end of the decade, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
“Higher interest begets more debt, and greater debt begets higher rates and higher interest. Eventually, the whole thing could come crashing down,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas said last month.
“That’s why Washington needs a fiscal intervention now, before it’s too late. The President, the Treasury Secretary, and Congressional leadership need to understand the severity of this issue. There are no easy fixes, and we can’t just wish this problem away.”
But so far, there’s no sign of much willingness to tackle spending or revenue. Trump has even called for a $5,000 “dividend” check to Americans if Republicans win the midterm elections and is already handing out “rebates” to millions of Medicare and Affordable Care Act enrollees.
Meanwhile, Bessent has argued that heating up the economy further can get the debt under control.
“With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this,” he said at Southern Methodist University last month. “We’ll get to the other side of this Iran conflict, and the underlying economy is very, very strong, and I think reaccelerating.”
But CBO Director Phillip Swagel said last week that faster economic growth is unlikely to keep U.S. debt in check . While stronger economic growth will help by bringing in more revenue for the federal government, it’s not that simple.
Federal spending also boosts growth, which lifts wages that in turn affect outlays on Social Security benefits, he pointed out. A robust economy also tends to send interest rates higher, which adds to debt interest costs.
Assuming interest rates of 4% to 5%, Swagel estimated that nominal GDP growth would have to reach 7%-8%, and real GDP growth would have to hit 5%-6% in order to stabilize the debt.
That’s more than double the latest real GDP pace of 2.2% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, even bullish Wall Street forecasts put full-year GDP growth at 2.5%.
“So growth will help, but it’s probably not plausible that growth alone will stabilize our fiscal trajectory,” he said. “So then we’re left with changes in revenues and changes in spending, and those are political choices.”
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan Wants to Make A.I. Chip Smuggling to China a Crime
articles.title_zh: Taiwan Wants to Make A.I. Chip Smuggling to China a Crime
articles.content_orig:
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
Anyone sneaking A.I. chips into China could soon face a criminal judge in Taiwan: The government in Taipei plans to tighten controls on exports of A.I. servers and advanced semiconductors to Chinese buyers. Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin confirmed the plans in an interview with Bloomberg. Unauthorized shipments would then be prosecuted as a crime under the Foreign Trade Act. Until now, they have counted merely as an administrative violation.
So far, Taiwan has relied on a blacklist. Since mid-2025, Huawei and the chipmaker SMIC have been on the list of strategic high-tech goods, and Taiwanese companies need a permit to supply them. Other Chinese buyers could usually still be served, as long as the chips did not fall under the 2022 U.S. export rules. Going forward, A.I. servers and cutting-edge chips are to be added to the list of controlled goods across the board, covering all buyers in China, Startup Fortune reports , citing Bloomberg. Chung Chia-pin, a lawmaker from the governing Democratic Progressive Party, has already drafted a corresponding amendment to the Foreign Trade Act. The penalties and the start date have yet to be decided.
The move also reflects Taiwan’s close ties with the United States. In January, Taiwan and the U.S. struck a trade agreement that cut U.S. tariffs on most Taiwanese goods from 20 percent to 15 percent. In return, Taiwanese companies pledged $250 billion (about €223 billion) in investment in American semiconductors, energy and A.I., backed by a further $250 billion in credit guarantees. The stricter export rules are in line with Washington’s effort to curb China’s access to A.I. chips.
At the same time, Taiwan is cashing in on the A.I. boom. Semiconductor exports hit a record $87.2 billion (about €77.8 billion) in September, up 60.9 percent from a year earlier. The biggest beneficiary, TSMC, recently reported a record profit .
The problem is real. According to Bloomberg, Nvidia chips reach Chinese buyers through smuggling networks in Southeast Asia. In May, Taiwan arrested suspected A.I. chip smugglers for the first time, and in July, prosecutors went after Super Micro managers, albeit on forgery charges. Existing export law lacked a criminal tool aimed specifically at diverted chips.
China is a big market for American chipmakers. In its last full fiscal year before U.S. licensing requirements kicked in, Nvidia generated more than 13 percent of its revenue in China, about $17 billion (about €15.2 billion). The tightened rules for its H20 chip cost the company about $4.5 billion (about €4 billion) in charges. At AMD, China accounted for more than 24 percent of revenue in 2024.
Both sides are escalating the technology conflict. China’s commerce and science ministries have put forward their own draft that would restrict or ban exports of 40 technologies, including A.I., chips and solar technology, The Associated Press reports. Beijing has not yet responded to Taiwan’s plans. For already jittery markets, it is another signal after A.I. and chip stocks fell sharply in recent days.

articles.title_orig: WaPo photojournalist beaten by settlers slams Netanyahu after surgery on nearly detached finger
articles.title_zh: WaPo photojournalist beaten by settlers slams Netanyahu after surgery on nearly detached finger
articles.content_orig:
United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has demanded Israel prosecute and jail those responsible for the attack on Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine in the occupied West Bank.
“Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Huckabee wrote on X on Saturday.
“Those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison,” he added. “We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.”
Levine was covering Palestinians’ annual harvest of olives on Friday in the occupied West Bank when Israeli settlers brutally attacked her and several Palestinians.
Israeli settlers stormed the area, beat her and stole her passport, telephone, wallet and equipment, according to witnesses.
The perpetrators, armed with bottles and slingshots, “were kicking me for like 10 minutes, and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag”, Levine said.
Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera that Levine “was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground.”
Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah.
The American photojournalist underwent surgery on her finger, which was nearly detached from her hand, and was left with a broken rib and multiple broken vertebrae, as well as lacerations, her daughter told The Associated Press news agency.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who wants to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base ahead of closely fought October 27 elections, claimed on Friday that Palestinians or “far-left” activists may have been responsible for the attack on Levine and other Palestinians.
Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has sharply criticised Israeli settler attacks against Americans, did not identify the culprits as settlers after Netanyahu tried to sow doubt as to their identity.
The ambassador, appointed by US President Donald Trump, met Palestinian-Americans in the occupied West Bank town of Turmus Aya in September to hear locals’ testimony about their experiences with pogroms. In August, Huckabee called a days-long Israeli settler siege an “act of terror”.
The US State Department criticised Friday’s attack using a cautious tone on Levine’s beating, stating condemnation of “criminal violence by any party”.

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar’s Sister’s Phone Was Seized Before Search of Lawmaker’s Home
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar’s Sister’s Phone Was Seized Before Search of Lawmaker’s Home
articles.content_orig:
Minnesota lawmaker’s attorneys asked for return of seized items and the preservation of any recordings of search
Ilhan Omar ’s attorneys have asked the US Department of Justice to return property that federal agents removed days earlier from her home during a search.
The lawyers for the Minnesota Democrat contended that the seizure as “neither justified nor lawful”, according to a letter that the Associated Press reported on Friday.
The federal investigation into Omar was launched just weeks ahead of the 3 November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot. Democrats accused Donald Trump, a Republican, of abusing his power as president to target a political opponent.
Omar’s attorneys wrote that there is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, according to the Wall Street Journal , which first reported on the lawyers’ letter.
“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the president’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” the congresswoman’s attorneys wrote.
The federal government has issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives, and seized her phone in its investigation of the congresswoman.
A justice department spokesperson said the letter from Omar’s defense team was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”, according to the AP.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” the spokesperson, Emily Covington, wrote in a text message on Friday evening.
The letter from Omar’s lawyers also accused the justice department of violating the agency’s longstanding policy aimed at avoiding potentially influencing an election. And they raised concerns about whether the investigators followed instructions from the magistrate judge who approved the search.
The attorneys demanded in the letter that the justice department preserve any audio and video taken during the search on Monday.
The justice department launched the investigation after years of Trump and conservative media figures promoting unsubstantiated rumors that Omar’s ex-husband is actually her brother – and that she married him so that he could obtain immigration status.
Omar, the most prominent Somali American in the US, has denied that allegation.
Citing sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News reported that the search on Monday was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork. Omar’s father filled out that paperwork when she was a child.
“I’m ok,” Omar posted on X after the raid. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
Omar also said the search was “just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation”.
The president has consistently launched racist attacks against Omar and other Somali Americans in Minnesota .
In December, he described them as “garbage” who “come from hell, and they complain, and do nothing but bitch”.
He said Omar “should be thrown the hell out of our country”.
After Monday’s search, Trump denied being involved in the investigation.
“I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: China proposes export controls on 23 AI technologies
articles.title_zh: China proposes export controls on 23 AI technologies
articles.content_orig:
China has proposed adding 23 artificial intelligence technologies to its list of technologies prohibited or restricted from export, while immediately requiring exporters to register covered transfers before they proceed.
The proposal is part of a broader revision covering 40 technologies across AI, biomedicine and solar power, according to a joint announcement issued on October 16 by China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology. Public comments are open through November 15.
The proposed additions span large AI models, AI agents, computing clusters and information-processing technologies. The ministries said 14 of the 40 technologies would be prohibited from export and 26 would be restricted.
Among the proposed prohibited technologies are systems that autonomously generate or modify malicious code, as well as certain core large-model technologies trained with sensitive national data. Proposed restricted items include AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and technologies connected to advanced models, agents and computing infrastructure.
The Associated Press reported that the draft also covers some chip-design technologies, including those used for AI processing and memory chips. It said models with at least two trillion parameters, or with specified globally leading capabilities, could fall under the restricted category. The proposal does not name individual commercial models.
The other proposed additions comprise five biomedicine technologies, including areas related to cell and gene therapy, and 12 solar technologies covering polysilicon, wafers and cell manufacturing. The official announcement said the solar scope can also include key equipment that carries the relevant technology.
The catalogue revision remains a draft, but the authorities have introduced temporary pre-export registration from October 16 until the final revision takes effect. Covered exporters must submit information through the commerce ministry’s technology-trade platform.
The registration requirement applies to transfers of technology ownership, overseas licensing, changes that place a domestic technology owner or controller under a foreign entity, and other transactions specifically identified by the commerce ministry. It also covers transactions that have begun but are not yet complete.
The filing asks for information on the exporter, the recipient, the destination, the technology and its intended use, and the expected value of the export. Registration is not the same as final approval under the proposed catalogue, but it gives regulators visibility into transfers while the consultation is underway.
In an accompanying policy explanation , the commerce ministry said technologies already in the public domain through open-source releases or academic publications would not be covered. It also said most AI technologies would remain freely exportable.
For technologies that do fall into a restricted category, overseas deployment may count as a technology export. However, Chinese companies operating their own overseas cloud or computing centers, conducting chip fabrication abroad, undertaking joint research, or participating in international standards work may qualify for simplified or automatic licensing procedures.
The ministry drew a distinction between transferring controlled technology and providing access to services built on it. Overseas use through APIs, websites, apps and software-as-a-service offerings would generally not be treated as a large-model technology export when no restricted technology is transferred. Lightweight deployment on overseas devices would also generally remain outside that scope.
Reuters reported that this distinction could allow Chinese developers to continue serving international users while giving Beijing greater oversight of sensitive model transfers and overseas deployments.
The ministries said the proposed controls are intended to prevent misuse, protect national security and keep sensitive AI capabilities under human control. The commerce ministry said the move does not target any particular country, region or entity.
The final catalogue may change after the consultation. Companies involved in cross-border technology licensing, overseas model deployment or changes in control will need to assess both the temporary registration rule and the detailed technical thresholds in the draft annexes.

articles.title_orig: Official warns of China poll risk
articles.title_zh: Official warns of China poll risk
articles.content_orig:
Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) yesterday warned of possible Chinese interference in next month’s local elections.
Shen made the remarks at the annual meeting of the Taipei-based Chinese Association of Political Science and an international conference titled “Rethinking Democracy: Continuity and Change in the Values and Practice of Modern Democracy.”
This year marks the 30th anniversary of Taiwan’s first direct presidential election. In 1996, despite missile threats from China, Taiwanese voters bravely went to the polls, marking a historic milestone in their ability to determine their own future through the ballot box, Shen said.
Over the past 30 years, Taiwan has held eight direct presidential elections and experienced three changes of ruling party, consolidating its democratic system while becoming a key partner in the global artificial intelligence and semiconductor supply chains, he said.
Shen stressed that the fundamental difference between Taiwan and China lies in their political systems: democracy versus authoritarianism.
Beijing has long sought to impose its “one country, two systems” framework on Taiwan and uses “united front” tactics to infiltrate the nation and spread political propaganda, with the goal of eliminating the Republic of China (ROC) and annexing Taiwan, he said.
However, Taiwan’s mainstream public opinion has firmly rejected “one country, two systems,” Shen said. Nearly 80 percent of the public supports maintaining the cross-strait “status quo” in which the ROC and the People’s Republic of China are not subordinate to each other, a reality that must be acknowledged in any discussion of cross-strait relations, he said.
The challenges facing democracies today extend beyond conventional military threats to include authoritarian powers such as China and Russia using “gray zone” tactics, information manipulation and infiltration to divide democratic societies and undermine public trust and unity, he said.
With local elections to be held this year, Beijing might continue to interfere in Taiwan’s democratic processes to influence voters’ independent judgement, he said.
In response, Taiwan must continue to bolster its democratic safeguards and societal resilience to ensure that its democratic system remains free from external interference and that people can exercise their democratic rights in a free and secure environment, Shen said.

articles.content_orig:

Expanding Next-Generation Network Capabilities and Accelerating the Innovative Convergence of Communication, Computing, and AI Laying a Solid Foundation for 6G Development in Hong Kong
HONG KONG, Oct. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- China Mobile Hong Kong Company Limited ("China Mobile Hong Kong") announced that it has taken the lead in realising a U6GHz network, successfully completing network testing and validation at its Mong Kok flagship store and advancing the exploration of Upper 6GHz band applications in mobile networks. Implementing China Mobile Group's strategy of "strengthening the network foundation and full-stack innovation", China Mobile Hong Kong aims to enhance network capabilities through new frequency band applications, drive collaborative innovation between terminals and the wider industry, and lay a robust foundation for Hong Kong's future 6G development.
Strategic Early Deployment of New Spectrum to Build Momentum for a 6G Future U6GHz, or the Upper 6GHz band, can provide continuous wide bandwidth and is a crucial spectrum resource supporting 5G-A and future 6G evolution. On 29 November 2024, Hong Kong completed its 6/7GHz spectrum auction, becoming the first region globally to auction this frequency band for public mobile services. China Mobile Hong Kong successfully bid for 100MHz of continuous spectrum and has made appropriate forward-looking deployments, advancing network capability validation and terminal adaptation to accumulate experience for future 6G commercialisation.
Expanding Network Capacity to Enable Smoother Smart Applications The newly added U6GHz spectrum can be utilised synergistically with existing frequency bands. Through various combinations with current spectrums, it can achieve download speeds of 3Gbps. The increased availability of spectrum helps enhance data transmission capabilities, accommodating more simultaneous user connections, improving the internet experience in highly congested areas, and supporting high-definition video and large-capacity data transmission.
As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into production and daily life, the demand for data transmission from devices such as smart glasses and AI robots continues to rise. China Mobile Hong Kong will promote the synergistic development of U6GHz and intelligent computing services, enhance connectivity between terminals and intelligent computing platforms, and explore AI image analysis, immersive interactions, and industrial applications. This will allow smart services to better integrate into everyday life and corporate operations.
Aligning with Mainland China and Hong Kong Blueprints to Consolidate the Foundation of Digital-Intelligent Development China Mobile Hong Kong will actively align with the Nation's "15th Five-Year Plan" and Hong Kong's first Five-Year Plan. Focusing on "AI+", computing infrastructure, and new industrialisation, the company will enhance communication and smart services through network upgrades to assist Hong Kong in building an international innovation and technology centre. Concurrently, China Mobile Hong Kong will collaborate with industry partners to accelerate the research, development, and testing of U6GHz products. By expanding hotspot coverage according to demand, it aims to drive the maturity of the industrial ecosystem and accelerate Hong Kong's 6G development. Looking ahead, China Mobile Hong Kong will continue to leverage its strengths as a central state-owned enterprise, providing high-quality digital infrastructure to serve Hong Kong and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, thereby fully contributing to the building of a cyber superpower and a digital China.
About China Mobile Hong Kong Limited China Mobile Hong Kong Company Limited ("China Mobile Hong Kong") is the wholly-owned subsidiary of China Mobile Limited (HKEx: 941), which is listed on the Fortune Global 500. China Mobile Hong Kong was incepted in January 1997 and was the first mobile network operator to launch PCS services in Hong Kong.
As the world's leading mobile network brand with the largest customer base*, The Company offers innovative and comprehensive 5G communications services, including voice, data, IDD and international roaming. The Company is committed to the development of 5G with new technologies such as artificial intelligence, internet of things, cloud computing and big data, integrating 5G applications in different industries, promoting the construction and development of smart city groups in Greater Bay Area.
* China Mobile (Hong Kong) Limited is a wholly-owned subsidiary of China Mobile Limited. As of 31 December 2025, China Mobile Limited had the largest number of mobile network subscribers in the world.

articles.title_orig: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen
articles.title_zh: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, arguing in an executive order Friday that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.”
Trump had signed the legislation, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., just last month. The bill took aim at Russia’s largest buyers of oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India.
Passed with bipartisan support , the bill was intended to target Russia’s revenue streams as the country continues to wage its war against Ukraine. Suspending the sanctions provides Russia a financial lifeline.
Trump’s decision to put a hold on the sanctions package comes after he announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar.
Trump has expressed frustration with Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure and has blamed them for the increase in fuel costs while downplaying the impact of the Iran war on the oil market.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that lifting sanctions was “wrong” and “only helps the Russians.”
In a Telegram post, he decried what he called an “American sanctions blackout,” adding that a “weakening of pressure on the aggressor, effectively serving as a financial reward for Putin—only encourages him to continue his attacks.”
“It seems to me that this won’t stop Putin,” he later told journalists in WhatsApp messages. “On the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that there is such support.”
The decision to waive the Russia sanctions drew swift condemnation from critics in Congress.
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., who’s running for re-election in a competitive district, said on Fox News Saturday that he does not support Trump’s decision, calling Putin “a vile dictator and thug.”
“I fully understand the need to get oil and diesel prices down, and we want to do that, but not at the expense of putting money in the pocket of Vladimir Putin so that he can continue to wage this illegal war in Ukraine,” Lawler said.
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, who also faces a battle for re-election this November, said in his own Fox News interview that he does not agree with waiving the sanctions, though quickly shifted to acknowledge Trump’s support for Alaska energy.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., called the move a “craven, cowardly action” in a statement.
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said on Fox News Saturday that the decision “was a mistake,” adding that “the current path, unfortunately, just, it benefits Putin, and that’s not a good idea.”
“I think the president, understandably, is focused on diesel prices,” Cruz said. “That being said, people are hurting. People are feeling real pain. But there are other ways to address gas and diesel prices.”
“Beyond irresponsible,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring at the end of his term, wrote on X. “What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?”
“If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin,” he added.
Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a staunch Ukraine ally who is also not seeking re-election next month, said “the president is prolonging the war, not ending it,” in a post on X .
“Lindsey would be appalled,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-TX, who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year, wrote.
Zelenskyy thanked both Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, and praised the late Graham for his prolonged vocal support for Ukraine.
“He always supported us very strongly and pushed for as much assistance to Ukraine as possible. It’s difficult without him, I’ll say frankly,” Zelenskyy said. “And I am grateful to his friends who supported him.”
Trump’s move to pause the sanctions comes as the price of diesel fuel has shot up almost 70% since the war in Iran began in February and comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, as cost of living remains a top issue for voters.
Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who co-sponsored the bill named for her late brother, has touted its success as a key part of her campaign to win a full term in his Senate seat. Graham is a fierce Trump ally, as his endorsement was critical in her GOP primary win. Graham has yet to criticize the president for his Russian oil deal or the decision to halt the sanctions.
Congress passed the legislation with strong majorities in both the House and Senate, though many Democrats opposed the bill because it granted the president new tariff powers.
The legislation states that before the administration waives the new sanctions, it must submit an unclassified report to Congress explaining its basis. In his executive order, Trump said the White House has sent the report to Capitol Hill.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.
Brennan Leach is an associate producer for NBC News covering the Senate.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Albanian police fire rubber bullets as student protests rage
articles.title_zh: Albanian police fire rubber bullets as student protests rage
articles.content_orig:
Police in Albania have fired rubber bullets at antigovernment protesters in the capital, Tirana, as violent clashes intensify over demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The clashes continued on Saturday for a fifth consecutive day after high school and university students joined a broader movement against Rama, whose governing centre-left Socialist Party has held power since 2013.
The unrest has brought growing anger over education, unemployment and alleged corruption into a wider confrontation with the government.
Protesters threw stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at police near Rama’s office and elsewhere in central Tirana.
Some set cars and rubbish bins alight, creating burning barricades across streets.
Police responded with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges as demonstrators pushed against security lines.
The AFP news agency reported that officers used rubber bullets for the first time since the demonstrations began.
National police chief Skender Hita confirmed their use at a news conference on Saturday, saying they had been deployed “in a limited manner”.
The Ministry of Health and Social Welfare said nine protesters and four police officers received medical treatment on Saturday.
Hita said 167 people had been arrested over five days of unrest, while 132 officers had been injured.
Seven police officers were also suspended pending investigations into allegations that they had exceeded their authority.
Rama, who is serving his fourth term and has refused to resign, visited businesses damaged during the unrest on Saturday. He promised to listen to students and protect their right to demonstrate, while warning against further destruction.
He also accused his conservative political opponents of encouraging the violence.
The students have complained about expensive university fees, poor educational facilities and limited employment opportunities, alongside allegations of government corruption.
At the start of Saturday’s demonstration, protesters set fire to a suitcase and threw it into the Ministry of Education’s courtyard. AFP reported that the gesture symbolised their determination not to leave Albania in search of better opportunities.
“We are demanding our rights, our future and a better country,” journalism student Sinan Billa told AFP.
The student demonstrations have added to months of antigovernment rallies organised by the Flamingo movement, which began as a campaign against a luxury tourism development on Albania’s southern coast.
The project is linked to an investment company founded by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.
The movement has since widened its demands to include Rama’s resignation amid allegations of corruption against his government.
The unrest has also spread beyond Tirana. Local media reported that protesters in the coastal city of Durres damaged a post office and blocked roads with burning barricades, extending the confrontations beyond the capital.

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
articles.content_orig:
Lawyers for Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota have demanded the return of property seized in a federal raid of her Washington, DC home, accusing the US Department of Justice of conducting a politically motivated investigation and failing to follow judicial instructions during the search.
“The political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day,” Omar’s lawyers wrote in a letter sent to federal prosecutors on Friday and obtained by The Associated Press news agency. “This search was neither justified nor lawful.”
In the letter, Omar’s lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, challenged an investigation into her immigration history, saying there was “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”.
The letter accuses federal agents of threatening the separation of powers and failing to comply with a magistrate judge’s instructions for the search of Omar’s northeast Washington home on Monday.
Federal agents searched Omar’s home on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud. Authorities seized her phone and passport, and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to The Washington Post. Her lawyers also asked authorities to preserve audio and video recordings from the search.
Omar’s lawyers claim that investigators did not provide a copy of the warrant to them in advance, nor did they contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel, which disregarded the magistrate judge’s orders. The notice would have allowed Omar to seek legal counsel and potentially leverage legislation that could have challenged the warrant.
Her lawyers said the procedures outlined by the judge are intended to protect Omar’s constitutional rights as a sitting member of Congress, and safeguard against the seizure of materials related to her legislative work.
Her lawyers also argued that the investigation was politically motivated due to its proximity to the November midterm elections.
“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions,” they wrote.
The Justice Department rejected the accusations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said.
Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.
Omar’s lawyers have requested records relating to the 2019 inquiry into her immigration history. The former investigation found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing to warrant a full investigation, according to The Washington Post.
The scope of the current investigation remains unclear.
The search took place days after Trump attacked Omar at a rally in Tennessee, describing her home country as a place of “crime and squalor” and suggesting that Vice President JD Vance and others were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump denied any involvement, telling reporters the matter was “really up to the DOJ”.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine still unable to intercept Russian drones due to Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine still unable to intercept Russian drones due to Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump.
"Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored."
Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory.
"Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems."
"Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity."
Denys Sienik, the chargé d'affaires of Ukraine to the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or SpaceX regarding its inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."
Sienik said "based on the data currently available to us, we cannot confirm that these capabilities have been fully restored."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating"
Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.
Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters.
"President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News on Saturday in response to a question about lifting the sanctions. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."
Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire.
In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.
On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted : "Time for Zelensky to go."
Olivia  Gazis contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: See it: Hawaii's Kilauea volcano erupts for 55th time since 2024 after rare two-month pause
articles.title_zh: See it: Hawaii's Kilauea volcano erupts for 55th time since 2024 after rare two-month pause
articles.content_orig:
Hawaii’s Kilauea volcano began its 55th eruptive episode since Dec. 23, 2024, just after 3 a.m. local time Saturday, following an unusually long two-month pause.
HAWAII VOLCANOES NATIONAL PARK, Hawaii — Hawaii ’s Kilauea volcano began its 55th eruptive episode since Dec. 23, 2024, just after 3 a.m. local time Saturday, following an unusually long two-month pause.
NEARLY 100 EARTHQUAKES SHAKE KĪLAUEA AS VOLCANIC UNREST PROMPTS PARK CLOSURE
Kilauea's 55th eruptive episode
Kilauea has seen episodic eruptions since 2024. But after the previous episode ended Aug. 25, USGS scientists said changes in activity at the summit — including a series of earthquakes and a shallow magma intrusion beneath the Halemaʻumaʻu crater in late September and early October — made it impossible to predict exactly when the next episode would begin.
SCIENTISTS CAN NO LONGER PREDICT WHEN KILAUEA WILL ERUPT DUE TO RECENT VOLCANIC ACTIVITY
A magma intrusion occurs when magma moves into cracks beneath the Earth's surface, causing earthquakes and cracks in the ground.
Kilauea Message 2026-10-17 04:21:15 HST. The north vent fountain has grown to about 250 feet (80 m) high and is at least as wide. The fountain is feeding a broad sheet of lava into Halema'uma'u crater. Wind is from the northeast and tephra is within the closed area of HVNP.
USGS volcano observers said lava fountains have reached 250 feet in height.
"The fountain is feeding a broad sheet of lava into Halema'uma'u crater," the agency said on social media.
CENTURIES-OLD LAVA ROCK ARCH IN HAWAI'I VOLCANOES NATIONAL PARK COLLAPSES INTO OCEAN FOLLOWING HURRICANE NOLO
Volcanic gas that's released during eruptions can impact people downwind, particularly those with respiratory issues or other sensitive populations. Eruptions can also release Pele's hair, which are strands of volcanic glass, and can irritate skin, eyes and respiratory systems.
The Halema'uma'u Trail and parts of Byron Ledge Trail in the national park are temporarily closed due to increased seismic activity earlier this month.
Kilauea spews sheets of lava during 55th eruptive episode (USGS)
Image of Kilauea's 55th eruptive episode since Dec, 23, 2024. (USGS)
Another view of the new ground cracks in the north part of Kaluapele, Kīlauea summit caldera, cutting through the recent tephra deposits on the caldera floor. New cracks were up to about 6 inches (15 cm) wide. The active vents of the ongoing eruption are visible in the upper right portion of the photo. (USGS photo by M. Patrick.)
Some of the new cracks that formed on Kīlauea caldera floor between September 30-October 1 were steaming and warm (about 60 dg Celsius, or 140 dg Fahrenheit) when they were measured by this thermal camera on October 6. This area has been covered in warm, steaming cracks for decades, however, and there was no sign of magmatic gas associated with the recent intrusive activity. (USGS photo by M. Patrick)
Lava fountaining from Mount Kilauea Volcano. (Hawaii Volcanoes National Park's / Facebook)
54th eruption of Mount Kilauea Volcano. (Hawaii Volcanoes National Park's / Facebook)
Lava fountains from Kilauea volcano during 53rd eruptive episode. (Hawaii Volcanoes National Park)
Kilauea's 53rd eruptive episode on Aug. 12, 2026. (USGS)
Previously, the somewhat regular activity at Kiluea was being driven by magma accumulating in a shallow reservoir beneath the Halemaʻumaʻu crater. Each eruptive episode released some of that pressure under the crater, after which magma would refill the reservoir, leading to a relatively regular pattern.
The episodes were generally separated by pauses of two or more weeks.
4 CLASSIC TYPES OF VOLCANOES
Nighttime video of Kilauea's 47th eruption since Dec. 2024.
(USGS via Storyful / FOX Weather)
However, several swarms of shallow earthquakes and a magma intrusion shook Kilauea in September and earlier in October, opening new cracks in the caldera, which may have contributed to the longest pause between episodes.
Kilauea is considered one of the world's most active volcanoes.

A Bowdoin College student was removed from Thursday’s U.S. Senate debate after he stood and began yelling that data centers “are poisoning our waters.”
The moment came about 15 minutes into the fourth and final televised debate between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democrat Troy Jackson. It led to Collins quipping that it “was obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson replied, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” Thursday’s debate was the only one of the four to feature a live audience.
Henry Elgie, 19, was the protester whom security removed from the Gracie Theatre at Husson University in Bangor, according to a news release from the Sunrise Movement , a national progressive group focused on young people who are “fighting to stop the climate crisis and win a Green New Deal.”
“I’m so sorry to interrupt, but I’m a young person and I’m terrified. AI data centers are destroying our climate,” Elgie, who appeared to be wearing a press badge, shouted as security moved to take him out of the venue. “They are poisoning our waters. You are taking corporate PAC money to an absurd degree.”
Event organizers said the person was not on the pre-registered media list but presented a Bowdoin Orient press badge and was allowed in. In a statement Thursday night, the editor-in-chief of the Orient said the student paper did not send anyone to the debate and that the credential must have been fabricated.
A Sunrise Movement spokesperson said Friday that Elgie lives and is registered to vote in Brunswick, where Bowdoin is located.
The Sunrise Movement news release that came out late Thursday night made clear that Elgie was directing his words at Collins. It included a statement from Elgie that criticized Collins and her campaign for receiving donations from billionaires and executives of artificial intelligence platforms.
“Instead of investing in real climate solutions, Susan Collins continues to prioritize endless war and tax cuts for billionaires. My generation deserves a livable future,” Elgie said in a statement.
Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen responded Friday by sharing a photo the campaign took of pro-Jackson and pro-Collins supporters who were outside of the Oct. 8 debate hosted by WMTW. A person in the photo was holding a fake check in the amount of $150,000 made out to 1820 PAC, a reference to the ProPublica story on pay-to-play allegations surrounding Collins.
The Collins campaign said the person holding the check last week was Elgie.
The Jackson campaign did not respond to a request for comment Friday morning.
Jackson supported the proposed moratorium on large data centers in Maine that Gov. Janet Mills, an outgoing Democrat, vetoed earlier this year . Mills cited concerns that the proposed pause on new centers until November 2027 would have killed a project in the mill town of Jay. (That project went on hold this summer, despite the veto.)
Collins aligned herself with Mills earlier this year, expressing support in August for projects at former mill sites and saying “there is usually hydropower right there, so there’s an energy source built in.” But Collins has also called for federal guardrails on data center development, including regulations on how much water and energy they use.
President Donald Trump has called for more data center development, despite public polling in Maine and nationally showing a majority of Americans from both parties oppose data centers getting built in their communities.

articles.title_orig: MN Senate candidates spar in the only debate before Election Day
articles.title_zh: MN Senate candidates spar in the only debate before Election Day
articles.content_orig:
It’s rare for a U.S. Senate race that doesn’t include an incumbent to only feature one debate, but that’s the case in the race to replace outgoing U.S. Senator Tina Smith.
Republican Michele Tafoya and Democrat Peggy Flanagan debated in the Minnesota Public Radio studio at noon Friday, sparring over everything from President Donald Trump to the war in Iran to fraud.
Tafoya initially supported the war, but now says it’s time to bring it to a close. “Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” she said, “but this has been going on now for seven months and Minnesotans and Americans writ large are hurting. The prices are too high. This war does need to end and it needs to end quickly. It also needs to end strategically. I would like to see the president lay out an exit strategy for the American people to listen to.”
Flanagan criticized Tafoya for her initial support for the war. “This war is costing us financially, but also in lives,” she said. “Twenty-one service men and women have lost their life, including a Minnesotan.  A mother. That’s unacceptable. We need to hold this president accountable.”
The two candidates also debated the impact of the Big Beautiful Bill, especially the lack of access to Medicaid and SNAP benefits for thousands of Minnesota families.
“This Big Beautiful Bill under Donald Trump has been absolutely terrible in Minnesota and Michele Tafoya has cheered it on,” Flanagan said.
Tafoya responded by criticizing Flanagan for doing nothing to prevent fraud during nearly eight years as lieutenant governor.
“And she’s talking about access?” Tafoya said, responding to Flanagan. “All of that money left the State of Minnesota, this historic fraud happened under her watch and suddenly she’s looking out for Medicaid and SNAP? Sell it to someone else Peggy.”
Recent polls show this race is too-close-to call. Our latest KSTP/SurveyUSA poll out this week shows Flanagan leading by three points, 45% to 42%, but within the margin of error of +/-4.2%. A Minnesota Star Tribune/KARE 11 poll showed Flanagan up by four points.

Last week, gamers still holding any hope that the GPU market would somehow stabilize had their hopes dashed. A while after Nvidia reportedly put the RTX 50 Super series on hold , rumors started flying that production of the already-rare RTX 5090 was stopping , likely to use precious silicon manufacturing capacity for more AI accelerators. Now, the company's senior VP Jeff Fisher reportedly said that card was not discontinued and would continue to be shipped. The statement comes after a myriad of websites, including Tom's Hardware , have asked the company for official comment, but to no avail.
The information comes from Taiwanese websites including 4Gamers and SJTV , which both are quoting a purported post-event interview where Fisher offered a brief explanation of the situation. According to the VP, supplies of the GPU are limited, but Nvidia is seemingly going all out to get the product to market (paraphrased from the Taiwanese reports).
"The supply chain (capacity) is indeed somewhat constrained, but NVIDIA is doing everything it can to get the product on the market. Although there are other variants of the RTX 5090 (chip), production has not been discontinued, and NVIDIA will continue to ship, which is very important," Fisher reportedly said to 4Gamers .
He also reportedly reiterated a common quote from Nvidia execs, stating that without GeForce, Nvidia wouldn't be where it is today, and likewise, the AI market wouldn't exist as it does today.
The claim that the card isn't gone after all merits some spot-checking, so we did a cursory browse of the common retailers. At Amazon , RTX 5090s are selling for about $8,500, but from third-party sellers. Best Buy has a grand amount of naught cards on offer, while Newegg lists 5090s for about $7,300, but from what are likely Chinese sellers, judging by the shipping time. The ever-famous U.S. tariffs would likely add quite a chunk of change to that price tag, too. Finally and perhaps most poignantly, the card remains absent from Nvidia's own marketplace and Micro Center as of this writing.
Some would say that these statements are nothing but a means to keep the company in gamers' minds, even though gaming-related revenue is now a vanishingly small piece of Nvidia's ever-larger money pie .
Jensen's firm isn't the only one seemingly keeping up appearances, as Intel has repeatedly stated that its long-awaited refresh of consumer GPUs isn't dead , and last year AMD said it still intends to deliver "the best mainstream gaming GPUs on the market." Yet there are no new GPU launches from any of the three, and their quarterly launch figures keep doubling down on AI.

Neocloud stocks like CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) are poised to cap off a horrible week in their relatively short time in public markets.
CoreWeave and Nebius stocks are both down about 15% just in the past five days.
While concerns about CoreWeave's financial health are being blamed for the neocloud stock routs, the reality is that it's not just a CoreWeave issue. The overall financial health of the AI economic system build-out is being more closely scrutinized in a land of higher-for-longer interest rates.
Goldman Sachs explained the pressure quite well in a new note on Friday.
US dollar high-yield AI-related debt spreads widened by 25 basis points between Oct. 13 and 14, reaching a new high of 360 basis points over Treasurys. By contrast, non-AI-related debt spreads were only two basis points wider and remain below their March peak, Goldman Sachs pointed out (see charts below).
Within AI-related debt issuers, the widening has been concentrated in AI-related corporate bonds and data center project finance.
"While some softer AI-related sentiment can move datacenter bonds wider, especially if there is a reassessment around off-taker credit risk, we view AI-related corporate bonds, from either neoclouds or firms with significant frontier lab exposure, as being at the epicenter of the funding cost debate," Goldman Sachs strategist Amanda Lynam explained. "Further removed AI-adjacent Energy and Utilities have been more resilient, in our view partly reflecting more diversified revenue streams and a relatively defensive earnings profile. We think the widening reflects a reassessment of the economics of the AI buildout, particularly for lower-rated borrowers that are more exposed to higher-for-longer rates and potential energy-cost pressures."
Lynam sees "some near-term reversal" of the recent sell-off in US high-yield debt tied to AI. But she acknowledges that "dispersion across AI-related issuers is likely to remain high."

articles.title_orig: The Iran war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, top economist says
articles.title_zh: The Iran war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, top economist says
articles.content_orig:
More than seven months into the U.S. war with Iran, sharply higher fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive and fly and adding to the cost of some goods, prolonging the strain on American households as the midterm elections approach .
Motorists and airline passengers have borne the clearest consequences as the fighting disrupts Middle East oil shipments. Some companies have raised delivery charges or prices on selected products. Yet the higher cost of making and moving goods has not translated into across-the-board price increases at stores.
Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. Many companies have absorbed at least part of their higher production and transportation costs. A September jump in wholesale prices suggests some businesses may eventually charge more if fuel prices stay elevated.
The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, Mark Zandi, estimated this week that the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 in higher energy prices, $540 in higher interest rates and $360 in military costs. The energy portion is growing by $50 a week at current fuel prices, Zandi said.
Here’s a look at price changes since the war began and which goods and services could be most susceptible to increases in the months ahead:
BEFORE THE WAR: Regular gasoline averaged $2.98 a gallon nationwide and diesel $3.76 almost eight months ago, according to AAA. Gas peaked at $4.56 in May, below its 2022 record, while diesel reached a record $6.53 in September.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: On Friday, the national average stood at $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, or 45% above its prewar level , and was up 68% for diesel at $6.33, AAA reported. Gas typically costs less in the fall, and this is the first October a gallon of regular gas has cost more than $4 on average, it said.
Expensive diesel is less apparent to most U.S. residents but contributes to overall inflation by raising the cost of moving goods.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains dangerous and constrained, prolonging uncertainty over oil supplies and fuel prices. The Energy Information Administration said this month that it expected winter heating costs to be 21% higher for the roughly 3% of households that rely on heating oil, most of them in the Northeast, assuming the weather is mild.
BEFORE THE WAR: Jet fuel averaged $99 a barrel worldwide before the war, doubled to $209 in April and climbed back to nearly $195 in September after a spring decline, according to the International Air Transport Association.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: Airlines have raised ticket prices and fees , trimmed schedules and shelved plans to add flights. Airfares cost about 22% more in September than they did a year earlier, the consumer price index showed. Average domestic airfares rose from $405 in late 2025 to $445 in the April through June period of this year, excluding optional fees, according to the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Fuel price volatility makes it harder for airlines to plan and could discourage them from lowering fares even when fuel prices start to fall, analysts said. United Airlines pulled some December flights and warned of further possible cuts in 2027. Fewer available seats could mean less pressure to hold ticket prices down.
Higher fares have covered substantial portions of higher fuel costs for domestic airlines but not enough to prevent a squeeze on their third-quarter profits, according to consensus estimates.
BEFORE THE WAR: The U.S. Department of Agriculture initially expected grocery prices to rise 1.7% this year, below the historical annual average. USDA now expects a still comparatively modest 2.4% increase.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Individual food prices can be volatile , and it’s not clear how much of this year’s expected increase is due to the war and how much is due to other factors, including tariffs, unfavorable weather and higher labor costs.
Cornell University economics professor Chris Barrett said he was surprised grocery prices haven’t risen faster given higher costs for diesel, fertilizer and refrigeration. USDA revised its 2026 fertilizer cost estimates for major crops upward by 9% to 13% and fuel, lubricant and electricity estimates by 33% to 41%.
Barrett suspects retailers are absorbing some increases to avoid alienating fed-up customers after multiple years of food inflation . Grocery prices in September were about 22% higher than five years earlier.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Experts have warned that fresh produce and other frequently replenished perishables could respond quickly to higher transportation and refrigeration costs. Barrett sees “very little prospect” of a significant reduction in fuel prices that could ease the pressure on farmers and truckers.
A strengthening El Niño weather pattern could damage crops through drought, heat or flooding, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization warned. That could lift commodity prices, although ample inventories and good harvests elsewhere may limit the impact on groceries.
BEFORE THE WAR: Nearly all shoes sold in the U.S. are imported, and roughly 70% of the materials in a synthetic shoe are petrochemical-based, according to Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America. The industry trade group opposed Trump administration tariffs last year.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Footwear prices were 3.4% higher in September compared to 12 months earlier, according to the consumer price index. Men’s shoes went up the most, by 4.5%.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: While import costs are down from a year ago, the footwear trade group said oil prices, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty are likely to keep retail shoe prices rising into 2027.
“Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers,” FDRA President and CEO Matt Priest said.
BEFORE THE WAR: The cost of moving goods and delivering packages was already increasing and depended on more than fuel.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: It’s not clear. September producer-price data showed that transportation and warehousing of goods sold to businesses as inputs cost 10.2% more than a year earlier. Prices for truck and water freight services each rose 19.3%. The indexes measure what transportation providers charged but do not show how much of the increase appeared in retail prices.
Consumers have felt the higher costs most directly when sending packages. The U.S. Postal Service raised base prices 8% in April for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select, citing increased transportation costs. UPS, FedEx and DHL also impose fuel surcharges on many shipments.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping costs could remain elevated during the holiday season even if oil prices ease. Third-party provider AFS Logistics and financial services company TD Cowen project record parcel costs this quarter and the highest truckload rates since early 2022.
“We expect fuel to drive elevated transportation costs for the foreseeable future,” AFS Logistics CEO Andy Dyer said.
Although UPS and FedEx surcharges could decline if diesel and jet fuel prices fall, changes to carrier surcharge formulas, holiday fees and tight trucking capacity could keep total shipping bills elevated, AFS said.
