articles.title_orig: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
articles.title_zh: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
articles.content_orig:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is performing even better than scientists anticipated after engineers completed an extensive series of tests and precision adjustments. The work has brought the observatory's powerful instruments into exceptionally sharp focus, with its main camera system now delivering image quality nearly 30% better than predicted.
The achievement marks an important step toward the telescope's ambitious mission to investigate dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe. Even the smallest improvements in optical precision could help Roman capture clearer images during its sweeping surveys of the cosmos.
"All of Roman's sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument," said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "Many of the mission's primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn't be possible without it, so it's both exciting and a huge relief to see that it's working well!"
NASA Puts Roman's Powerful Camera System to the Test
Following the activation of the Wide Field Instrument in September, engineers began a comprehensive testing campaign to confirm that each component worked properly on its own and as part of the complete system.
Their first priority was examining the instrument's 18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note, along with the electronics that operate them. The team then evaluated the element wheel, a rotating mechanism equipped with filters and other optical components. These allow selected wavelengths of light to reach the detectors and can separate incoming light into its individual colors.
Next came the instrument's internal calibration system. Engineers activated its light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which function as adjustable light sources that can produce different colors and brightness levels under commands from Earth. By measuring how the detectors respond to these controlled signals, scientists can identify differences in sensitivity and make the corrections needed for accurate observations.
Engineers also tested the instrument's alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the sharpest images. They finished by checking the thermal control system, which maintains the temperatures required for the instrument's various components to function correctly.
"Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."
A Space Telescope Already Close to Perfect Alignment
While one group concentrated on preparing the Wide Field Instrument, another worked to refine the telescope's overall optical alignment.
The results were encouraging from the beginning. Roman's mirrors and other optical components were already positioned with remarkable accuracy, meaning engineers needed to make only minor corrections.
"The telescope's performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch," said Matthew Bolcar, Roman's optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. "All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment."
Achieving that level of precision is especially challenging for a spacecraft. The forces experienced during launch can cause tiny shifts in sensitive equipment, and conditions in orbit differ significantly from those on Earth. Roman launched on August 30, carrying optical systems that had been meticulously tested before leaving the ground.
"Our ground testing couldn't exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity," Bolcar said. "And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted."
A Mirror Adjustment Smaller Than a Human Hair
Roman relies on an intricate arrangement of mirrors and optical components to collect light from distant cosmic objects and direct it toward its two scientific instruments. For the resulting images to remain sharp, the light must follow an extremely precise path.
Even a microscopic misalignment can affect how accurately the telescope brings light into focus.
Fortunately, Roman's optical system was already so well aligned that only incredibly small movements were necessary to improve its performance.
"We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair," said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. "This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the Empire State Building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower."
Although nearly impossible to appreciate at a human scale, such a small adjustment can make an important difference when a telescope is designed to study objects across vast cosmic distances.
The team initially concentrated on Roman's Coronagraph Instrument, which had been producing images that were slightly out of focus. The problem was less severe than engineers had anticipated, making it relatively straightforward to correct.
The coronagraph now meets the team's demanding performance expectations. Engineers will continue refining its camera settings and determining the optimal configurations for its deformable mirrors, which can change shape to make extremely precise corrections to incoming light.
In the coming weeks, the team plans to test the coronagraph's ability to block unwanted light, an essential capability for observing faint objects near much brighter ones.
Once the coronagraph's focus had been optimized, engineers returned to the Wide Field Instrument for another round of adjustments.
Roman's Image Quality Exceeds Expectations by Nearly 30%
The final measurements revealed an especially impressive result. Roman's Wide Field Instrument achieved optical performance nearly 30% better than the team had predicted.
Before launch, engineers established an image quality requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square). This measurement describes the amount of optical error in the system, or how far the incoming light deviates from an ideal, perfectly focused wavefront.
To put that scale into perspective, 90 nanometers is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a human hair. At these tiny dimensions, even seemingly insignificant imperfections can influence the sharpness of astronomical images.
After the latest corrections, however, engineers measured an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS, substantially better than the original requirement.
That improvement means Roman should be capable of producing even sharper images than its designers initially expected, strengthening its ability to carry out detailed observations across enormous regions of the sky.
"All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Jurling said. "It's a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing."
With both scientific instruments meeting or surpassing their expected performance, Roman has cleared another important milestone in its preparation for routine observations. The results highlight the extraordinary precision of the telescope's design and offer a promising outlook for its upcoming investigations into the hidden structure a

Verizon will offer Apple's new iPhone Handoff feature for iOS 27, but it will cost you $10 a month. The carrier says the feature is "coming soon" to its network in its announcement , where it also revealed that it was offering the iPhone Duo . If you'll recall, the feature launched on T-Mobile in the US, which charges $5 a month for it, and Deutsche Telekom in Germany. iPhone Handoff lets you use the same eSIM number on two devices, as long as they're both running iOS 27 and share the same Apple ID.
The phones can't use the same number at the same time, though — you'll have to choose which one is actively using the shared number at any given time. You will, however, be able to switch primary devices anytime you want. Your calls, messages and Find My automatically move to the iPhone you're currently using, and your iCloud backups are synced across devices.
To set up iPhone Handoff, go to Settings > Cellular > Set up Cellular or Add eSIM on your newer phone. Select iPhone > Continue > Transfer . To switch between your two iPhones, just unlock the device you want to start using. You don't have to do anything else: You'll just see a message that says "Switched to this iPhone" at the top of the screen of the iPhone. Apple advises making sure your iPhones have passcodes to remain in control of which one is actively using your number.

articles.title_orig: Cardinal Bernardin: An example for the Church and the world
articles.title_zh: Cardinal Bernardin: An example for the Church and the world
articles.content_orig:
We are publishing the full text of the Lecture delivered Friday evening, 16 October 2026, by Cardinal Blase Joseph Cupich, Archbishop of Chicago, as part of the initiatives carried out at Fiera di Primiero, in Trento, in memory of Cardinal Joseph Louis Bernardin thirty years after his death.
Cardinal Bernardin, born in the U.S. state of South Carolina to parents of Trentino origin who had immigrated to the USA, led the archdiocese of Chicago from 1982 until 1996, the year of his death.
The Italian towns of Rovereto and Trento are also taking part in the initiatives, which were promoted by the archdiocese of Trento. The three-day event concludes Saturday evening with the celebration of a Mass presided over by Cardinal Cupich in the cathedral of the Trentino capital.
I, who come from the city that Cardinal Bernardin called home, feel honoured to be here at Fiera di Primiero, where the Cardinal equally felt at home, thanks to your welcome and your esteem. Tonight, I would like to reflect briefly with you on how Joseph Bernardin took the best of what he learned from Trentino's rich culture and matured into a world-class figure whose impact on the Church and the world has not yet faded.
The historic speech he delivered at Fordham University in 1983, with which he introduced his famous âconsistent ethic of lifeâ approach to the examination of crucial issues of the contemporary world, as well as the leadership role he played in the drafting of the pastoral letter on peace written by the American bishops, offer insights into appreciating this impact.
There were three truly revolutionary beliefs that guided him. He was first of all convinced that it was necessary to follow up on the invitation of the Second Vatican Council to read the signs of the times. The Cardinal understood that the Church can only be credible if fully engaged in the world and attentive to what happens in peopleâs real lives, as well as to the forces that influence politics and public opinion. In many ways, he anticipated the famous phrase of the late Pope Francis: âReality is superior to the idea.â
His reading of the signs of our times led him to the conclusion that it was useless to address issues such as abortion, capital punishment, nuclear proliferation, use of military force, or anything else separately. He realized that this approach was motivated in large part by the fact that such issues were already divisive in themselves. But he was also convinced that an all-encompassing commitment to respect for life as a true principle connecting these issues would benefit them all. In his words: âThe purpose of proposing a consistent ethic of life is to argue that success on any one of the issues threatening life requires a concern for the broader attitude in society about respect for human life.â¦ The viability of the principle depends upon the consistency of its application.â
Second, the cardinal was convinced that the comprehensiveness of the Church's social doctrine made it distinctly capable of guiding the definition of such issues in the public arena. As a case in point, he asked how it was possible that only Catholic bishops strongly opposed both abortion and the nuclear war policies of the United States. It was the completeness of the doctrine, that is, its consistency, that distinguished the Church. Consequently, the social doctrine of the Church could not be confined to one of the political categories that characterize American public life. Yet this is precisely why the consistent ethic of life has attracted criticism. It affirms that the doctrine of the Church cannot be shaped according to our political divisions nor should it be diminished by minimizing the importance of its fundamental social teachings, even to approximate important political objectives. Along the same lines, Pope Leo recently observed that one cannot define oneself as a defender of Life if one opposes abortion but at the same time is in favour of the death penalty or does not oppose the inhuman treatment meted out to immigrants.
Finally, the Cardinal was convinced that the Church can count on a unique position to incentivize the promotion of the common good, through a redefinition of public policies. The way we cultivate faith, pastoral life, the ministries of health care and education: all demonstrate the completeness of the social doctrine of the Church. So much so that Cardinal Bernardin readily admitted that he chose a Catholic university to introduce his approach of coherent ethics of life, as he appreciated the particular role that Catholic universities have in shaping public debate.
The moral framework of a âconsistent ethic of lifeâ championed by the Cardinal is essential today, at a time when deep social divisions set people against one another in extreme ways. His sound counsel invites us to reflect on the risks of living in âbubblesââsurrounded by people like ourselves, yet fearful of engaging in genuine dialogue on a range of critical issues. Many of these are, in fact, matters of life and death: the healthcare crisis exposed during the pandemic; the scourge of racial injustice, which diminishes the dignity of immigrants; and the threat that climate changeâbecoming more evident with each passing yearâposes to all life on Earth.
The theological and moral legacy of Cardinal Joseph Bernardin remains one of the most influential currents of thought within the modern social doctrine of the American Church. As Archbishop of Chicago, Bernardin articulated a vision that wove various moral imperativesâfrom nuclear disarmament to the protection of the unbornâinto a cohesive whole. His legacy is fundamentally linked to two landmark moments: his leadership in drafting the pastoral letter on peace (âThe Challenge of Peace: Godâs Promise and Our Responseâ, 1983) and his lecture at Fordham University, where he introduced the âconsistent ethic of lifeâ.
Although he faced detractorsâeven among his fellow bishopsâhis insights were remarkably prescient, mirroring the holistic moral vision later developed by John Paul II in Evangelium vitae . It is no exaggeration to say that in Evangelium vitae , Pope John Paul II affirmed Bernardinâs broader synthesis, explicitly placing direct attacks on innocent human lifeâsuch as abortion or euthanasiaâon the same level as wider, structural threats to human life, including war, poverty, and ecological degradation. In doing so, he reinforced the principle that a true culture of life must take into account every threat to human dignity.
In more recent times, Bernardinâs words have gained new life and strength through the teachings of both Pope Francis and Pope Leo; both have championed a culture of encounter, mutual listening, and discernment, aimed at a shared path forward. We are the privileged heirs to the gentle and wise spirit that animated Cardinal Bernardin. As a successor to that good cardinal, I am truly delighted to be with you to celebrate his memory and his historical legacy. His words and his example continue to inspire us in our work for peace, the education and formation of young people, the promotion of understanding and collaboration among Christians and non-Christians alike, and, of course, the respect for life in all its precious forms.
I pray that the prophetic voice and the legacy of our beloved Cardinal Bernardinâwhich remain as relevant as everâwill continue to inspire us all toward an even deeper mutual solidarity, as members of the same family of God. We need this now more than ever.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says Russia's claimed territorial advances are 'an illusion'
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says Russia's claimed territorial advances are 'an illusion'
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's General Staff has refuted claims by Valery Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, that Russian forces have captured 92 settlements since early September, including Kostiantynivka and Dobropillia, and advanced to within 5 kilometres of the outskirts of Zaporizhzhia.
Source: Andrii Kovaliov, spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Quote: "Due to the lack of significant battlefield successes, the Russian military leadership continues to create an illusion of major victories for its own political leadership and domestic audience. The latest example is a briefing by Valery Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, based on blatant lies, manipulation and exaggeration.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has evidence that refutes the Russian command's false claims about the situation along the contact line."
Details: Kovaliov recalled that in his briefing, Gerasimov claimed that since 1 September, Russian forces had captured more than 1,800 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements.
The spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this was untrue. "In fact, thanks to active operations by Ukraine's Defence Forces, more territory has been liberated since the beginning of autumn than the enemy has managed to capture," he said.
Kovaliov also stressed that Gerasimov's claims about the capture of Dobropillia were equally false, adding that the city remains under Ukrainian control.
"This is not the first time the Russian leadership has presented wishful thinking as reality. On 1 September, Putin claimed that Sviatohirsk had been captured when, in fact, it was and remains under the control of Ukraine's defence forces," he recalled.
In addition, the General Staff described claims that Russian forces had captured Kostiantynivka and Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka and reached the outskirts of Kramatorsk as false.
"As of the morning of 17 October, Ukraine's defence forces still have positions in Kostiantynivka, where fighting is ongoing. Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka has also not been captured by the enemy, and claims that Russian forces have reached Kramatorsk do not reflect the actual situation on the battlefield," Kovaliov said.
The spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said claims that Russian forces were advancing in the outskirts of Sloviansk and controlled more than 50% of Mykolaivka were also untrue.
"In fact, a small enemy group infiltrated the southern outskirts of Mykolaivka. Ukraine's defence forces are conducting strike-and-search operations to eliminate it," he clarified.
Kovaliov also commented on Gerasimov's claims about fighting for Orikhiv and the capture of Novopavlivka and Novoandriivka.
"In fact, as of 17 October, all three settlements remain under the control of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," he said.
According to the spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the claim that Russian forces had advanced to within 5 kilometres of the southern outskirts of Zaporizhzhia is also false. The contact line has remained 22 kilometres from the regional capital for a considerable time.
"Another fabrication is the claim that Velykomykhailivka in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast has been captured. Russian forces have repeatedly claimed to have captured this settlement, attempting to present wishful thinking as reality. As of 17 October, Velykomykhailivka remains under Ukrainian control, and the contact line is 8 kilometres east of the settlement," Kovaliov said.

articles.title_orig: La Via Campesina takes to streets against World Bank-IMF in Bangkok, Thailand
articles.title_zh: La Via Campesina takes to streets against World Bank-IMF in Bangkok, Thailand
articles.content_orig:
Bagnolet, 17 October 2026 | Press release
For The Food Sovereignty for our Peoples, Against the World Bank and IMF policies! Our Future, Not the World Bank’s Choice!
Bangkok: On 16 October 2026, hundreds of La Via Campesina members, our member organisation in Thailand, the Assembly of the Poor (AOP), and allied organisations took to the streets of Bangkok to denounce the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) during their Annual Meetings in Thailand.
Their message was clear: peasants are fed up with the World Bank and IMF and their destructive policies. Chanting, “Down, down, World Bank! Down, down, IMF! Let’s Feed the People, not the Bank!” , protesters denounced decades of policies that have harmed communities, undermined livelihoods and threatened their future.
The AOP peasants and fisherfolk sang a powerful song that exposed the state violence and repression that many peasants face whenever they rise up to demand that their voices be heard. “We love one another so we are determined to destroy and annihilate. We love one another so we claim our father with such recklessness. We love one another so we burn our homes we burn our country. We love one another so we are led astray by wicked leaders.” The song’s bitter irony laid bare the contradiction between political leaders’ rhetoric of unity and love and the violence, destruction and suffering their actions bring upon the people.
“ Our struggles are connected. They are about the self-determination of peoples everywhere. The World Bank and the IMF have failed to support this right. We demand an end to imperialism and to economic policies that harm people rather than meeting their needs,” Hakech Mohamed from Morocco.
The placards told the story of how investment projects promoted by these Bretton Woods institutions affect people’s everyday lives. The peasants demanded: “Community Forests Are Life, Not Corporate Carbon Markets,” “Stop Blue Carbon Greenwashing,” “Stop Data Centres,” “The Future We Didn’t Choose! Our Future, Not the World Bank’s Choice,” “High-Spending Tourism Means Expanding Poverty,” and “Stop Land Grabs!”
For decades, large-scale infrastructure investments and economic reforms mainly in the low-income and lower-middle-income countries of the Africa, Asia and Latin America backed by the World Bank and IMF have contributed to the disruption of peasant livelihoods and the dispossession of communities.
Anuka from Sri Lanka, echoed similar calls to resist corporate takeover of our countries.
“ We are not here to negotiate. We demand our government to listen to us, the people. Mandates come from us, the people and not the World Bank. Cancel the debt! We don’t want to pay the debt!
“ We’ve come here to deliver our solidarity statement because people around the world are dying of hunger, and this hunger is linked to the debt crisis. Our governments are unable to take care of their people. At the same time, power is being taken away from food producers and transferred to multinational corporations that produce food, but that food doesn’t necessarily reach the people who need it .” Said Themba Chauke from South Africa
Peasants did not simply denounce the World Bank and IMF; they asserted their right to determine their own development, their future, and their relationship with their land and territories. Their demands included “Our Land, Our Voice, Our Future,” “Free Seeds, UNDROP Now,” “Peasant Agroecology Is the Solution,” and “Farmers’ Welfare: Restore Fair Crop Price Support.”
“Today is a day of resistance. For us, the Indigenous peoples and peasants, women and men from Latin America, we say no to debt and no to the Bank. The World Bank’s politics are politics of debt, poverty and the destruction of our peoples and territories. We have a proposal for life. We want to build a social contract in which peoples’ sovereignty and food sovereignty are prioritised,” said Maria Macz from Guatemala.
On this day, La Via Campesina marked the International Day of Action for Peoples’ Food Sovereignty and Against Transnational Corporations , denouncing the neoliberal policies of the World Bank and IMF and demanding an alternative grounded in food sovereignty and financial sovereignty.

articles.title_orig: A 26-year-old felt her concerns were being dismissed. Then she was diagnosed with breast cancer.
articles.title_zh: A 26-year-old felt her concerns were being dismissed. Then she was diagnosed with breast cancer.
articles.content_orig:
Andrea de Armas knew the ultrasound technician thought she was overreacting.
De Armas was 26. She had no known family history of breast cancer . But she had found a lump in her breast. Before beginning a rigorous program to train as a physician assistant, she wanted to get it checked out.
Being that young in a waiting room filled with older patients getting routine scans was already unsettling, she said. Then the technician seemed to dismiss her concerns.
"The tech had 'Why are you here?' vibes. Without her explicitly saying that, that's exactly what she told me. I felt belittled and just weird," De Armas recalled. "I was like, 'I have a mass, I feel something on my chest or breast.' And they were like, 'Oh, really?' ... It was just really uncomfortable the entire visit."
After the scan, a radiologist reviewed it and recommended that De Armas get a biopsy immediately. It was a sharp turn from the technician's skepticism, De Armas said, adding that she "had a lot of emotions and felt so conflicted" about the experience.
De Armas made an appointment at Baptist Health's Herbert Wertheim Cancer Institute, which did another scan and biopsy. Four days later, the day before her physician assistant program was set to begin, she learned the lump was malignant. She had breast cancer .
"Words can't describe it. It's just sensory. I was in a paused state, where I was just listening," De Armas said. "Then the words went through my head, and I felt like I was in go mode. Like, I need to do something about this, because tomorrow, I start PA school. So we need to do something about this."
About one in 10 new breast cancer diagnoses are in women under 45, according to the American Cancer Society's website , though only about one in 1,344 women are diagnosed in their 20s. Breast cancer incidence rates have also increased by about 1% per year, and there are slightly more new cases being diagnosed in women under 50 than women above 50, the ACS says.
Young women tend to be diagnosed with breast cancer at a later stage and tend to have "more aggressive" tumors or be diagnosed with rarer disease subtypes , said Dr. Mary Gemignani, the director of the Women's Early Onset Cancer Program and chief of the Division of Breast Surgery at NYU Langone.
Despite those statistics, some young women still face dismissal, Gemignani said.
"I've seen many women over the years who will give the story that they were told they were too young to have breast cancer," said Gemignani, who has been seeing patients for over 25 years, in a 2025 interview with CBS News. Gemignani was not involved in De Armas' care.
Further testing found De Armas had a genetic mutation associated with increased breast cancer risk. Learning that helped De Armas feel in control as she began treatment.
"It was a bit of relief, in the sense of understanding where this could have come from, and that there were things out of my control," De Armas said. "It's also pretty empowering for my family. People can get the screenings they need and get ahead."
De Armas was determined not to let the diagnosis disrupt her life. She had a lumpectomy in early June, a month after her diagnosis, during a break in her school schedule. To balance her program and chemotherapy, she went for treatment at 6:50 a.m., then spent the afternoon in class. She scheduled a bilateral mastectomy and reconstruction during winter break.
Gemignani said it's not unusual for young women to have "unique needs" when it comes to cancer treatment, since they may be juggling school, work or family obligations with less support or resources than older generations.
Dr. Cristina Lopez-Penalver, a surgical oncologist at Baptist Health's Herbert Wertheim Cancer Institute who treated De Armas, said the unusual treatment schedule allowed her to stay on track at school while maintaining her health.
"We worked together as a team," Lopez-Penalver said. "She was really not about ready to let this breast cancer get in her way."
De Armas graduated as a physician assistant in 2025. One month later, she was working in the field. In September, she celebrated her first anniversary at that job.
Now 30, De Armas says she is cancer-free. The days of surgery and chemotherapy are behind her. But because of the makeup of her cancer, she remains on hormone therapy. The medication put her into temporary menopause, which Gemignani said is another unique concern for young breast cancer patients . She also had to make fertility decisions earlier than she expected. She continues to see her oncologist for regular follow-ups.
"I'm really lucky. I feel like I'm doing OK," De Armas said. "It took me a little bit to kind of adjust. It wasn't immediate; it took time. It took understanding the kind of changes my body was going through. But I'm able to live a pretty normal life for a 30-year-old."
De Armas said she hopes sharing her story will inspire others to trust themselves and push for answers when something feels wrong. Being nervous about a scan or medical intervention is "a valid experience," she said, but someone should "never let the fear of the unknown freak you out."
"It's always in your hands, and you just need to just take the step together with community and people around you," De Armas said. "Just do what's in your best interest, always. We're all human beings. The things we're genetically predisposed to are out of our control. So to feel empowered, do the things that we know are in our control. It's a cliché that knowledge is power, but it is so true."
Edited by Lucia I Suarez Sang

articles.title_orig: CDC to send ‘disease detective’ to help tackle Pennsylvania measles outbreak
articles.title_zh: CDC to send ‘disease detective’ to help tackle Pennsylvania measles outbreak
articles.content_orig:
State has confirmed six measles-related deaths and county at center of outbreak lacks its own health department
The county at the center of Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is at a clear disadvantage because, local officials say, it lacks its own health department and it will now get special assistance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
As of Wednesday, Pennsylvania had confirmed 1,222 measles cases, up from 86 the week before. Six measles-associated deaths have also been confirmed by the state.
The CDC announced on Thursday it would send a scientist – specifically, a “disease detective” – from the agency’s epidemic intelligence service to help tackle Pennsylvania’s growing outbreak.
“CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” a CDC spokesperson told NBC News on Thursday.
The spokesperson also added that the CDC director, Dr Erica Schwartz, recommends the MMR vaccine “as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection”.
The network also reported that in addition to the deployment of the “disease detective,” the CDC was releasing nearly $4m to aid the measles response efforts in Pennsylvania.
Lancaster county, the focus of the state’s outbreak with more than 415 confirmed cases as of 9 October, is the largest county in the state to not have its own health department. The plain community, or Amish, who have historically had lower rates of vaccination, make up about 8% of the county’s population.
The Guardian reported earlier this month that the state was bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials sharing concern that it was “only a matter of time” until the disease spread beyond the outbreak’s center.
The outbreak also comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by growing vaccine skepticism, particularly because of the influence of the controversial health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr . Kennedy has also notably had a public dispute with the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, who has lambasted the administration and Kennedy for spreading vaccine misinformation.
“I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said in August during a briefing to report two measles deaths in his state, their first in three decades.
He continued: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation. There’s real-life consequences to scaring people.”
Alice Yoder, who was elected to the Lancaster county board of commissioners in 2023 and previously worked as a critical care nurse, told the Guardian that county officials were “very concerned” about the outbreak and that, without its own health department, the county was at a clear disadvantage.
“It’s a lot for our state to handle from a communication standpoint,” Yoder said. “They’re perhaps doing the best that they can, knowing that Pennsylvania has 67 counties, with 60 being under the auspices of the centralized state system rather than having their own health departments.”
She added: “By having a local health department, particularly one of our size, I believe it would mean we would have local data, it would be in real time, and we would have that information quickly. And most importantly, we would have an established staff, which has established relationships with a variety of partners within our community, which means that once we find a sign of an outbreak we would be able to respond to it really quickly.”
Yoder, who is now advocating for the county to establish its own health department, added that because the county doesn’t have one, she and her colleagues find out about measles cases and deaths only through media announcements at the same time as the general public.
“I never thought I would see measles again in my lifetime, but once it occurred I thought that we probably should have been prepared for it,” she said.
An advantage for counties in Pennsylvania that do have their own health departments, such as Montgomery, is their ability to work with local community health initiatives, like coalitions aimed at promoting immunity.
Susan Wenrick, vice-chair of the Montgomery County Immunization Coalition, which is made up of members of county government, healthcare professionals and other community members, said one of the coalition’s main goals was to improve access to vaccines.
“The biggest challenges to vaccinating people in Montgomery county have been access and availability, but one positive thing that came out of the pandemic was the public-private partnerships that were created to bring vaccines to communities, along with addressing the uninsured and underinsured barrier,” Wenrick said.
She added: “These are challenging times due to the amount of misinformation that is available, along with the average person turning to Google or social media for their health information instead of consulting their healthcare professional. A big part of MCIC’s efforts is to provide trusted resources for all.”
As of Friday, the CDC reported 4,410 measles cases nationwide, marking an ​increase of 330 from its update last week. As noted by Reuters , ​the CDC “shifted to using mortality data from ​the National Center for Health Statistics for measles-related deaths, rather than ‌relying ⁠on state health departments, a change that has drawn scrutiny”.

articles.title_orig: Ranked: The World’s Most and Least Free Countries
articles.title_zh: Ranked: The World’s Most and Least Free Countries
articles.content_orig:
Political freedom has been declining globally for more than a decade, raising questions about the strength of democratic institutions and individual rights, even in advanced economies.
This visualization ranks 171 countries using the Atlantic Council’s 2026 Freedom Index , which measures the freedom to participate in politics, own property, and live under fair and predictable laws. Scores reflect conditions in 2025.
Luxembourg (91.8) and Sweden (91.5) follow Denmark at the top of the index. Just 3.6 points separate the world’s 10 freest countries, highlighting how closely clustered the leading nations are.
Several Asian economies have also moved up the rankings. South Korea climbed from 33rd to 25th, recovering some of the ground lost during its recent political crisis. Japan advanced from 18th to 14th.
Freedom also carries economic implications. According to Atlantic Council research, countries undergoing democratization see GDP per capita rise by 8.8% over 20 years, on average, relative to autocratic peers.
Afghanistan ranks last with a score of 19.0, followed by Turkmenistan (24.3). Many of the lowest-ranked countries face longstanding authoritarian rule , conflict, or fragile institutions.
China ranks 147th globally, alongside Guinea and DR Congo, despite having the world’s second-largest economy . Its freedom score fell from 42.9 in 2024 to 41.7 in 2025, highlighting the contrast between its economic influence and restrictions on individual freedoms.
Russia ranks 154th, with its freedom score falling from 47.3 in 2019 to 39.2 in 2025. The 8.1-point decline reflects growing restrictions on political opposition, independent media, and public dissent, particularly since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The United States has a freedom score of 79.9, ranking behind Canada (19th), the UK (20th), and Japan (14th). Its decline from 22nd to 37th represents one of the largest annual drops in the index.
Other measures point to a longer-term trend. In 2025, America’s democracy score fell to its lowest level since 1965.
The U.S. decline illustrates how even established democracies can experience setbacks in political rights and institutional safeguards.

Explore who receives weapons from the world’s biggest arms exporters, from U.S. shipments to Saudi Arabia to military aid for Ukraine.
The world’s biggest weapons exporters supply countries across the globe, but their largest recipients reveal some of the most important relationships in international security.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) , international transfers of major weapons increased 9.2% between 2016–2020 and 2021–2025.
The following table ranks the world’s leading arms exporters and identifies their biggest recipients, using SIPRI’s 2021–2025 transfer-volume data.
The figures highlight how arms trade relationships reflect geopolitical alliances and regional security priorities. Some countries supply weapons to a broad network of partners, while others depend heavily on a handful of recipients.
The data reveals two distinct patterns. Major exporters such as the United States supply weapons to a wide range of countries, while others have more concentrated relationships, with a single recipient accounting for a majority of their exports.
These differences can reflect longstanding defense partnerships, regional security concerns, or the immediate demands of ongoing conflicts.
Saudi Arabia was the world’s third-largest arms importer in 2021–2025, obtaining 77% of its imported major weapons from the United States.
The relationship spans decades of security cooperation. American-made aircraft, air-defense systems, and other advanced equipment play a central role in Saudi Arabia’s military capabilities, particularly as the country seeks to deter regional threats and protect critical infrastructure.
These purchases also sustain commercial relationships with American defense manufacturers, part of a broader global industry that includes some of the world’s largest arms companies .
Not every international weapons transfer represents a commercial purchase. Some weapons are provided as military assistance, particularly during active conflicts.
Ukraine was the world’s largest recipient of major arms in 2021–2025, following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Transfers from countries including the United States, Germany, and Poland reflect the scale of international military support.
Weapons can also serve different purposes. Some replenish equipment consumed in active conflicts, while others modernize militaries, strengthen deterrence, or build reserves against future threats.
This distinction matters when interpreting the rankings. SIPRI measures the volume of major weapons transferred, rather than their financial value or whether they were ultimately deployed.
Explore how China’s nuclear weapons arsenal climbed 71% since 2020 , highlighting another dimension of the changing global military balance.
The U.S. and Iran supplied 86% of military drones exported in 2022–2025, mostly to opposite sides of the Ukraine war, while Türkiye had the most customers.
Military drones have moved from the margins of warfare to the front line, yet only a handful of countries export them at scale.
The U.S. and Iran dominate the trade, with most of their exports supplying opposite sides of the war in Ukraine.
This graphic ranks the 14 countries that exported military drones over 2022-2025, using data from the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database .
SIPRI counts drone aircraft weighing at least 150 kg, plus one-way attack drones and loitering munitions, which are built to strike once and be destroyed. The figures include drones sent as aid or built in the buyer’s country under license, but largely exclude small FPV and commercial drones.
The U.S. exported 7,593 military drones and Iran 6,800, each more than six times as many as third-ranked Germany (1,000). Nearly all went to a single war: 95% of U.S. drones went to Ukraine, while 99% of Iran’s went to Russia.
The table below shows how many military drones each country exported from 2022 to 2025, along with its share of the global total:
Almost all of these drones were built for a single use. One-way attack drones and loitering munitions make up 97% of the global total, which helps explain how a few wartime transfers can add up to thousands of units. Every drone the U.S. sent to Ukraine during this period was of this type.
Nearly all of Iran’s exports were Shahed-136 drones that Russia also assembled and produced under license, which SIPRI still counts as Iranian exports. Iran built up its drone industry in response to a UN arms embargo that tightened over time before expiring in 2020.
Below the top two, exports drop off quickly. Only Germany (1,000) and Poland (690) delivered more than 500 drones, while the bottom seven exporters, from Czechia to Sweden, delivered 89 combined.
Drone export patterns for the two largest suppliers shifted sharply in 2025. U.S. exports climbed from 1,010 in 2022 to 3,219 in 2024, then fell to 402 in 2025, the same year new U.S. military aid to Ukraine came to a halt .
Iran, meanwhile, continued delivering about 2,000 drones a year from 2023 through 2025, making it the largest exporter in 2025 by a wide margin.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV calls world hunger a ‘terrible offense’ against human dignity
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV calls world hunger a ‘terrible offense’ against human dignity
articles.content_orig:
The pontiff, still hospitalized after surgery, sent a message for World Food Day on Friday.
Pope Leo XIV on Friday called world hunger a “terrible offense” against human dignity and emphasized that adequate food is a basic human right.
“It is a terrible offense against human dignity to prevent bread from reaching any person or to destroy the means by which it is produced,” the pontiff wrote in a message published for World Food Day.
Still recovering from surgery at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, Leo addressed his message to Qu Dongyu, director general of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). World Food Day, celebrated every year on Oct. 16 to highlight world hunger, also marks the organization’s founding in 1945.
In his message, Leo lamented the challenge of world hunger and questioned how some can speak of technological innovation while food shortages persist.
“Hunger cannot be considered a statistical anomaly, for it is caused mainly by a lack of political will and collective charity,” Leo said.
“Today, people speak of innovation with great confidence,” Leo said. “However, this term is often used only in reference to the development of devices and algorithms, or the optimization of performance merely for the sake of financial gain.”
According to FAO’s annual report for 2025, an estimated 645 million people worldwide experienced hunger, mainly distributed across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. According to the same report, 35.5 million children were severely malnourished, and war remained the “primary driver of acute food insecurity and malnutrition.”
Leo also said that food shortages should never be “used as a weapon of war” and encouraged the United Nations to work toward a “new global food order” in which technology ensures food for all.
“Regular access to safe, adequate and sufficient food, in keeping with the dignity of every person, is a basic human right,” the pope wrote.
“A new global food order is essential — one in which technological innovation is unconditionally subordinated to respect for God-given human dignity and the universal common good.”
The pope’s remarks on world hunger follow his June visit to the headquarters of the World Food Programme in Rome, where he emphasized the need to focus on humanity to combat hunger worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Chicago 'No Kings' protest locations near me: Rallies against Donald Trump, ICE, happening in Evanston, Arlington Heights and more
articles.title_zh: Chicago 'No Kings' protest locations near me: Rallies against Donald Trump, ICE, happening in Evanston, Arlington Heights and more
articles.content_orig:
Movement shifts focus from protest to voter turnout drive
CHICAGO (WLS) -- "No Kings-Vote Early" rallies took place in several neighborhoods across the Chicago area as organizers encouraged residents to vote early and participate in upcoming midterm elections.
The events marked a shift for the No Kings movement, which organizers say began with nationwide marches opposing President Donald Trump and his policies and has now evolved into a more localized effort focused on increasing voter turnout.
Neighborhood resident Michael Burke said frustration with the president motivated him to participate.
"We're so frustrated with our current president and we just need to do anything we can in reaction to him," Burke said.
Supporters of the effort said voting is the most accessible form of civic engagement.
"It is the one thing that everybody can do. Some people can't march. Some people can't, you know, organize crowds or whatever, but everybody can vote," neighborhood resident Caty Norman-Burke said.
One of the events, the "Chalk the Walk-Voting Is Our Superpower" rally at Horner Park on Chicago's Northwest Side, had a community-focused atmosphere as organizers engaged residents. Organizers said it was the fourth installment of the neighborhood event.
Rachel Costa, a neighborhood resident, said she is concerned about how the results of the upcoming midterm elections will be received.
"I think my biggest concern is that results would not be accepted, That in the process of counting the votes. They'll be people who want to not pay attention to that and disregard it," Costa said.
Organizers said earlier rallies were intended to send a message, but the movement is now focused on turning public frustration into political participation, with an emphasis on increasing early voting.
"Democracy is at stake and we need to do all we can to stand up for our neighbors for our community and turn the tide in this country so we are stressing the importance of voting. Make a plan to vote. Encourage others to vote and vote early," said Alison Anselmo, lead of the Indivisible Chicago Northwest chapter.
The Oct. 17 rally was one of thousands of No Kings-Vote Early events taking place across the country. Volunteer Steve Roberts encouraged residents to verify their voter registration and make a plan to cast a ballot.
"They try to restrict voting by taking people off the voter rolls saying they don't live where they say they live and the other thing I know he's talked about messing with mail in voting," Roberts said.
Beyond voter turnout, organizers said election protection was also a key focus of the rallies. They pointed to Trump administration policies and legislative efforts such as the failed SAVE America Act, which opponents say would create unnecessary barriers for eligible voters.
Organizers said the broader effort is aimed at both increasing participation and safeguarding access to the voting process.
One of the larger events Saturday was in Arlington Heights at North School Park. Another was an early vote rally in Hyde Park at East 57th Street and Hyde Park Boulevard. Both events began at 2 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar's turbulent week explained: The dueling probes that threw the Somali-born progressive into chaos
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar's turbulent week explained: The dueling probes that threw the Somali-born progressive into chaos
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, defends her immigration timeline outside their DC residence that Homeland Security Investigations raided on Monday amid a criminal fraud investigation. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
It was a week of legal turmoil for one of America's most recognizable members of Congress.
Early Monday morning, federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant on the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn.
The raid was part of an ongoing criminal probe into Omar's immigration status, with sources telling Fox News Digital that authorities are scrutinizing whether she or her father committed fraud when filling out paperwork for her to become a U.S. citizen.
A day later, U.S. Attorney for the District of Washington, D.C., Jeanine Pirro, announced her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures , which had previously been subject to public scrutiny and congressional oversight, but never by authorities.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is seeking another term in Minnesota’s heavily Democratic 5th Congressional District. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital breaks down what we know so far about each investigation:
In May 2025, Omar filed financial disclosure forms for the year 2024, a requirement for every member of Congress to complete every year. It showed that she had between $6 million and $30 million in assets connected to two businesses run by her husband, Tim Mynett. One was a venture capital firm, and the other was a California winery.
Her financial disclosures from the year prior, covering 2023, said those assets were only valued at between $15,000 and $51,000 total.
The now-defunct winery, eStCru LLC, saw its reported valuation jump from between $15,000 and $50,000 in 2023 to between $1 million and $5 million in 2024. Rose Lake Capital LLC showed an even sharper increase, rising from a reported value of between $1 and $1,000 in 2023 to between $5 million and $25 million the following year.
The massive reported spike in net worth over the one-year span raised eyebrows, leading a watchdog group called the National Legal and Policy Center to file a complaint with the Office of Congressional Conduct in February of this year.
'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP
Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) sits with husband Tim Mynett during the first day of the Democratic National Convention at the United Center on August 19, 2024, in Chicago, Illinois. Delegates, politicians and Democratic Party supporters are in Chicago for the convention, concluding with current Vice President Kamala Harris accepting her party's presidential nomination. The DNC takes place from August 19–22. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Less than a month after the complaint was filed, Omar amended her 2025 disclosure form. The new filing reduced the couple's combined reported assets to between $18,004 and $95,000 and said the businesses had zero value after accounting for liabilities.
ILHAN OMAR'S OFFICE SAYS SHE'S ‘NOT A MILLIONAIRE’ AFTER $30M FILING REVISED DOWN TO UNDER $100K: REPORT
Omar blamed an accounting error and has since repeatedly insisted that she is not a millionaire.
In September, the Office of Congressional Conduct voted 5-1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss misconduct allegations stemming from the financial disclosures.
But the hubbub caught the eye of Pirro, who confirmed on Fox News' "America Reports" Tuesday that her office is investigating the discrepancies.
Further details about the investigation have not yet been released.
U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro announces charges related to an international car theft ring during a press conference at the Justice Department in Washington, D.C., on April 22, 2026, alongside D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser. (Nathan Howard/Reuters)
Monday's judicially authorized raid of Omar's Washington, D.C., home sent shock waves through the political world, with many critics calling it politically motivated because it occurred three weeks before November's general elections.
The Trump administration has denied those accusations.
DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’
HSI agents spent several hours at Omar's home, and The Wall Street Journal reported that the lawmaker's personal cell phone, computers and passport were seized during the search. She has not been seen publicly since before the raid.
Sources told Fox News Digital that investigators are scrutinizing whether Omar or her father fraudulently filled out immigration paperwork when Omar became a U.S. citizen decades ago. The Journal also reported that the goal of the probe is to strip Omar of her citizenship.
A dozen people, including family members, were subpoenaed in relation to the investigation.
FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. According to reports, the search is part of an ongoing criminal investigation. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
"Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully," President Donald Trump said Monday of the raid. "I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me."
"I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is ... a non-country, and then she comes over here, and she complains about our Constitution," he continued. "I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it."
On Tuesday, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital after rallying for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Tyler, Texas, Vice President JD Vance echoed a similar sentiment.
"We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that — where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," Vance said. "We really want to let the law, the facts drive this. And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to."
Rep. Ilhan Omar dismissed Vice President JD Vance’s claims that the Justice Department is investigating her for alleged immigration and fraud violations, referring to House Republicans' attention to the matter as politically motivated. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION
Vance made it clear that taking that unprecedented step of denaturalizing a sitting member of Congress is possible, but only if the law requires it based on the facts of the case.
"And to the question of it being unprecedented, I mean, what I'd say is that Ilhan Omar herself is a very unprecedented person," Vance said.
"We have very rarely had a person in Congress who seems to have such disdain and such rage at the country that gave her a better life," Vance said. "Now, that's not a crime."
"But we're going to see whether she did commit a crime. And if she did, we're obviously going to follow the law."
A spokesperson for Omar did not return multiple requests for comment throughout the week.
However, Omar has responded on social media.
"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said.

articles.title_orig: Susan Dell is the one running the Dells’ $10 billion giving operation
articles.title_zh: Susan Dell is the one running the Dells’ $10 billion giving operation
articles.content_orig:
Michael Dell is the sixth-richest man in the world with a net worth of about $232 billion. He and his wife, Susan, have given away about $10 billion of that fortune—and she is calling a lot of the shots on where the money goes.
She is the co-founder and chair of the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, established in 1999. The organization currently manages more than 800 projects worldwide each year, particularly in the U.S., Africa, India, Israel, and their home state of Texas, where they live on a sprawling 33,000-square-foot estate .
The organization’s focus areas are education, jobs and livelihood, and health—causes she’s cared about deeply since childhood. Her father was a surgical oncologist and “sparked her lifelong passion for health,” the foundation says. As a girl, she would even stop strangers at the grocery store to tell them not to smoke.
“People matter to her,” Janet Mountain , head of the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, said in a statement . “And because people matter to her, solutions matter to her.” Mountain also previously served as an executive at Dell before joining the foundation in 2003.
Recently, Susan has focused largely on the foundation’s livelihood pillar through the Dells’ commitment to Trump Accounts. In December 2025, the couple committed $6.25 billion to provide $250 contributions to 25 million U.S. children.
The donation is intended to benefit children age 10 and under who aren’t eligible for the federal government’s separate $1,000 contribution for children born between 2025 and 2028. The Dells’ money will go to children in ZIP codes with median incomes of $150,000 or less, giving millions of families a chance to start building wealth early.
“We believe that when children have a future that they can see is worth saving for, then that will help build hope and opportunity and prosperity for generations to come,” Susan said during the White House announcement in December.
The couple initially considered limiting their contribution to Texas, Michael explained at the event, before deciding to expand the initiative nationwide. But their home state has long been central to the Dells’ philanthropy, particularly when it comes to health care.
In April, the Dells became the first donors to surpass $1 billion in lifetime giving to the University of Texas at Austin. Their latest commitments will support a new advanced research campus, an AI-focused medical center, scholarships, student housing, and expanded supercomputing capabilities.
That milestone builds on decades of Dell investments in health care across Central Texas. In 2013, the foundation committed $50 million to establish Dell Medical School at UT Austin, along with another $10 million for local health care initiatives.
“A medical school at UT Austin further establishes Central Texas as a center of excellence for family health and research,” Susan said at the time.
The foundation has also supported Dell Children’s Medical Center , which opened in 2007, and the Dell Pediatric Research Institute , helping expand access to specialized children’s care and medical research in the region.
Beyond her philanthropic work, Susan had a career of her own. A fashion entrepreneur , she founded three labels, including luxury brand Phi (which closed during the recession ). She’s also an endurance athlete who has competed in marathons, triathlons, and the Ironman World Championships in Hawaii.
In 2018, she was inducted into the Texas Women’s Hall of Fame for helping families recover from Hurricane Harvey. She and Michael committed more than $43 million to rebuilding and recovery across 41 counties. In 2025, she and Michael also received the History-Making Texan Award, recognizing their contributions to the state and beyond.
And despite decades of philanthropy, Susan has long viewed the foundation’s work as far from finished.
“The reality is, you know, we’re just getting started,” she said during a 2017 discussion about the future of philanthropy.
Sydney Lake is an associate editor at Fortune , where she writes and edits news for the publication's global news desk.

articles.title_orig: Katie Zacharia ousted as White House press secretary
articles.title_zh: Katie Zacharia ousted as White House press secretary
articles.content_orig:
President Trump's embattled new press secretary Katie Zacharia was forced out Friday after less than a week on the job.
Zacharia confirmed widespread reports that Trump had let her go in a post on X just after 9 p.m. ET Friday, alongside a photo of the two of them in the Oval Office. "President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man," she wrote. "I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him."
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung told CNN in a statement that Zacharia "will continue to support the President as she transitions to a new role."
Zacharia is the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in U.S. history.
Her five days on the job fell well short of Anthony Scaramucci's 11 days as Trump's communications director in 2017. Trump is unlikely to name a new press secretary anytime soon, two sources familiar with his thinking told NBC News .
Earlier Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia was on her way out, telling reporters that he had asked Zacharia to "reconsider" whether she "need[s] this."
"I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy and I don't think you could ever be happy in this job,'" Trump said.
Asked if he was planning to "fire" Zacharia, the president said no. But, he added, "I want her to have a good life. I don't want [her] to have a life like she's led in the last three days. She is being brutalized by the media."
Around the same time, multiple outlets reported that Zacharia had already been let go. Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had "fired" Zacharia. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role, and CBS News, Politico and the Washington Post published similar reports.
Zacharia was in the middle of an interview with the Wall Street Journal at her West Wing desk shortly before 1 p.m. Friday when she was called away, the Journal reported . She had just told the reporters, "There are no staffing changes that are happening."
Senior Trump adviser Jason Miller then knocked on her door and said Vice President JD Vance wanted to talk. "JD wanted to chat with us real quick," Miller said, according to the Journal. Zacharia left and never returned to the interview.
The president announced on Friday, Oct. 9, that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August.
Zacharia started at the White House on Monday and gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than Trump's agenda.
In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State.
In media appearances, Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer.
But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia."
Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China."
In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper. "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One. And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question."
Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job.
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia looks on as President Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn on Oct. 13.
In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time.
On Thursday, Zacharia confirmed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China."
On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer."
White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome."
Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added.
Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law."
"I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'"
On Thursday night, Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her halting explanation .
"Why not just say, 'I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn't pass it'?" Hannity asked. "Why get into this long drawn-out thing about the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?"
"When I moved back to the United States, I didn't retake the bar," Zacharia said. "I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law."
Hours before she was forced out, Zacharia told "Fox & Friends" on Friday that no one had asked whether she passed the bar before she was hired. "Those questions weren't asked," she said. "I'm being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel," according to The Hill .
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the Briefing Room on Oct. 13.
Zacharia's first briefing lasted 15 minutes, most of which was taken up by her opening statement.
"I am so honored to work for President Trump and the American people as the new White House press secretary," Zacharia told reporters in the Briefing Room. "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time."
She took questions from three news outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — before ending the briefing.

When a couple from Xinjiang took their quintuplets home on a 36-hour train journey, the babies became favourites of both the train crew and fellow passengers, who took turns caring for them.
The five babies were born on February 26 at a major hospital in Wuhan, in central China’s Hubei province. Their father, known as Abu, and their mother, Dili, are both from Hotan in northwestern China’s Xinjiang region.
The 24-year-old mother conceived naturally despite having previously been diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome, a condition that can make pregnancy difficult, Hubei Daily reported.
After their birth, the quintuplets – one boy and four girls – were cared for in Wuhan by their parents and their aunt.

articles.title_orig: IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
articles.title_zh: IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
articles.content_orig:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has a responsibility to help poorer nations struggling with rising debt, high inflation and price shocks caused by war spillovers, the head of the global lender says.
Speaking as the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok wrapped up on Saturday, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said discussions with global policymakers showed both “optimism and worry”.
“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia,” Georgieva told reporters. “But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.”
Georgieva said vulnerable nations are missing out on the AI investment boom that is driving growth in richer countries while at the same time dealing with higher borrowing costs.
Higher global interest rates mean low-income countries now spend 8 to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, up from previous years, she said.
“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” Georgieva said.
The warnings came as low-income, oil-importing countries take the strongest hit from rising global energy costs. Prices have soared since February when the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran , leading to retaliatory strikes in the Middle East and disrupted oil and gas flows.
“Escalating conflicts ‌and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” said a statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC).
The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender.
Georgieva said her organisation has a responsibility to help countries restructure debt if needed to assist with domestic resource mobilisation, bring in international finance and create conditions for private investment.
Such countries need to set spending targets that prioritise growth and protect the most vulnerable people, she said, adding that the IMF has a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”.
“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people,” she said.
Georgieva also said the IMF plans to back Iraq “very firmly” with a requested loan programme while talks with Lebanese authorities are making progress.
“We will get to Iraq both money and policy support,” she said. “In the case of Lebanon , we are in very intense discussions with Lebanese authorities. We have made significant progress towards the programme. We have still a bit more work to do together, and I’m confident we will be successful.”

articles.title_orig: China urges joint efforts to address risks, challenges in nuclear field
articles.title_zh: China urges joint efforts to address risks, challenges in nuclear field
articles.content_orig:
UNITED NATIONS – China's ambassador for disarmament affairs, Li Chijiang, on Friday called on the international community to work together to address the risks and challenges in the nuclear field.
Li made the appeal at the thematic debate on nuclear weapons at the Disarmament and International Security Committee of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
Over the past year, confrontation within multilateral nuclear arms control mechanisms has further intensified. The international community is increasingly concerned about the risks of a nuclear arms race and nuclear war, he said.
The Cold War mentality is the primary source of deterioration of the international strategic security environment, the envoy noted.
Double standards are the greatest challenge to the international nuclear non-proliferation regime, and unilateralism is the greatest obstacle to global governance in the nuclear field, he added.
"The international community should work together to address the risks and challenges in the nuclear field following the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security," said Li.
Relevant nuclear-weapon states should abandon their policy of nuclear deterrence based on winning a nuclear war and the first use of nuclear weapons, he said.
The international consensus on the nuclear test ban must not be challenged, Li said, adding that the commitments on "moratorium on nuclear testing" must be honored.
The state with the largest nuclear arsenal should effectively fulfill the special and primary responsibility for nuclear disarmament by making drastic and substantive reductions in its nuclear arsenal, rather than pursuing "the world's most robust, credible and modern nuclear deterrent," Li said.
Efforts to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons should not undermine the right of developing countries to the peaceful use of nuclear energy. The peaceful use of nuclear energy must not be used as a cover for nuclear proliferation, he said.
A certain non-nuclear-weapon state accumulates large amounts of plutonium of no credible civilian use, promotes the revision of the "Three Non-Nuclear Principles," and openly advocates the possession of nuclear weapons. The international community must be vigilant and exercise strict constraint, Li said.
The Three Non-Nuclear Principles, formally adopted by the Japanese parliament in 1971, refer to not possessing, not producing, and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons into the country.
China's position of advocating the complete prohibition and thorough destruction of nuclear weapons remains firm, its policy of no-first-use of nuclear weapons is consistent, and its efforts to maintain global strategic security and stability have never ceased, he said.

articles.title_orig: US: California wildfires destroy homes, leave thousands without power
articles.title_zh: US: California wildfires destroy homes, leave thousands without power
articles.content_orig:
At least six expensive properties have been engulfed by fast-spreading wildfires on the southern coast of California, prompting thousands of people to evacuate.
The Orange County Fire Authority said on X that the so-called Norte fire had scorched about 465 acres (188 hectares) and that at least four homes had been impacted in the affluent San Juan Capistrano municipality.
Black smoke billowing from the hills was visible for miles as firefighters tried to contain the fast-moving blaze.
The agency said firefighters were "aggressively attacking the fire from ground and air" and repeatedly requested people to stay away from the area.
The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano.
The National Weather Service warned of "high risk for large fires and rapid fire growth," especially over Los Angeles and Ventura counties, as well as the mountains and foothills of San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties
The wildfires have continued to worsen due to the intense Santa Ana winds, low humidity and unseasonably high temperatures.
According to forecasters, wind gusts of up to 50-70 miles (80-110 kilometers) per hour were recorded in the mountains, with coastal and valley areas seeing gusts between 35 and 55 miles per hour.
Authorities have turned off the electricity supply to reduce the risk of electrical sparks that the heavy wind gusts could carry, leaving thousands of people in the state without power.
