articles.title_orig: 'Our land, our Albania': young lawmaker demands new future as protests rage
articles.title_zh: 'Our land, our Albania': young lawmaker demands new future as protests rage
articles.content_orig:
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë and Vlora in the west, Gjirokastër in the south and Korçë in the east.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.
The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.
The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.
Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."
Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.
"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.
"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.
The UK government has urged visitors to check media for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

articles.title_orig: Canada’s Mark Carney makes final appeal against Alberta separation ahead of referendum
articles.title_zh: Canada’s Mark Carney makes final appeal against Alberta separation ahead of referendum
articles.content_orig:
EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path toward independence in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty.
With U.S. President Donald Trump waging a trade war and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted.
“Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up.
“This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he said.
Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation.
Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier Friday, the Liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence.
Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies.
“I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta.
Smith noted that Carney grew up in Alberta and remains an Edmonton Oilers fan.
“He can’t be all bad, right?” she joked.
“Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us. Never. Never,” Carney warned Friday in Edmonton, repeating a warning he made a day earlier in Calgary.
At Thursday’s Calgary rally and Friday’s Edmonton rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the United States.
Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies.
“Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said.
But he also emphasized his deep ties to the province.
“Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said.
Outside the Edmonton rally venue Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading “Say no to Carney’s new world order.”
Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22% of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high.
Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism.
But some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote.
“I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada.
Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline.
Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions.
Carney’s chief political rival, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, also urged Albertans Friday to remain in Canada.
“Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said.
Despite their agreement on keeping Alberta in Canada, Carney and Smith remain divided over nine other questions on Monday’s ballot involving immigration and provincial powers. Smith wants voters to approve them, while Carney has urged their rejection.
“For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.

articles.title_orig: Senegal-sized Antarctic glacier melting faster than thought: Why it matters
articles.title_zh: Senegal-sized Antarctic glacier melting faster than thought: Why it matters
articles.content_orig:
The world’s largest glacier is melting much faster and could add twice as much to global sea levels as previously expected over the next century.
New research published this week by a team of glaciologists has found that the Thwaites glacier in West Antarctica is losing mass rapidly because warm seawater is pushing underneath it and melting its core. This could add 1.2 inches (30mm) to water levels even if global warming does not accelerate as predicted.
The findings, published in the journal Nature Communications, add to a growing body of evidence that shows that the glacier, which has been receding for decades, is now losing mass even faster than scientists thought.
Researchers at the University of California in the United States collaborated with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory for the study. Here’s what we know about the findings:
Nicknamed the “Doomsday Glacier”, Thwaites is the largest glacier on Earth, spanning an area of around 192,000sq km (74,130sq miles) or roughly the size of Senegal – and larger than the US state of Florida.
It is located on the Walgreen Coast of Marie Byrd Land in remote western Antarctica and forms part of the great West Antarctic ice sheet, which includes other glaciers and is 14 times the size of Thwaites.
The glacier was first mapped in 1947 and is named after the late American glaciologist Fredrik T Thwaites, although he never visited it.
In the 1980s, scientists discovered that Thwaites is melting rapidly and have closely monitored its melting process as concerns have grown ever since.
Because it is so big, the glacier’s collapse would sharply raise global sea levels by a catastrophic amount – although researchers don’t project that will happen for many decades, or even a few centuries.
Together, Thwaites and other glaciers such as the Pine Island glacier – an ice stream in West Antarctica which flows into Pine Island Bay in the Amundsen Sea – act as a barrier that holds back the vast and vulnerable West Antarctic ice sheet. If melted, the ice sheet could cause many coastal cities to be submerged around the world.
At present, ice loss from Thwaites contributes around four percent of all global sea-level rise. Studies have calculated that the glacier has lost more than 1,000 billion tonnes of ice since 2000, and continues to lose 50 billion tonnes of ice per year.
The main drivers are warm ocean water which is actively melting the Thwaites glacier from underneath it, according to several studies.
Ocean warming is caused by human-induced climate change, in particular from the burning of polluting fossil fuels.
In a 2019 study, the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory discovered a giant underwater cavity beneath the Thwaites glacier that spread across an area two-thirds the size of Manhattan, which researchers said was likely speeding up the glacier’s thinning.
Rising temperatures have caused glaciers to lose about five percent of their ice since 2000, according to the European Space Agency.
Thwaites could add as much as 1.2 inches (30mm) – double the current estimates – to sea levels by 2100, even without any additional global warming, the study found.
The researchers said they used new computer models that paint a clearer picture of melting activity under the threatened glacier at its grounding line – the boundary where it transitions from resting entirely on bedrock to spreading out over the sea in the form of ice shelves.
Where other ice sheet models conclude a grounding line is fixed, the scientists said they developed the concept of a broader “grounding zone” instead. In this scenario, seawater lifts and lowers the ice in a “tidal pumping” process that allows warm water to reach “deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting,” lead author Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA, told media.
That melting process is accelerating the Thwaites’ “unpinning” from the Mouginot Ridge – an important underwater bedrock currently stabilising the glacier from below. The study concluded that there is a 60 percent chance that Thwaites could unpin from the ridge by the end of the century.
However, experts say more studies are needed to accurately predict the volume of Thwaites’ ice loss.
In separate findings, scientists from the British Antarctic Survey concluded that Thwaites will continue losing ice for at least the next 150 years, even under the most extreme ocean cooling conditions imaginable.
The study, which used computer simulation models that examined the melting effects of the ocean over the next century and a half, was published in Geophysical Research Letters in July.

articles.title_orig: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia show the Yemeni rebels’ growing strength
articles.title_zh: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia show the Yemeni rebels’ growing strength
articles.content_orig:
Iran spent years building influence in Yemen through Hezbollah recruiters and Revolutionary Guards officers, a former Yemeni pro-democracy activist told Iran International, and is now using the Houthis to carry the war to Saudi Arabia and its Western allies.
Baraa Shiban, an associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in London who took part in Yemen’s 2011 uprising and later negotiated with the Houthis, told Iran International’s Eye for Iran podcast that Tehran’s involvement began long before the group became a major regional force.
His account comes as Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and energy infrastructure have opened another front in the wider war, threatening aviation and trade routes already disrupted by the confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz.
“I think we’re entering phase three,” Shiban said, describing what he sees as Tehran’s strategy of extending the economic cost of the war to US allies.
Iran, he argued, had kept the Houthis in reserve as a strategic asset until it needed them. Their attacks now serve Tehran’s interests while advancing the group’s own ambitions inside Yemen.
From democracy conferences to an IRGC handler
Young Yemenis who took part in the 2011 Arab Spring were invited to conferences in Lebanon that were presented as discussions of democratic reform, Shiban said. Those who went found that Hezbollah operatives were behind them.
Activists receptive to Iran’s revolutionary ideology were introduced to a Revolutionary Guards officer working in Lebanon under the alias Abu Hadi, he said, and some went on to Tehran.
“We were calling it the Arab Spring. The Iranians called it the Islamic Awakening,” he said. Tehran, he said, wanted to present Yemen’s uprising as an extension of Iran’s 1979 revolution.
Shiban identified the officer as Hassan Irlou , who in 2020 became Iran’s ambassador to the Houthi authorities in Sanaa, a post the United States said was held by a Quds Force official. Irlou died in December 2021.
Hezbollah ran much of the operation at first, Shiban said, before Revolutionary Guards personnel took a more prominent role.
The recruitment reached beyond political activists to women invited to conferences in Iran, some of whom came back converted to the Islamic Republic’s ideology. Shiban said he was shocked by one woman he knew as very liberal, who had protested alongside him and returned from Iran repeating Tehran’s case for crushing the Syrian revolution.
“She has absorbed that propaganda of what the Iranians were saying about the Syrian revolution and why they need to kill all of those protesters until the last one, given this woman herself was protesting with us,” he said.
People drawn into these networks went on to help set up the Houthis’ political bureau in Sanaa, Shiban said. Iran International could not independently verify the full extent of the recruitment he described.
The account has new weight after Saudi Arabia disclosed on Thursday that the Houthis had rejected an invitation to negotiations in Oman in July.
Riyadh had sought talks to settle outstanding differences before the fighting escalated, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Rayed Krimly said.
The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh 20 times in October. At least 19 people have been killed in the recent attacks across the kingdom, according to Saudi officials.
Yemen analyst Fatima Alasrar said on X that the Houthis’ refusal reflected Tehran’s timetable rather than an effort to resolve their long-standing demands over airport access, and warned that Iran could keep leverage through the Bab el-Mandeb strait even if it reached a deal with Washington over Hormuz.
The Houthis also have their own aims, among them consolidating control over Yemen and forcing Saudi Arabia to end its support for rival Yemeni forces.
A second strategic chokepoint
The war has put Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow passage between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, at the center of the regional confrontation.
Iran saw the leverage that disrupting Hormuz gave it and wanted the same at a second shipping route, Shiban said. “It saw how valuable and important the Strait of Hormuz was and it wanted to add another choke point.”
The consequences are visible inside Yemen. On Thursday, Houthi missiles struck the presidential palace compound in Aden, killing five people, according to Yemeni authorities. Houthi advances around Taiz have intensified fighting and displacement.
The escalation could prove costly for Tehran, Shiban said, having already antagonized Saudi Arabia and pushed Yemen’s internationally recognized government toward wider war. But Iran’s leaders appear willing to take that risk, he said, on the calculation that Western governments will hesitate to act decisively.
“I think right now they’re counting on the United States is going to be hesitant,” he said.
Even a long confrontation could suit Tehran, he said, if it raises the economic pressure on the Persian Gulf states and strains their ties with Washington.

Iran has executed a 28-year-old Iraqi man convicted of spying for Saudi Arabia, a charge he denied, according to the Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights.
Ayoub Mohammad Nabil, from Haditha in western Iraq, was hanged on Sunday morning at Lakan Prison in Rasht, the capital of Gilan province on the Caspian coast, the group said. Iranian officials and domestic media had not reported his sentence or his execution by the time it was announced.
Nabil had entered Iran legally on his passport and was working as a caretaker at a private villa when Intelligence Ministry agents arrested him in the nearby town of Fouman on August 26, 2025. He had no prior security record, Iran Human Rights said.
A source told the group he was held for about five months at the Intelligence Ministry’s detention center in Rasht, where he was subjected to severe psychological torture. He denied any link to Saudi Arabia or groups tied to it, and said he had been accused because he was a practicing Sunni Muslim, wore a beard and taught the Quran to local children in his guardhouse.
Despite no evidence of any political activity, the source said, Branch One of Rasht’s Revolutionary Court sentenced him to death for “moharebeh,” or waging war against God, through spying for Saudi-backed proxy groups.
The Kurdish rights group Hengaw, citing its own sources, said Nabil was moved to solitary confinement for execution on October 8, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis intensified.
He is at least the 17th person executed in Iran on espionage charges this year, and the third Iraqi, according to Iran Human Rights. Thirteen were accused of spying for Israel or the United States; the other two Iraqis were accused of spying for an unnamed Arab country, and an Afghan man for an unnamed state. Fifteen of the 17 were executed after the war began in February.
More than 70 political prisoners have been executed in Iran since the January protests, and at least 20 more face execution on political charges, Iran International has found.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a report on Thursday that capital cases in Iran, especially security cases, involve systematic violations of fair-trial rights, including forced confessions, closed trials lasting minutes and restricted access to independent lawyers. He called for an immediate halt to executions.
The rights group HRANA said last week that at least 2,003 people were executed in Iran in the year to October 8, up 29 percent on the previous year.

articles.title_orig: With flying Roadster, Tesla waves goodbye to the car business
articles.title_zh: With flying Roadster, Tesla waves goodbye to the car business
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Nearly a decade after Tesla first announced its second-generation Roadster , the company debuted the car in a flashy demo that seemed to challenge the laws of physics.
The sleek white sports car drove upside down, thrust itself into the air and performed a flip over a lineup of other Tesla vehicles.
It accelerated from  0 to  60 miles per hour in under a second, with Tesla Chief Executive Elon Musk saying it will eventually be able to travel as fast as half the speed of sound.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation into Elon Musk’s Cybercab one day after its launch in Austin, Texas.
“Let’s take it to the limits and way past the limits,” Musk said at Thursday’s event in McGregor, Texas. “You’re gonna see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company.”
Here’s what to know about Tesla’s latest electric model .
At the demo event, Musk said production will begin in 2028.
The second-generation Roadster, a nod to the company’s first-ever car, was originally unveiled in 2017. The plan then was for production to begin in 2020.
“Delaying something for nine years, if that was Mazda, no one would stand for that. Tesla just seems to get a pass on everything like that,” said Brian Moody, an analyst at Capital One Auto Navigator.
Tesla’s AI splurge triggers profit squeeze and rare cash burn.
The original Roadster hit roads in 2008 and was discontinued in 2012.
Tesla does not have a good track record of meeting its own deadlines. Musk has long promised to perfect self-driving technology and make it available in existing Tesla models.
Since 2017, Tesla has collected numerous deposits of $50,000 from customers who wanted to reserve their Roadster. Many of those customers have taken to social media to complain that the wait has been too long.
Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, posted a series of screenshots on X in 2025 that showed him asking Tesla for a refund of his Roadster reservation. His email to the company bounced back.
“I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays. But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait,” Altman wrote on X.
It turns out, to make Ford Motor’s electric pickup truck a sales champion, the company just had to stop making it.
At the Texas demo, the Roadster didn’t exactly soar through the air — it thrust itself off the ground for brief moments using thrusters on the bottom of the vehicle.
The version of the car that’s capable of leaving the ground won’t be publicly available and does not have approval for use on public roads.
Dubbed the “Rocket” package, the thruster-enabled Roadster will be sold only to invited customers. It will seat one person and be equipped with a multi-mode suction system and cold-gas thrusters that can boost it into the air.
The technology is a collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX , both run by Musk.
The electric ride hailing service Green SM, founded in Vietnam in 2023, is making its first entry into the U.S. market in Los Angeles.
“A tease like that has a little bit more reality to stand on when it’s coming from a company that can send things to the moon and bring them back intact,” Moody said.
The “Thrust” package, which will see a limited release, comes with thrusters positioned on the rear of the vehicle that can propel it forward at record speeds.
“It’s gonna crush every track record that’s ever existed,” Musk said Thursday.
Customers can now reserve a “Performance” version of the Roadster that can be driven on regular roads. Musk did not announce a price for the vehicle, but it is expected to cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Tesla’s electric vehicle sales have been falling, and Musk has made clear he’s orienting the future of his company around AI, self-driving technology and robotics.
With Chief Executive Elon Musk playing a prominent role in the Trump administration, many Tesla drivers are no longer happy about supporting the car brand.
The company recently discontinued its Model S and Model X electric vehicles, and in turn unveiled the Cybercab, a golden robotaxi that can carry two passengers and lacks driver’s parts like a steering wheel and gas pedal.
The new Roadster demo gave Tesla shares a short boost, but they quickly came back to Earth. Its stock price fell 2% Friday to trade near $355.
Like the original Roadster, the new version isn’t intended to be a mass-market vehicle, said iSeeCars.com analyst Karl Brauer. It’s likely to cost more than $250,000.
“This car, like most exotic cars , does not pay the bills,” Brauer said. “They’re supposed to be attention-getters. They’re supposed to reflect the advanced capabilities of the company.”
The Trump administration’s efforts to erode California’s emissions authority are slowing the state’s EV transition, but not stopping it.
The Roadster could generate new excitement around the company, but it won’t make revenues surge.
Though Tesla has die-hard fans, Musk’s reputation was battered in 2025 when he briefly led President Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency. An overall cooling of the electric-vehicle market under the Trump administration has also slowed sales of mainstream Tesla models.
“His last all-new vehicle, the Cybertruck, everyone has pretty much agreed that’s an official flop,” Brauer said. “From a reputation point of view, Musk does need this one to be a hit.”

articles.title_orig: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
articles.title_zh: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
articles.content_orig:
A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed. During deep sleep, the body releases growth hormone, a powerful chemical messenger that helps build muscle, strengthen bones, and regulate fat metabolism. For teenagers, getting enough sleep is especially important because growth hormone plays a major role in reaching their full height potential.
Scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production. What remained unclear was exactly how the brain controls this process, particularly during non-REM sleep, the deep, restorative stage that typically dominates the earlier part of the night.
Now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship. In a study published in the journal Cell , the team identified the neurons that regulate growth hormone release during sleep and discovered a previously unknown feedback system that helps maintain a delicate balance between hormone levels and wakefulness.
The discovery reveals that the relationship works in both directions. Sleep stimulates growth hormone production, but growth hormone also sends signals back to the brain that influence when we wake up.
The findings could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to treating sleep disorders associated with metabolic diseases such as diabetes, as well as neurological conditions including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.
"People know that growth hormone release is tightly related to sleep, but only through drawing blood and checking growth hormone levels during sleep," said study first author Xinlu Ding, a postdoctoral fellow in UC Berkeley's Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute. "We're actually directly recording neural activity in mice to see what's going on. We are providing a basic circuit to work on in the future to develop different treatments."
Why Deep Sleep Matters for Growth and Metabolism
Growth hormone is best known for its role in childhood development, but its importance extends well into adulthood. It supports the maintenance of muscle and bone, helps the body regulate how it uses stored fat, and influences blood sugar levels.
When sleep is consistently disrupted, growth hormone regulation can suffer. Because this hormone helps control glucose and fat metabolism, inadequate sleep may contribute to an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.
To understand how the brain coordinates these processes, the Berkeley researchers focused on a region called the hypothalamus. Located deep within the brain, this small but essential control center helps regulate hunger, body temperature, hormone production, and the daily cycle of sleeping and waking. Its basic functions have been preserved throughout mammalian evolution.
Within the hypothalamus, the researchers examined neurons that produce growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and two distinct types of neurons that produce somatostatin.
These chemical messengers have opposing functions. GHRH encourages growth hormone secretion, while somatostatin suppresses it. Together, they help control how much growth hormone enters the bloodstream, largely by regulating its release from the pituitary gland, a small hormone-producing structure at the base of the brain.
The scientists also investigated how growth hormone influences the locus coeruleus, a region in the brainstem involved in alertness, attention, thinking, and the drive to explore new or unfamiliar experiences.
Disruptions in the activity of this region have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders.
"Understanding the neural circuit for growth hormone release could eventually point toward new hormonal therapies to improve sleep quality or restore normal growth hormone balance," said Daniel Silverman, a UC Berkeley postdoctoral fellow and study co-author. "There are some experimental gene therapies where you target a specific cell type. This circuit could be a novel handle to try to dial back the excitability of the locus coeruleus, which hasn't been talked about before."
Scientists Map the Brain Circuit That Controls Growth Hormone
The research was conducted in the laboratory of Yang Dan, a professor of neuroscience and of molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley.
To investigate how the circuitry works, the team studied mice using electrodes implanted in their brains. The scientists recorded neural activity while using light to stimulate specific neurons in the hypothalamus, allowing them to observe how different parts of the system responded.
Mice are particularly useful for studying sleep regulation because their sleep patterns differ significantly from those of humans. Rather than sleeping through one long stretch each night, mice typically sleep in brief episodes lasting only several minutes, scattered throughout the day and night.
This gave the researchers repeated opportunities to examine how neural activity and growth hormone regulation changed as the animals moved between sleeping and waking.
Using advanced techniques to trace connections between brain cells, the team discovered that GHRH and somatostatin behave differently depending on the stage of sleep.
During rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the stage commonly associated with vivid dreaming, activity involving both GHRH and somatostatin increases. Although these hormones normally exert opposing effects, their coordinated activity during this stage contributes to increased growth hormone release.
During non-REM sleep, the pattern changes. Somatostatin activity decreases, reducing its inhibitory influence, while GHRH activity rises moderately. This combination also promotes growth hormone secretion.
The discovery helps explain how different sleep stages can support the release of the same essential hormone through distinct patterns of brain activity.
Growth Hormone Also Helps Control When We Wake Up
Perhaps the most surprising finding was that growth hormone does not simply respond to signals from the sleeping brain. It also influences the brain circuits that control wakefulness.
As growth hormone gradually builds up during sleep, it stimulates neurons in the locus coeruleus, increasing their activity and helping promote the transition toward waking.
This creates a feedback loop in which sleep encourages growth hormone release, and the resulting hormone activity helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.
The researchers also identified an unexpected complication. Although greater activity in the locus coeruleus generally promotes alertness, excessive stimulation can have the opposite effect.
In an earlier study published the same year, Silverman demonstrated that when neurons in this region become overexcited, they can paradoxically promote sleepiness rather than wakefulness.
Together, these findings reveal a carefully regulated system in which the brain must balance competing signals to maintain healthy sleep and hormone activity.
Scientists describe this type of self-regulating process as homeostasis, the body's ability to maintain stable internal conditions even as its environment and physiological demands change.
"This suggests that sleep and growth hormone form a tightly balanced system: Too little sleep reduces growth hormone release, and too much growth hormone can in turn push the brain toward wakefulness," Silverman said. "Sleep drives growth hormone release, and growth hormone feeds back to regulate wakefulness, and this balance is essential for growth, repair and metabolic health."
A Surprising Connection Between Sleep and Brain Health
The newly identified feedback system may have implications that extend beyond physical growth and metabolism.
Because the locus coeruleus helps regulate attention, alertness, and cognitive function, growth hormone's influence on this region suggests it could also play a role in how effectively the brain functions after waking.

articles.title_orig: China: Japan needs to face history and reflect on past crimes
articles.title_zh: China: Japan needs to face history and reflect on past crimes
articles.content_orig:
Japan can only truly move toward the future by thoroughly reflecting on its wartime aggression and sincerely repenting for its crimes, the Chinese defense ministry said on Friday.
Senior Colonel Chen Xi, spokesman for the Ministry of National Defense, made the remarks when commenting on renewed public attention to the atrocities committed by Unit 731 of the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II.
His comments came after documentaries in Singapore and Japan drew renewed attention to Unit 731. A Singapore-produced documentary, Inside Unit 731: Japan's Secret Human Experiments, was recently named the best history documentary and has drawn more than 1.45 million views on YouTube.
Japan's public broadcaster NHK also aired a documentary titled The Secret Unit: The Silent Postwar Era, which used newly discovered photographs and testimony from people with firsthand knowledge to examine crimes committed by Unit 731.
Chen said Unit 731 carried out inhumane experiments on living people and conducted biological warfare during Japan's invasion of China, acts that seriously violated international law and constituted grave crimes against humanity.
"The historical truth will not disappear, and the evidence of the crimes committed by the invading Japanese forces is irrefutable and cannot be denied," Chen said, citing views expressed by people in Japan who have called for an honest reckoning with the country's wartime history.
He also said recent attempts by Japanese right-wing forces to use emerging technologies to tamper with data and distort public understanding of history had again raised concerns in the international community.
Chen said efforts to whitewash Japan's wartime aggression or deny historical facts would not change the record of what happened.

articles.title_orig: Brush fires trigger evacuations in Los Angeles, Orange counties amid Santa Ana winds across SoCal
articles.title_zh: Brush fires trigger evacuations in Los Angeles, Orange counties amid Santa Ana winds across SoCal
articles.content_orig:
The Bryson Fire burns in Malibu, Calif., on Oct. 15, 2026. The brush fire in the mountains west of Los Angeles prompted evacuation warnings from officials, as powerful Santa Ana winds risked spreading the blaze rapidly.
Southern California towns are on high alert as the first Santa Ana winds of the season have arrived, igniting multiple blazes across the region.
The red flag warning put out by the National Weather Service (NWS) Wednesday evening followed a relatively quiet wildfire season so far in California . Only 300,000 acres had burned since Jan. 1, compared to the over one million acres that fires have usually burned by mid-October.
Santa Ana winds blow in from the desert, typically between the months of September and May. The winds bring warmer temperatures and drier air to Southern California. They also greatly increase the risk of wildfires—warm winds coupled with summer drought can often make for a dangerous combination. The January 2025 fires that tore through the Pacific Palisades and Altadena were fueled by Santa Ana wind gusts that reached 100 m.p.h.
This week’s winds will not be as strong , according to NWS predictions. But that doesn’t mean the area is in the clear. The NWS warned that, if any fires ignite, “conditions are favorable for extreme fire behavior.”
The largest fire, named the Henderson fire, erupted Thursday afternoon around Camp Pendleton, a San Diego Marine Corps training base, and had burned through 1,404 acres by Friday morning. Two other fires have burned through 200 acres and 43 acres in Los Angeles county.
The NWS issued a red flag warning on Oct. 15 for the Los Angeles County San Gabriel Valley forecast zone that will stay in effect until Saturday evening. The most extreme conditions are expected in the Ventura and Los Angeles County valleys and mountains, particularly Santa Clarita, Thousand Oaks, and Simi Valley.
As of Thursday night, Southern California Edison shut off power to tens of thousands of customers. Nearly 90,000 PG&E customers were also left without power. Shutting down power helps stop downed power lines or aging infrastructure from sparking fires.
If you live in an impacted area, sign up for local emergency alerts, plan for power outages, and avoid any outdoor activities that might ignite sparks like BBQs, campfires, or discarded cigarette butts.
One Southern California town is even encouraging residents to secure hallowed decorations—the giant skeleton and inflatable pumpkins haunting front lawns. High winds can turn Halloween decorations into hazards,” the city of Pasadena said in a Facebook post. “Secure them before winds pick up.”

articles.title_orig: Trump: White House didn't impede satellite system in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Trump: White House didn't impede satellite system in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.
Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions."
Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you."
Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian.
The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.
On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far."
Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.
SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Iran Is Giving Houthis Targeting and Intelligence for Attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.title_zh: Iran Is Giving Houthis Targeting and Intelligence for Attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.content_orig:
Iran spent years building influence in Yemen through Hezbollah recruiters and Revolutionary Guards officers, a former Yemeni pro-democracy activist told Iran International, and is now using the Houthis to carry the war to Saudi Arabia and its Western allies.
Baraa Shiban, an associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in London who took part in Yemen’s 2011 uprising and later negotiated with the Houthis, told Iran International’s Eye for Iran podcast that Tehran’s involvement began long before the group became a major regional force.
His account comes as Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and energy infrastructure have opened another front in the wider war, threatening aviation and trade routes already disrupted by the confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz.
“I think we’re entering phase three,” Shiban said, describing what he sees as Tehran’s strategy of extending the economic cost of the war to US allies.
Iran, he argued, had kept the Houthis in reserve as a strategic asset until it needed them. Their attacks now serve Tehran’s interests while advancing the group’s own ambitions inside Yemen.
From democracy conferences to an IRGC handler
Young Yemenis who took part in the 2011 Arab Spring were invited to conferences in Lebanon that were presented as discussions of democratic reform, Shiban said. Those who went found that Hezbollah operatives were behind them.
Activists receptive to Iran’s revolutionary ideology were introduced to a Revolutionary Guards officer working in Lebanon under the alias Abu Hadi, he said, and some went on to Tehran.
“We were calling it the Arab Spring. The Iranians called it the Islamic Awakening,” he said. Tehran, he said, wanted to present Yemen’s uprising as an extension of Iran’s 1979 revolution.
Shiban identified the officer as Hassan Irlou , who in 2020 became Iran’s ambassador to the Houthi authorities in Sanaa, a post the United States said was held by a Quds Force official. Irlou died in December 2021.
Hezbollah ran much of the operation at first, Shiban said, before Revolutionary Guards personnel took a more prominent role.
The recruitment reached beyond political activists to women invited to conferences in Iran, some of whom came back converted to the Islamic Republic’s ideology. Shiban said he was shocked by one woman he knew as very liberal, who had protested alongside him and returned from Iran repeating Tehran’s case for crushing the Syrian revolution.
“She has absorbed that propaganda of what the Iranians were saying about the Syrian revolution and why they need to kill all of those protesters until the last one, given this woman herself was protesting with us,” he said.
People drawn into these networks went on to help set up the Houthis’ political bureau in Sanaa, Shiban said. Iran International could not independently verify the full extent of the recruitment he described.
The account has new weight after Saudi Arabia disclosed on Thursday that the Houthis had rejected an invitation to negotiations in Oman in July.
Riyadh had sought talks to settle outstanding differences before the fighting escalated, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Rayed Krimly said.
The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh 20 times in October. At least 19 people have been killed in the recent attacks across the kingdom, according to Saudi officials.
Yemen analyst Fatima Alasrar said on X that the Houthis’ refusal reflected Tehran’s timetable rather than an effort to resolve their long-standing demands over airport access, and warned that Iran could keep leverage through the Bab el-Mandeb strait even if it reached a deal with Washington over Hormuz.
The Houthis also have their own aims, among them consolidating control over Yemen and forcing Saudi Arabia to end its support for rival Yemeni forces.
A second strategic chokepoint
The war has put Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow passage between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, at the center of the regional confrontation.
Iran saw the leverage that disrupting Hormuz gave it and wanted the same at a second shipping route, Shiban said. “It saw how valuable and important the Strait of Hormuz was and it wanted to add another choke point.”
The consequences are visible inside Yemen. On Thursday, Houthi missiles struck the presidential palace compound in Aden, killing five people, according to Yemeni authorities. Houthi advances around Taiz have intensified fighting and displacement.
The escalation could prove costly for Tehran, Shiban said, having already antagonized Saudi Arabia and pushed Yemen’s internationally recognized government toward wider war. But Iran’s leaders appear willing to take that risk, he said, on the calculation that Western governments will hesitate to act decisively.
“I think right now they’re counting on the United States is going to be hesitant,” he said.
Even a long confrontation could suit Tehran, he said, if it raises the economic pressure on the Persian Gulf states and strains their ties with Washington.
You can watch Eye for Iran on YouTube or listen on any podcast platform.
Iran has executed a 28-year-old Iraqi man convicted of spying for Saudi Arabia, a charge he denied, according to the Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights.
Ayoub Mohammad Nabil, from Haditha in western Iraq, was hanged on Sunday morning at Lakan Prison in Rasht, the capital of Gilan province on the Caspian coast, the group said. Iranian officials and domestic media had not reported his sentence or his execution by the time it was announced.
Nabil had entered Iran legally on his passport and was working as a caretaker at a private villa when Intelligence Ministry agents arrested him in the nearby town of Fouman on August 26, 2025. He had no prior security record, Iran Human Rights said.
A source told the group he was held for about five months at the Intelligence Ministry’s detention center in Rasht, where he was subjected to severe psychological torture. He denied any link to Saudi Arabia or groups tied to it, and said he had been accused because he was a practicing Sunni Muslim, wore a beard and taught the Quran to local children in his guardhouse.
Despite no evidence of any political activity, the source said, Branch One of Rasht’s Revolutionary Court sentenced him to death for “moharebeh,” or waging war against God, through spying for Saudi-backed proxy groups.
The Kurdish rights group Hengaw, citing its own sources, said Nabil was moved to solitary confinement for execution on October 8, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis intensified.
He is at least the 17th person executed in Iran on espionage charges this year, and the third Iraqi, according to Iran Human Rights. Thirteen were accused of spying for Israel or the United States; the other two Iraqis were accused of spying for an unnamed Arab country, and an Afghan man for an unnamed state. Fifteen of the 17 were executed after the war began in February.
More than 70 political prisoners have been executed in Iran since the January protests, and at least 20 more face execution on political charges, Iran International has found.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a report on Thursday that capital cases in Iran, especially security cases, involve systematic violations of fair-trial rights, including forced confessions, closed trials lasting minutes and restricted access to independent lawyers. He called for an immediate halt to executions.
The rights group HRANA said last week that at least 2,003 people were executed in Iran in the year to October 8, up 29 percent on the previous year.

articles.title_orig: China Could Fully Stop Production Of Cars With Hidden Door Handles
articles.title_zh: China Could Fully Stop Production Of Cars With Hidden Door Handles
articles.content_orig:
China's market regulator has drafted rules that would sharply limit fully electric hidden door handles starting January 1, 2027. Doors would still need to open if the power fails.
The draft also sets a July 1, 2027 paperwork deadline for models already on sale and spells out when a hidden-handle design could trigger a production halt.
The retractable door handles of the Tesla Model S
From January 1, 2027, any manufacturer applying to register a new vehicle design in China would have to submit extra technical data and safety-validation material if that design uses what regulators call an "innovative" feature, with hidden door handles high on the list. The rule targets fully flush, power-retracting handles that sit level with the body and pop out electronically.
Under the draft, fully electric external handles that depend on power to present and release would be banned. Semi-hidden or recessed designs could stay, but only if the handle can be operated mechanically and offers a grab space of at least 2.4 inches by 0.8 inch for a hand to pull.
The draft does not stop at door handles. The same rules would require physical controls for safety-critical functions like exterior lights, windshield wipers, and defogging, shifting those tasks away from touchscreen-only menus.
Vehicles already approved for sale in China are not exempt from the new rules. Automakers have until July 1, 2027 to submit extra technical and validation materials for any already certified model, including the China-market BMW iX3 without pop-out handles . A separate door-handle safety standard gives those in-market vehicles a longer transition period to complete any hardware changes.
Recessed Door Handle Design
Compliance is not just about adding a lever. Reports on the draft describe 51 additional parameters regulators want documented for new vehicle registrations, covering structural and software reliability, environmental adaptability, heating and cooling performance, and sealing against water and dust.
Innovative designs also face real-world durability testing with at least 18,600 miles.
That does not mean every car with flush handles gets pulled from the road. The production-halt and recall rules only apply to vehicles that miss the documentation deadline and are later found to carry a genuine safety risk.
The risk sits with automakers that let the July 2027 deadline lapse on a model with an undocumented or weakly tested design. In that case, the draft calls for an immediate production stop and a recall plan filed with the regulator, similar to the Tesla door handle recall in China .

ATLANTA -- Hassan Kariem 's family is remembering him as a dedicated father, husband, and brother.
"He loved everything about Atlanta. He loved kids. He loved technology," said Joshua Nelson, Kariem's brother-in-law.
SEE ALSO | Six Flags Over Georgia to reopen as planned Friday as Goliath coaster remains closed after fatal fall
Kariem's wife and daughter, along with his niece, all went to Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday to celebrate a birthday. Kariem's daughter was turning 13 years old.
"His last words were to my daughter, and they were, 'This is my favorite ride. I'm so excited to be here,'" Nelson said.
Investigators say Kariem was ejected from the Goliath coaster and fell to his death on Monday. Nelson says his daughter sat right next to Kariem.

"How she described it was, he went up. I guess as the ride was going, he would go up, he went down, went up, down, and the third or fourth time it happened, the latch came undone, and that's when he fell out," Nelson said. "When it first happened, she called me when they got her off the ride, crying. She was like, I don't know where he went."
The Georgia Office of Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire says the Goliath was last inspected in March and showed no warning signs . But Nelson says the family is patiently holding out for answers.
"We're banding together and once the investigation is done, give him the proper sendoff," he said.

articles.title_orig: Reflections | How China’s macabre practice of human sacrifice in burials came to an end
articles.title_zh: Reflections | How China’s macabre practice of human sacrifice in burials came to an end
articles.content_orig:
In China, elites were buried with human companions as far back as the Neolithic period. Over time, symbolic figures replaced real people
Archaeologists have long found a disturbing pattern in the graves of ancient rulers: the dead were sometimes accompanied by other dead. Around royal tombs, the remains of people – who appear to have been killed specifically to follow their masters into the afterlife – lie alongside precious objects and weapons.
A new study from Egypt has brought this practice back into the news. At the ancient royal cemetery of Abydos, archaeologists re-examined the skulls of people buried around the tombs of early rulers. They found signs of serious injuries on many of the skulls, including fractures consistent with powerful blows inflicted around the time of death.
The pattern suggests that at least some of these people did not simply die naturally and happen to be buried near their rulers. They may have been deliberately killed to accompany them into the next world.
Human sacrifice was part of funerary rites of the powerful across the ancient world, from Egypt and Mesopotamia to Europe and the Americas. The practice was also a feature of elite society in ancient China, where it rested on the belief that the dead continued to exist in another world and would need servants, attendants and companions.

articles.title_orig: How many people in the world identify with a particular religion?
articles.title_zh: How many people in the world identify with a particular religion?
articles.content_orig:
Religious compositions vary a lot from country to country.
In my own country , the United Kingdom, Christianity is the most popular, and following no religion is becoming increasingly common, particularly among young people. But I struggle to get a sense of how these differences stack up globally.
The Pew Research Center publishes estimates of religious affiliation across the world. You can see the global breakdown in the chart for 2020 (the most recent year available). It shows the number of people who identify with each religion. Pew counts people by the religion they report, regardless of their beliefs or practices.
You can see that Christians are the largest group, with 2.3 billion people, followed by Muslims, with 2 billion. People with no religious affiliation come close behind.
Those not affiliated with any religion are among the largest groups in the world. But this undersells religion’s reach: when we add up all religious groups, most people in the world — around three in four — identify with a religion. Those with no religious affiliation are still a minority.
According to the latest data from the World Health Organization, the global death rate from malaria has almost halved since the year 2000.
The chart above puts this recent progress into a larger historical perspective. It combines the latest estimates from the WHO and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation with those for the 20th century published by the late malaria researcher Richard Carter. Since 1900, the global death rate has declined by 96%. If it were still as high as it was then, around 16 million people would die from malaria every year instead of 610,000.
Behind this long-run decline is a shift in the distribution of the burden of malaria. In the first half of the 20th century, most malaria victims died in the Asian tropics. It was the substantial progress there — as well as in the Mediterranean and in the Americas — that made this vast improvement in human health possible.
Today, more than 9 out of 10 malaria deaths occur in Africa. This means that the recent progress shown in the chart is, above all, Africa’s progress.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero.
Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong : many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart.
In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million.
Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines .
Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:
Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.
The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.
The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.
From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.
People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
But it tells us none of that.
It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index.
When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable.
As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most.
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.

articles.title_orig: Evacuation orders issued as wildfire burns in Orange County, California - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Evacuation orders issued as wildfire burns in Orange County, California - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The Norte Fire has damaged or destroyed multiple homes, officials said.
Evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Orange County, California, as firefighters work through the night to contain a fast-spreading fire.
There are some 4,600 hundreds and nearly 16,000 people, in the evacuation zone , according to officials with the Orange County Fire Authority.
The Norte Fire ignited midday Friday in San Clemente and has burned at least 465 acres so far, according to fire officials.
"Due to weather and topography, this fire moved fast," Orange County Fire Authority Fire Chief T.J. McGovern said at a news conference Friday evening, calling the wind "relentless."
The vegetation fire threatened multiple structures, with at least six homes damaged or destroyed so far, officials said. No residents have been injured but two firefighters have been hurt, fire officials said.
"Crews are aggressively attacking the fire from the ground and air. Please continue to avoid the area," the Orange County Fire Authority said.
Several schools in the area were dismissed early on Friday due to the fire "out of an abundance of caution," Capistrano Unified school officials said.
The fire comes amid critical fire weather conditions in the region, including strong Santa Ana winds and high heat.
Red flag warnings are in effect for Los Angeles and Ventura counties and the Antelope Valley foothills through Saturday night.
This fire is burning about 20 miles north of the Henderson Fire at Camp Pendleton in San Diego County, which has burned 2,079 acres.
Some 400 firefighters were working to contain the fire with another 400 en route, officials said.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Malibu wildfire rages, triggering evacuations in Southern California
articles.title_zh: Malibu wildfire rages, triggering evacuations in Southern California
articles.content_orig:
The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection was busy Friday tracking multiple fires across the state Friday, and the weather will provide little relief over the weekend.
Critical fire conditions are expected to persist as a threatening combination of strong Santa Ana winds, low humidity and dry vegetation will make it more difficult to contain wildfires in the region, Los Angeles County officials said Friday.
In San Diego County, the day-old, 2,080-acre Henderson Fire was burning at Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, and, just north of the base, in San Juan Capistrano, was the 465-acre Norte Fire.
A blaze in Malibu known as the Bryson Fire has triggered evacuations in the famed Southern California beach community. It was at 146 acres and was 17% contained Friday evening.
Firefighters worked overnight to suppress the fire, said Lindsey P. Horvath, supervisor of the Los Angeles County’s third district.
“It is still red flag alert,” Horvath said in a news conference Friday morning, adding that such conditions are expected to last at least until Saturday night. “Be vigilant and be prepared.”
Flames from the Henderson Fire at Camp Pendleton on Friday licked the northbound shoulder of Interstate 5 , the main artery between the state’s two largest cities, Los Angeles and San Diego, and prompted the California Highway Patrol to shut it down for more than four hours.
Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner line between the two cities announced a track closure and warned its customers of “significant delays and/or cancellations” on Friday.
Neighborhoods near Calle Delgado in San Juan Capistrano faced mandatory evacuation orders as the separate-but-nearby Norte fire “continues to grow,” the Orange County Fire Authority said on Friday afternoon.
An estimated 16,000 residents were subjected to mandatory evacuation orders, Orange County Fire Authority Chief TJ McGovern said at an evening news conference about the Norte Fire.
Among them was U.S. Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., who said he had to abandon his longtime home in San Juan Capistrano. He thanked firefighters for keeping it standing.
“You saved our entire neighborhood today,” Levin said at the news conference.
Two of the estimated 400 firefighters assigned to the Norte Fire were stabilized at a hospital after sustaining unspecified injuries battling the blaze, McGovern said.
At least six homes have been damaged or destroyed since the fire was reported about 11:30 a.m., he said.
Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office said the state secured a grant from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to help fund the firefight in Orange County. Firefighters and equipment were staged in the county Thursday in anticipation of Friday’s fire weather, it said.
The governor’s office blamed “a significant wind event” for imperiling Southern California communities and fanning the Norte Fire, which is also beset by low humidity and summer-like temperatures.
It warned residents that utilities may shut off power as a precaution intended to avoid live lines sparking wildfires
Federal forecasters said the Norte Fire was thriving in 96-degree temperatures, with offshore winds clocking speeds as great as 30 mph.
The Bryson Fire began just before 5 p.m. Thursday on Encinal Canyon Road’s rugged terrain in the Santa Monica Mountains.
No fatalities and no structure losses or damages have been reported as of Friday morning. Los Angeles County Fire Chief Anthony Marrone said he estimates that more than a hundred structures in the general area of the Bryson Fire are threatened.
At least one firefighter had minor injuries from working to contain the fire Thursday night. That person was transported to a hospital and is expected to recover, Marrone said.
Evacuation orders for the Encinal, Trancas and Zuna Canyon areas have been issued, meaning residents must leave immediately as they face an immediate threat to life and property because of the Bryson Fire .
Over 400 firefighters are continuing to work on containing the Bryson Fire alongside more than 75 “ground and aerial resources,” Marrone said.
Winds from up to 35 mph are expected to heighten fire weather threats in the area, according to the National Weather Service, with gusts forecast to reach up to 70 mph.
These conditions could potentially help spark new fires or allow existing fires to rapidly spread. The risk for fires will be highest on Friday for western Los Angeles County, Ventura County and southeastern Santa Barbara County.
“As wildfires continue to burn faster and push deeper into our built environment, I urge residents to continue to monitor high-risk weather conditions,” Marrone said.
Hours before the Bryson Fire began Thursday, another wildfire erupted in the city of Azusa, located north of Los Angeles.
The Peak Fire burned 43 acres on Thursday and briefly prompted evacuation orders for a neighborhood in the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains. Forward progress on the blaze had been stopped by Thursday night after firefighter managed to contain 41% of it.
Nicole Acevedo is a news reporter for NBC News.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: HP Googlebook 14 Review: Great laptop, shame about the OS
articles.title_zh: HP Googlebook 14 Review: Great laptop, shame about the OS
articles.content_orig:
HP’s first crack at a Googlebook laptop is a winner, or at least as much of one as the platform allows. While Googlebook as an operating system leaves a lot to be desired, the HP Googlebook 14 checks every single box for a fantastic laptop.
Kicking things off with the hardware, HP really has built a very good laptop here.
The design is subtle at a glance, but I appreciate the sharp corners of the underside where the feet hold the laptop up for air circulation. There’s a decent-sized gap in the back for airflow as well which almost feels like a handle when you’re carrying the closed laptop. It’s a far cry from something as flat and edgeless as a MacBook Air, but I’ve really come to like it while using the HP Googlebook 14.
The machine is just 10.9mm thick, and weighs in at 2.74lbs (despite an error that doubles the weight on HP’s website). The aluminum build is sturdy with minimal flex in the deck, and it mostly passes the one-handed opening test.
The keyboard has been a tremendous highlight. Despite the thin design, there’s a ton of travel in this keyboard and it’s wildly comfortable to type on. The keys have a satisfying clack without being too loud to be used in public spaces, and the spacing is great, while the backlight is also perfectly pleasant. It took just a few minutes to feel completely at home typing, though Googlebook’s keyboard shortcuts do take a moment to settle into. The top row of function keys are simple and straightforward for the most part, but the window fullscreen toggle (F4) and screenshot tool (F5) both need better iconography — the screenshot key is incredibly vague.
The trackpad is also quite good. While I still struggle with Google’s premium push on Googlebook’s first wave, I’m glad that haptic trackpads were mandated, though HP’s implementation feels just a tiny bit hollow. The placement of the trackpad going right up to the spacebar might prove troublesome for some users, but I never ran into any issues in my testing period.
As for the display, the 14-inch OLED panel is gorgeous. It’s crisp and colorful, and just bright enough. I’d love if it were a bit brighter for outdoor usage, but it’s perfectly acceptable as long as you’re not in direct sunlight.
Battery life is good enough, though not quite at the level of something like a MacBook Air. That’s a bit of a tough pill to swallow given Googlebook OS’ inherent limitations, but this is a far cry from the dark days of laptop battery life and easily on par with a Snapdragon-powered Windows machine. Standby time is good, and it’s actually quite nice having Android’s typical battery usage stats at the ready. Windows is far behind in this regard. Charging has been very quick and I commend HP for including a charger that feels like it belongs in this decade, though I typically stuck with whatever USB-C chargers I had at the ready both in at-home use and on a recent trip.
Performance on the Snapdragon X Elite with 16GB of RAM is unsurprisingly excellent. Seeing as Googlebook is built on Android, it’s a clear formula for a speedy machine. While I’ve absolutely run into my fair share of hiccups here or there, boot times are near-instant, and the overall performance is impossible to complain about.
HP Googlebook 14 has every piece of a great laptop, but sadly it all comes down to the software, and Googlebook is a drag on this machine.
Our Abner Li has already delivered a pretty in-depth review of Googlebook OS as a whole, so this is basically my own personal addendum on that.
My view of Googlebook is that, frankly, it seems a bit pointless in this day and age. Google has rebuilt ChromeOS on top of a new foundation that, yes, presents more possibility for the future, but also fixes virtually none of the existing problems. Like ChromeOS, Googlebook has an incredibly limited library of desktop-class software, even more so given that Linux support has regressed tremendously. One could point at obvious examples like the Adobe suite here, but it really comes down to the niche apps and tools that have been built out for Windows, macOS, and Linux for decades now. That’s an impossible task for any new platform to deal with, but Googlebook feels as though it is actively ignoring that clear gap in functionality. As mentioned, Linux app support has been largely decimated, which was a major boon to the app situation on ChromeOS. There’s also no way to emulate apps for other platforms here, which would be another good way to meet the needs of users not satisfied by what can be found on the Play Store or the web. Google literally has the tools to do this and, yet, none of them can be found here.
In launching this platform, Google’s repeated line about who this is for is “it’s a laptop for Android users.” I’m absolutely sick of hearing that. It’s utterly meaningless.
In a smartphone-dominated society, smartphones are the tentpole. Yes, you want integration between devices, but you’re not buying a laptop for smartphone integration. You buy a laptop to do the things that your phone can’t, and Googlebook can’t really do much more than your phone, at least not yet.
HP did a great job building out a very good laptop for Googlebook. The hardware is just let down by the software. You’d have a much better time using this laptop with Windows or even Linux compared to Googlebook right now. Especially at a time when the cost of laptops continues to skyrocket, I cannot recommend that anyone invests $1,200 into a Googlebook when you can get a Windows laptop, or even a MacBook, for the same price, if not less. There’s simply no reason to get less functionality for the same price. Fast-forward to when Googlebook is available on less expensive hardware and it might be a different story, but right now, eh .
