articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Faces Weekly Loss on Tech Stock Slump — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slid on Friday as traders notched a mostly losing week amid a shift away from tech and artificial intelligence-related names as well as a rise in oil prices.
The S&P 500 lost 1.09% and ended at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 2.14% to close at 26,140.03. Both indexes ended the session below their 50-day moving averages. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41. The sell-off sent the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months .
Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 3%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH slid 10% week to date for its biggest weekly decline since April 2025.
Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, dragged the S&P 500 to a losing week. The benchmark index fell about 2% this week, while the Nasdaq shed more than 4% for its worst week since June. The Dow, on the other hand, advanced 0.7% on the week.
Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down nearly 12%, bringing the stock's week-to-date losses to 25%.
"The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now."
Other areas of the market such as energy saw gains Friday, with stocks like Chevron helping to keep the Dow's losses in check. Oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions between the U.S. and Iran as well as between Russian and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate crude futures increased 3.51% to settle at $101.41 per barrel, while Brent crude futures advanced 3.72% to $109.86.
Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 82% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
The three leading U.S. indexes ended Friday's session with losses.
The S&P 500 dropped 1.09% to finish at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41.
As the market sell-off intensified Friday afternoon, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) rose to levels it last closed at four months ago.
The VIX rose to 21.32, as of 3:10 p.m., rising more than 4.8 points on the session. It's on pace for its highest close since June 10, when it closed at 22.22.
Typically, when the VIX is above 20 that indicates greater fear in the market. The index last closed above that level on July 29 , when markets fell after the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its meeting that month. The next day , stocks rose, and the day marked a bottom in a market where many AI-related stocks had been selling off in the previous month .
The Nasdaq Composite was down about 2.5% in afternoon trading on Friday, bringing its loss on the week to almost 5%.
With that move, the tech-heavy index on pace for its worst weekly performance since the week ended April 4, 2025, when the index recorded a roughly 10% drop.
Communication services and information technology led the S&P 500 lower on Friday.
The two sectors were down 2.7% and 2.4%, respectively, becoming the two biggest laggards among the 11 S&P 500 sectors. Consumer discretionary followed behind them, falling 1.5%.
However, a look beneath the surface showed that the S&P 500 — which was last down 1.3% — was more evenly split despite the losses at the index level. There were about 280 losers in the index and 222 gainers.
In total, five out of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were in positive territory, led by energy with its 2.1% gain and utilities with its rise of 1.2%.
— Sean Conlon and Sarah Min
U.S. crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz this week and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 2.9% to $100.78 per barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was 3.3% higher at $109.37 per barrel. Read more .

Early in the "SaaSpocalypse" that roiled software companies this year, Manish Gupta, a portfolio manager at First Eagle Investments, added to Workday as he parsed through the wreckage for some bargains.
In recent months, that bet has paid off for the value investor. After falling about 40% in the first quarter of 2026, during which the enterprise software stock at various points was trading at not even three times revenue, the stock went on to surge more than 55% in the third. It's also outperforming this week, rising more than 2% amid a broader tech sell-off as investors exit for safer assets.
Gupta, who attended the company's analyst day this week, remains confident in Workday, which he said is trading at a discount to similar businesses in the private markets. Workday is a top 10 holding in the First Eagle Global Fund (SGENX) , which he co-manages and which had nearly $75 billion in total net assets as of Sept. 30.
"The price has moved up, but the business has also become better," Gupta said. "The 'SaaSpocalypse' has also turned around, but the stock's still attractive."

articles.title_orig: DHS Secretary Mullin calls Ilhan Omar probe a "strong case," says agents executed multiple search warrants
articles.title_zh: DHS Secretary Mullin calls Ilhan Omar probe a "strong case," says agents executed multiple search warrants
articles.content_orig:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal agents executed multiple search warrants on the same day they searched Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home. While appearing on a podcast Friday, Mullin described the ongoing investigation as a "strong case" while suggesting cases of coordinated immigration fraud could be prosecuted under federal racketeering laws.
In an interview with Andrew Kolvet, who hosts the "Charlie Kirk Show," Mullin volunteered that multiple warrants had been served on Monday, adding that a judge had authorized the enforcement action and that investigators expected to present their case to a grand jury.
Omar has not been charged with a crime. She has called the investigation politically motivated.
"She wasn't – or it wasn't the only place we served the warrant," Mullin said, referencing the D.C. residence of the Minnesota congresswoman. "There was multiple other warrants served on that same day."
"We had a judge sign it, and we expect to be able to take the case to a grand jury," Mullin said, revealing new details about the scope of the operation. "But I will tell you, we wouldn't move forward, and President Trump didn't want to move forward either, unless we knew that it couldn't be politically driven. Now they want to try making it political driven. This individual wants to try making it about themselves. This was about enforcing once again our nation's laws, and it's a strong case."
President Trump previously stated he didn't know anything about the investigation, which is being handled by DHS' Homeland Security Investigations division and the Justice Department. Asked about the Omar probe on Monday, Mr. Trump told reporters: "I think she's a terrible person, but that's really up to the DOJ."
Mullin's remarks came amid a federal investigation into possible fraud involving immigration documents submitted by Omar's family decades ago. The documents in question date back to Omar's childhood, involving paperwork completed by her late father when she was a child, CBS News reported earlier this week . Multiple relatives of Omar received grand jury subpoenas as part of the investigation, and the lawmaker's personal cellphone was taken by DHS, sources told CBS News.
During the interview, Kolvet also asked Mullin about a hypothetical scenario involving a former foreign warlord who entered the United States as a refugee with his daughter. Mullin did not establish that the circumstances applied to Omar's family. But the DHS secretary did use the hypothetical to suggest that those who submit fraudulent immigration documents and enable others to enter the country under the same purported scheme could very well be prosecuted under U.S. law.
Such conduct, he said, could potentially constitute a violation of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, or RICO, a federal law used to prosecute organized criminal enterprises.
"If someone … fills out their paperwork illegally, and they claim that they are this person and this is their background, and then underneath that individual, a lot of other people come in. And I'm just saying hypothetically across a whole bunch of cases that's out there, then that can be considered a RICO case, right?" the DHS secretary offered. "Because there was conspiracy to deceive the American government, and therefore everything else that came in with it could then be looked at [part of] the same case."
Mullin suggested that a racketeering prosecution could allow investigators to examine conduct extending back decades, arguing that statutes of limitations generally would not apply to such cases.
Under federal law, criminal RICO prosecutions are generally subject to a five-year statute of limitations, although in certain cases prosecutors can incorporate older acts into a timely prosecution involving an ongoing criminal enterprise or conspiracy.
In Grunewald v. United States, the Supreme Court held in 1957 that prosecutors cannot indefinitely extend a conspiracy simply because perpetrators covered it up after it ended.
Mullin did not explicitly indicate that prosecutors were pursuing RICO charges against Omar. But his remarks did suggest investigators are considering whether alleged immigration violations could be examined as part of a broader conspiracy rather than simply as isolated offenses. He said Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents had worked closely with the Justice Department to build out the case.
It is unusual for federal officials to speak openly about ongoing criminal investigations beyond confirming that a court-authorized search was conducted, in part due to due process protections and grand jury secrecy rules.
CBS News has reached out to Omar's attorney for comment.
Earlier this week, Omar — a staunch Trump critic who has drawn the president's ire for years — denied all wrongdoing and said she "will not be silenced."
"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," she wrote on X . "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation."
Sarah N. Lynch contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.title_zh: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the operation, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications, at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing green vestments while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
The head of the Roman Catholic Church "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
Also on Friday, the Pope phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin from hospital to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where access to food and water has been cut off for thousands .
"The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope's request will indeed be carried out," said Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state.
Without mentioning a ceasefire, the Kremlin said: "The Vatican's intention to help create the conditions necessary to ensure the safety of the town's population and to organise vital supplies has been supported."
It added: "It has been agreed to co-operate on this matter."
The UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Turk, made a similar plea to address what he described as a "desperate" situation in Oleshky.
The Pope's doctors said on Friday that tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his surgery.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
The pontiff first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

articles.title_orig: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
articles.title_zh: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
articles.content_orig:
The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies
W hen Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods.
“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China . “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.”
She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario.
Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.”
Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”.
Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments.
At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster.
“I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.”
It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations.
The offering are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake.
Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country.
In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis.
“The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.
But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction.
In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside.
In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck.
“I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.”
Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered.
In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine”.
Entry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says.
“There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang.
Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

articles.title_orig: Apple’s updated App Store rules go after ‘nudify’ AI apps
articles.title_zh: Apple’s updated App Store rules go after ‘nudify’ AI apps
articles.content_orig:
The terms more explicitly ban apps that create ‘nonconsensual intimate imagery.’﻿
The terms more explicitly ban apps that create ‘nonconsensual intimate imagery.’﻿
Apple’s App Store rules now more explicitly ban so-called “nudify” apps that generate intimate images of people without their consent using AI tools.
The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors . Apple didn’t pull X or Grok from the App Store, though it told senators that it threatened to yank Grok . At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did .
As part of updates announced Friday , Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps. Developers who “fail to implement adequate safeguards” or “don’t remedy violations after notice” may be removed from the App Store. Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved.
Apple’s rules also more clearly spell out that any apps that “facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children” will be pulled from the App Store and “blocked from alternative distribution.”

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave stock plunges 12%, but Wall Street analyst says buy the dip
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave stock plunges 12%, but Wall Street analyst says buy the dip
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
CoreWeave (CRWV) stock plunged 12% on Oct. 16, putting the AI infrastructure company on track to finish the week down 25% as concerns over AI funding continued to weigh on market sentiment.
Earlier this week, Bloomberg reported a sharp rise in CoreWeave's bond yields, raising questions about whether the company can generate enough cash flow to support its rapid expansion.
CoreWeave's bond yields climbed to around 15%, while the cost of insuring its five-year debt against default rose by as much as 74.5 basis points to 1,194.5 basis points, an all-time intraday high, according to Bloomberg. That could mean odds of more than 60% that CoreWeave would default sometime in the next five years.
CoreWeave has been spending heavily on data centers and Nvidia (NVDA) chips to meet soaring demand for AI computing power.
The company has secured major contracts with AI developers and technology companies, but building the infrastructure needed to fulfill those agreements requires substantial upfront investment.
The Friday, Oct. 16, decline came after CoreWeave stock rebounded the prior day, following comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that helped ease some concerns.
"CoreWeave's strength is improving every day," Huang said at a Bloomberg event in Stockholm. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing."
Nvidia holds roughly 47.2 million shares of CoreWeave, representing about a 10% stake in the company. CoreWeave is also a major customer of Nvidia's chips.
However, Huang's reassurance failed to sustain the rebound.
Peer Nebius (NBIS), another company investing heavily in AI computing infrastructure, dropped about 12% on Oct. 16 and was also headed for weekly losses. Nvidia also invests in Nebius.
Also read: Dell stock price tumbles 6.8% after epic 271% run
In August, CoreWeave reported second-quarter results that topped Wall Street expectations.
The company posted an adjusted loss of $1.03 per share, narrower than the $1.20 loss analysts expected. Revenue came in at $2.58 billion, up 112% from a year earlier and above the $2.56 billion estimated by Wall Street.
For the third quarter, CoreWeave guided for revenue of $3.4 billion to $3.6 billion, implying 158% growth at the midpoint. Analysts surveyed had expected $3.43 billion, CNBC reported.
CoreWeave also reported a revenue backlog of more than $100 billion. That means it hasn't earned that money yet.
Despite the recent sell-off, Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Brett Knoblauch believes investors are focusing too heavily on CoreWeave's debt and overlooking its improving business fundamentals.
In a research note, Knoblauch said CoreWeave's debt-yield spike reflects concerns about financing massive AI capital expenditures rather than weakening demand, according to StockTwits , citing The Fly.
Also read: Micron stock tumbles despite analyst calls semiconductor sell-off
Knoblauch said demand remains strong, with nearly all of CoreWeave's 2027 capacity already sold and Nvidia providing a backstop for unsold capacity. He also pointed to improving economics, including rising revenue per megawatt and contribution margins, which have shortened the payback period for AI chips to 2-2.5 years.
Knoblauch believes improving unit economics and asset-backed financing can help CoreWeave sustain its rapid growth, despite concerns about borrowing costs.
Cantor Fitzgerald maintained its overweight rating and $176 price target on CoreWeave shares, recommending that investors buy the dip.
CoreWeave stock trades at around $61 as of writing.

articles.title_orig: How China Has Quietly Taken a Lead in International Agency Staffing
articles.title_zh: How China Has Quietly Taken a Lead in International Agency Staffing
articles.content_orig:
The front of the World Health Organization building in Geneva, Switzerland, on December 3, 2019. China has sought to staff the middle ranks of the international civil service, write Mike  Kuiken and Leland Miller. (Shutterstock/Diego Grandi)
Since 2020, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission has published a ledger of Chinese citizens holding senior positions across the international system, agency by agency, and the April 2026 edition lists five at the International Seabed Authority (ISA), an institution few Americans have even heard of. Under the World Health Organization ( WHO ), which everyone has heard of, it lists none.
Earlier this month, Beijing nominated Song Li, a National Health Commission official who has spent years on WHO technical committees, for the post of WHO director-general. This leadership contest is only one part of China ’s effort to shape international institutions. Across international institutions, Beijing is seeking to fill middle- and senior-level posts where officials (whose tenures often outlast leadership terms) draft standards, interpret procedures, process applications, and shape the choices that reach leadership for approval. Washington counts Beijing’s people at the top. The more consequential question is who holds the pen underneath.
In Kingston, Jamaica, the official who runs the office that processes applications to mine the deep ocean floor is Yongsheng Cai , a former Chinese foreign ministry official. He sits at the International Seabed Authority , which regulates mining on the half of the planet’s seabed that lies beyond any nation’s jurisdiction, and applications to explore and eventually extract the metals that go into electric-vehicle batteries cross his desk before they reach anyone else. He is one of five Beijing-aligned appointees in senior staff and oversight posts at the authority, and none of them arrived there by accident.
For years Washington has measured Chinese influence by the top jobs, and by that measure Beijing peaked in 2020 , when Chinese officials ran four United Nations agencies at once: food and agriculture, telecommunications, civil aviation, and industrial development. By 2023 , they had left three of those four top jobs, with only Qu Dongyu winning a second term at the Food and Agriculture Organization. Beijing’s candidate also lost the 2020 race for the World Intellectual Property Organization leadership. At Interpol, China’s candidate, Meng Hongwei, won the presidency in 2016; Beijing summoned him home two years later and imprisoned him (his resignation letter arrived from custody).
That run of departures may seem like proof that Beijing is in retreat. But it obscures an influence strategy that has been underway beneath the agency heads. Beijing’s influence in that layer persists through leadership changes, even as its WHO bid signals renewed ambition for the top jobs—just when Washington has walked away from the table.
Plenty of serious people in Washington, in both parties, regard these institutions as sluggish, politically captured, and venues for anti-American speeches. They are not wrong. However, the institutions exist anyway, and they decide who mines the seabed, who gets which radio frequencies, and how international trademark-registration systems operate, whether or not the United States is in the room. Every American city has a zoning board that will rule on the building next door whether or not you show up, and the people who do show up write the rules.
In intellectual property, Binying Wang , the Chinese nominee who lost the 2020 contest for Director General of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), remained deputy director general for its brands and designs sector for years afterward. WIPO’s current leadership listing identifies her successor as Shen Changyu , who ran China’s patent and trademark office for 12 years. The individual has changed; Chinese representation in the portfolio that administers the international trademark and design-registration systems has continued.
In civilian technology, the Standardization Administration of China serves as the secretariat for 95 Technical Committees and subcommittees of the International Organization for Standardization, including the one drafting global standards for brain-computer interfaces. These systems connect brain activity to computers. Technical standards bodies may sound obscure, but the point is simple: standards built around a country’s existing technologies can give its companies a head start, leaving competitors to adapt their products.
The International Telecommunication Union ( ITU ) coordinates international use of the electromagnetic spectrum, the radio waves that carry everything from cell signals to satellite internet, and the Commission’s April 2026 ledger lists no Chinese citizen in its General Secretariat, which again looks like a retreat until you check the layer below. Witnesses at the Commission’s April 2025 hearing on China’s space program cited Chinese filings covering more than 74,000 low-earth-orbit satellites. Every one of those filings has to clear the union’s coordination rules, which are written by consensus at its conferences and interpreted by a twelve-member board, so whoever controls the room and the board controls the orbits. They described Beijing’s practice of flooding union and World Radiocommunication Conference sessions with enough personnel to overwhelm consensus.
For the telecommunications union’s elections in Doha this November, Beijing has nominated Cheng Jianjun , an executive vice president of China Mobile, for another term on the 12-member Radio Regulations Board , which interprets the Radio Regulations and handles associated disputes. A government able to send more people than anyone else to handle problems such as these does not especially need the secretary-general’s office.
The private sector needs the tools to defend itself from unconventional drone or cyber threats.
Foreign and malign actors constantly exploit weak ownership reporting requirements to launder money throughout the United States.
The frozen conflict in Cyprus is a major roadblock to integrating one of NATO’s most powerful militaries into European defense initiatives.
The International Monetary Fund’s ( IMF ) general counsel is Yan Liu , a Chinese citizen. Her department helps shape the IMF’s sovereign debt policies and supports the Common Framework and the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable , processes where China’s role as a major creditor is consequential. China is the largest bilateral lender to the developing world and has a well-documented record of lending on secret terms in Zambia, Sri Lanka, and across the countries that have joined the Belt and Road Initiative . When those debts come up for restructuring, her office writes the IMF’s positions, a proximity to the referee no other creditor would be allowed.
A recent Center for Global Development study found that China’s formal voting power in these institutions still lags compared to the size of its economy, which is true. Yet that’s beside the point, because Beijing’s strategy isn’t to outvote anyone so much as staff the offices that write the rules the votes are about.
Congress rightly saw this problem coming years ago and wrote remedies into the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 , including a binding duty for the National Institute of Standards and Technology ( NIST ) to coordinate American participation in international standards bodies, and a pilot grant program to pay for the people who would do it. Congress gave the duty to NIST because setting standards is what NIST exists to do, and has done for the United States and much of the world since Congress created it in 1901.
Four years on, Congress should ask what that mandate has delivered: how many American experts are participating, which committees they lead, and where gaps remain. NIST announced a $15 million, five-year cooperative agreement with ASTM International in O

articles.title_orig: On World Food Day, We Must Take Real Action on Global Malnutrition Crises
articles.title_zh: On World Food Day, We Must Take Real Action on Global Malnutrition Crises
articles.content_orig:
Save the Children Renews Call for Global Food Security Strategy
FAIRFIELD, Conn. (Oct. 16, 2026) — This World Food Day, Save the Children is calling for renewed action to ensure every child has access to the food and nutrition they need to survive, learn and thrive. Whether they face acute malnutrition in a humanitarian crisis or rely on nutrition programs here in the United States, children need consistent access to healthy food to reach their full potential.
As more than 43 million children across the globe suffer from severe malnutrition, [1] Save Children is also reiterating its call for the U. S. government to release its overdue Global Food Security Strategy.
The Global Food Security Act requires a new Global Food Security Strategy every four years. The strategy due in 2026 is yet to be released. At a time when hunger is worsening in many parts of the world and a “Super” El Niño is expected to worsen hunger and malnutrition in many parts of the world, the strategy can help guide U.S. efforts to identify emerging crises and support early and effective action – before children face serious health complications.
In an op-ed published by The Hill earlier this month, Save the Children President and CEO Janti Soeripto wrote : “The new Global Food Security Strategy should be built on a clear picture of where hunger is worsening, who is most vulnerable and which interventions stop a crisis before it becomes a catastrophe. It should treat early warning, early financing and early action as inseparable, strengthening tools like the Famine Early Warning Systems Network with better technology, nutrition data and information from frontline workers and communities.”
This year’s El Niño weather event – predicted to be one of the strongest in decades – is expected to deepen hunger and malnutrition further, because of dangerous droughts, crop failures, flooding and livestock losses.
Children in Somalia, Yemen and other countries facing conflict, extreme weather and economic instability need urgent support to prevent hunger from becoming a catastrophe.
World Food Day is also a reminder that child hunger remains a challenge in the United States . Federal nutrition programs, including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Child and Adult Care Food Program and school meals, help millions of children access healthy food and support their learning and development. Children cannot reach their full potential when they are hungry.
While acute malnutrition is both treatable and preventable, prevention requires sustained investment in nutrition, health systems, resilient food systems and early action before crises escalate.
Save the Children supports policies that reduce child hunger, improve nutrition and strengthen food security for children and families in the U.S. and around the world. Investing in children’s nutrition is one of the most effective ways to improve health, education outcomes and long-term opportunity.
In its programmatic work, Save the Children takes a comprehensive approach, investing in prevention, treating malnutrition and strengthening health systems while delivering food to children in need.
This World Food Day, Save the Children urges policymakers to prioritize actions that prevent hunger, protect children’s nutrition and help to build a future in which every child has the opportunity to grow up healthy and thrive.
[1] Levels and Trends in Child Malnutrition. Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates: Key findings of the 2025 edition; May 2025. UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Group/JME-Brochure-UNSDG-regions-2025-v23.pdf
Save the Children believes every child deserves a future. Since our founding more than 100 years ago, we've been advocating for the rights of children worldwide. In the United States and around the world , we give children a healthy start in life, the opportunity to learn and protection from harm. We do whatever it takes for children – every day and in times of crisis – transforming the future we share. Our results , financial statements and charity ratings reaffirm that Save the Children is a charity you can trust. Follow us on Facebook , Instagram , LinkedIn , X and YouTube .

articles.title_orig: Pour One Out for the Leap Second
articles.title_zh: Pour One Out for the Leap Second
articles.content_orig:
Leap seconds have driven a raging debate in the metrological community for three decades. Now, that argument has been put to rest: The leap second is officially dead.
Doing away with an obscure metric the average person has been blissfully unaware of may seem like a novelty, but killing the leap second has major ramifications for technology you rely on every day. It also helps stave off what could’ve been a dangerous moment in time: The possibility of the world’s first negative leap second.
The International Bureau of Weights and Measurements (known by its French acronym BIPM) on Thursday said that in May 2027 it would stop issuing leap seconds, 32 of which have been added since 1972 to adjust what’s known as Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
The world implemented the leap second in 1972 due to a growing gap between time measured with atomic clocks and time based on the Earth’s rotation. The reason for the discrepancy? The latter is slowing down due in large part to tidal friction caused by the moon and Earth’s rotation not lining up. The molten core of the Earth as well as oceans and the atmosphere also affect the spin rate.
Leap seconds are a way to keep atomic-clock-driven UTC in line with astronomically kept Universal Time (UT1). Think of it like adding a little extra track for a train to keep running exactly parallel with another one. Rather than happening on a set interval—like a leap year—BIPM uses the average of hundreds of atomic clocks around the world and compares their time calculations to astronomical time to determine when a leap second is necessary. The most recent one was added in 2016.
Of course, adding track is no small effort, and it may seem like a lot of hassle for a measly second. But UTC is vital for all sorts of technology given the number of APIs and databases that rely on it. Introducing a leap second helped keep UTC and UT1 aligned, but it also wrought havoc on various systems running on UTC and forced companies to figure out how to deal with them when they were added every few years.
A number of tech companies like Google and Meta use “a ‘smear’ method of dealing with leap seconds,” Judah Levine, a fellow at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, writes in an email. In essence, they spread a leap second out over the course of a day or so in tiny increments. But leap seconds have thrown off other systems ; the airline Qantas, for example, saw its booking system borked by a leap second in 2012 .
Adding a leap second is hard enough as it is. But the odds of having to add a negative leap second have been rising in part because Earth has picked up rotational speed in recent years due to climate change. (There’s always a climate angle.) Melting ice has caused a shift in the planet’s gravity so extreme that a negative leap second may have been required as soon as 2029, according to a 2024 Nature study . Part of the calculus of ditching the leap second altogether was that going negative isn’t worth the risk.
“There are continuing problems with positive leap seconds even after 50 years, and the concern was that the negative leap second would be much more serious because its effects had never been tested,” Levine says.
BIPM time department director Patrizia Tavella confirmed those concerns in an email to WIRED. “The probability of a negative leap second convinced us [to] set the application date in 2027,” she wrote, adding that there was added urgency following tests by an industry standards group that “showed several failures with a negative leap.”
Tavella says the group is waiting until May 20 2027 to implement it because it's the anniversary of 1875 signing of the Metre Convention, creating BIPM, as well as Metrology Day. In other words, it’s the perfect time to mark the passing of time—or more accurately, the lack thereof.
The death of the leap second makes life easier for everyone now. “The nice fact is that we have nothing to do!” Tavella says. “Just continue to accumulate second[s] and ‘normal’ minutes of 60 seconds.”
Levine concurs, writing that “life will have one less hassle.”
But kicking the can on adding leap seconds doesn’t mean atomic time and astronomical time won’t continue to drift apart. That’s why BIPM also agreed to create a leap hour. Given how long it takes leap seconds to add up, a leap hour is millennia away. (There are, after all, 3,600 seconds in an hour.)
“We do not speak of leap hour yet,” Tavella says. “If systems rely on UTC, they have nothing to do. If they rely on UT1, they have to be able to use the information UT1-UTC which, in [the] future, will be larger than 1 second.”
In other words, not our problem, and good luck to future generations!

It was likely their final face-to-face showdown in a race with potentially major national implications.
Over the hour, Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson disparaged each other's records, portrayed the other as beholden to political interests far from Maine and drew laughs from the audience with their sharp barbs. At one point, Jackson even told Collins to "shut up" after she quipped that a protester obviously came from his camp.
But they occasionally agreed on issues, such as about the pernicious effects of the "dark money" that is pouring into Maine to attack and prop up both candidates.
Here are a few key takeaways from Thursday night's debate co-sponsored by Maine Public, NEWS CENTER Maine and the Portland Press Herald.
As he'd done throughout their three previous joint appearances, Jackson sought to portray Collins — a 30-year Senate veteran — as a key cog in a Republican majority in Congress that he says refuses to stand up to what he believes is a dangerous president.
"They will not stop Donald Trump and I do think our democracy is risk," Jackson said before accusing Trump of trying to suppress the vote in November. "Donald Trump is trying every trick in the book to keep power. And we've already seen what he will do on Jan. 6 when he led an insurrection."
And he repeated one of his favorite statistics — that Collins allegedly votes with Trump 96% of the time.
"The reality is that 100% of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there," said Jackson, a professional logger and former Maine Senate president who entered the race in July after former Democratic nominee Graham Platner withdrew. "The votes that she throws away are managed votes that she already knows the outcome."
As she's done in previous debates, Collins accused Jackson of cherry-picking a number from a study that only examined about one-third of the votes that have been taken. The real figure, she said, is about 72%. And Collins, who chairs the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, pointed to years of analysis consistently showing her the most or one of the most bipartisan senators from either party.
"He is going to be an automatic vote for the Democratic position no matter what," Collins said of Jackson. "We have lost a lot of the centrists and one of the reasons is we need people who will work across party lines."
It's probably a safe assumption that both candidates have wanted to say this to the other at some point (or lots of times) during the three previous tense debates. But it took an unexpected disruption to bring it out.
The brief scene began when an audience member began shouting at Collins about the environmental impact of data centers as she started answering a question on an entirely different topic.
"So this is obviously one of Troy's supporters," Collins said, leaning slightly into the microphone.
"Oh shut up," Jackson shot back. "I did not ... I don't even know that kid."
"Oh right," Collins said sarcastically.
Just before Collins' initial remark, Jackson had been frowning and shaking his head in the direction of the protester. And from the audio and video, it seems like Jackson's "oh shut up" was more flippant than mean-spirited. The two rivals even seemed to exchange snarky smiles before the debate quickly resumed without future disruption.
Not surprisingly, the Senate Leadership Fund — one of the super PACs spending millions of dollars to support Collins — called attention to Jackson's statement in an email blast.
The protester was later identified as Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old Bowdoin College student. A press release from the Sunrise Movement — a self-described "youth movement to stop climate change and create millions of jobs in the process" — said that Elgie was part of a pattern of students confronting politicians on the campaign trail.
Despite this being the fourth debate, the two panelists — Maine Public chief political correspondent Steve Mistler and NEWS CENTER Maine host and political reporter Phil Hirschkorn — managed to get the candidates to weigh in on some new issues.
In some cases, they almost agreed.
Both Jackson and Collins said they were opposed to so-called "dark money," which is when political donors hide their contributions by giving to organizations that don't have to disclose their sources, such as politically active 501(c)(4) nonprofits. According to Mistler, Collins and Jackson have benefited from at least $75 million in dark money spending so far.
Collins said she has supported sweeping campaign finance reforms in the past that did not pass constitutional muster.
"I still think that there are reforms that could be made, and one of them is full disclosure of everyone who is contributing," Collins said.
"I'm 100% for overturning Citizens United," Jackson said, referring to the Supreme Court decision that opened the door to unlimited spending on campaigns and, by extension, the creation of super PACs. "I mean, billionaires have bought Congress and everyday people can't afford to buy them back."
On the issue of guns, Collins reiterated that she would support a ban on so-called bump stocks that allow semi-automatic guns to function more like a machine gun and would support "reasonable" limits on magazine capacity. She also said would be "open" to increasing the age to purchase an assault weapon from 18 to 21.
Jackson said he opposes increasing the minimum age. But unlike Collins, he would support a ban on the purchase of assault weapons — but would not support taking them away from people who already own them.
But the rivals disagreed sharply on whether the Supreme Court should be expanded.
Some progressives are pushing to add justices to counteract the court's 6-3 conservative majority. Jackson supports the idea and also called for term limits on justices and ethics reforms.
"We have the best Supreme Court that money can buy right now and I think that has to be turned over," Jackson said.
But Collins said adding justices would amount to political interference.
"It's inconsistent with the whole idea of the Supreme Court being insulated from politics ... that would make it a total political body," Collins said.
The last time Congress added seats to the Supreme Court was in 1869.

articles.title_orig: Trump hits Georgia to rally Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state
articles.title_zh: Trump hits Georgia to rally Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state
articles.content_orig:
The unpopular president is rallying to support Republican nominees ahead of midterms
Sign up for the Breaking News US email
Donald Trump’s speech to a small crowd of supporters in Dalton, Georgia, was just disrupted by protesters holding up signs against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), who were forced out of the crowd by Trump supporters, including a man wearing a yellow Gadsden flag as a cape.
Two of the signs denounced the idea of sending ICE officer to the polls on election day, which the administration has refused to rule out.
After he began speaking again, Trump praised “the woman in the yellow cape”.
“She went up there, ripped them out of their seats and threw them the hell out of here. Where’s the woman with the yellow cape, then? She was great,” Trump said.
As Donald Trump continues to rail against senator Jon Ossoff at his rally in Georgia, it is worth noting that Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent and a fierce Trump critic, said on Thursday that he would be “delighted for the president to come every day between now and the election”.
Speaking on MS Now, Ossoff said Trump was welcome to campaign against him in Georgia because “the public is turning against this administration.”
“They see, on the one hand, the total incompetence,” Ossoff continued. “The nation plunged recklessly into a war that they don’t know how to win or to end, a global energy crisis, record high diesel prices, record high prices for healthcare.”
“It costs more today than ever before in our country’s history to fill up your truck, to stock your fridge, to power your home,” the Democratic senator continued. “And then everybody can see that at the same time, the first families raking in billions of dollars from all over the world. The president’s adorning his office in gold. People are fed up and they’ve had enough.”
Donald Trump’s remarks to supporters in Georgia are mainly a rehash of previous speeches, filled with false claims we have debunked repeatedly, suggesting that the president is not a regular reader of the Guardian.
“Less than two years ago, our country was dead. Now we have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” Trump said, before claiming, as he has in the past, that this was an observation made to him by the Saudi king during his visit to that country last year.
“So that statement was true. The king of Saudi Arabia, when I was over there, he said, ‘A short time ago, you had – you were a laughingstock’ – meaning our country was a laughingstock, all the way, all the way around the world, everybody was laughing at the USA,” Trump said. “‘And in a very short period of time, you made it the hottest country,’” the president continued, attributing this remark to the Saudi king.
As the Guardian has reported previously, Trump did not meet the Saudi king, who is elderly and not often seen in public, during his visit last year. Instead, he was hosted by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. There is also no evidence that the Saudi prince made this statement to Trump, but there is video of Trump making a version of that claim to Prince Mohammed during an address to a US-Saudi investment event in Riyadh on 13 May 2025.
“The days of economic misery under the last administration are rapidly giving way to the greatest economy in the history of the world,” Trump said before directly addressing the crown prince in the audience. “We are rocking. The United States is the hottest country, with the exception of your country, I have to say, right? … No Mohammed… You’re hotter. At least as long as I’m up here, you’re hotter. But groceries, gasoline, energy and all other prices are down with no inflation. We have no inflation.”
Two weeks after his return to the US, Trump began saying that this observation had been made not by him, but to him. “I went to Saudi Arabia,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on 28 May 2025. “The king told me, he said, ‘you got the hottest com-’ we have the hottest country in the world right now.,” Trump said. “Six months ago this country was stone cold dead. We had a dead country.”
As he repeated the story, again and again, Trump began to also attribute his own claim, that the US was “dead” under Joe Biden, to the Saudi king as well. In remarks at the Nato summit in the Hague in June 2025, Trump insisted that the Saudi king had told him: “A year ago, your country was dead. You had a deadhead running it. You had a country that was dead”.
Since then, Trump has repeated the tale dozens of times.
Speaking in Georgia, Donald Trump is spending most of his time defending his record as president, rather than discussing Republican candidates at the rally who are up for election next month.
Much of what he said was simply not true.
To take one example, the president repeated an entirely imaginary story he has repeated frequently in recent weeks, about how he was supposedly blamed for high prices by reporters on the second day of his term, in January 2025.
“When I came in, it was January 20th. I came in and on January 21st I had a news conference and some of those same people were at the news conference and they were screaming at me. I was only there for less than one day, substantially less than one day. And I’m having a news conference. I thought it would be a victorious conference. I thought the fake news would be saying, ‘Oh, sir, what a great race you ran,’” Trump said.
“My first news conference, January 21st. So I take office on the 20th. I figured maybe I won’t have a news conference. So the next day I have a news conference and I’m waiting for accolades from the press. And they said, what about the cost of eggs? What about the cost of beef?” Trump claimed.
In fact, a review of the transcript from that news conference reveals that no such exchange took place on 21 January 2025, when he was mainly pressed on the pardons he signed the day before for Capitol rioters convicted of violence against police officers on January 6 2021, in support of his attempt to stay in power despite losing the 2020 election.
Donald Trump’s speech to a small crowd of supporters in Dalton, Georgia, was just disrupted by protesters holding up signs against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), who were forced out of the crowd by Trump supporters, including a man wearing a yellow Gadsden flag as a cape.
Two of the signs denounced the idea of sending ICE officer to the polls on election day, which the administration has refused to rule out.
After he began speaking again, Trump praised “the woman in the yellow cape”.
“She went up there, ripped them out of their seats and threw them the hell out of here. Where’s the woman with the yellow cape, then? She was great,” Trump said.
As he has in the past, Donald Trump just bragged to supporters in Georgia about what he called his key role in helping to defeat Democrat Jon Ossoff in a 2017 special election for a Georgia House seat, but made no mention at all of the fact that he also campaigned hard against Ossoff in the 2020 Georgia Senate race that Ossoff won, when he defeated the Trump-backed Republican David Perdue.
“Ossoff was leading by a lot and they called me in to help. It was a special election,” Trump recalled. “And I came in and I held a massive rally for the person, very nice woman. And we ended up beating Ossoff. So I beat him. And that was in 2017. I beat him once and now we’re going to beat him more importantly a second time.”
Trump failed to mention that the second time he campaigned against Ossoff was at a rally in Valdosta, Georgia, on 5 December 2020 – ahead of the runoff election Ossoff won in January 2021.
That rally was supposed to encourage Georgia Republicans to vote for Perdue, and a second Republican Senate candidate, Kelly Loeffler, but Trump devoted most of his speech to complaining about his loss in the 2020 presidential election and giving voters the idea that the elections were “rigged” against Republicans.

articles.title_orig: Presidential adviser says Ukraine is in talks to lift speed limit on military satellite network
articles.title_zh: Presidential adviser says Ukraine is in talks to lift speed limit on military satellite network
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.
Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions."
Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you."
Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian.
The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.
On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far."
Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.
SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Man Charged in Fatal Fentanyl Overdose and Rape of FIT Student
articles.title_zh: Man Charged in Fatal Fentanyl Overdose and Rape of FIT Student
articles.content_orig:
The suspect is accused of waiting 45 minutes before seeking help.
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Two teens are facing federal charges this week accusing them of supplying the fentanyl that killed one New York City college student and poisoned a second.
According to the newly unsealed indictment, Moises Freire, 19, brought fentanyl he obtained from Brian Peralta, 18, to the victims' undergraduate residence hall at Fashion Institute of Technology on March 18.
Officials said Freire falsely claimed the drug did not contain fentanyl and was "pure cocaine."
Freire encouraged the victims to ingest the substance and almost immediately both women lost consciousness, prosecutors said.
While the victims were incapacitated, Freire allegedly raped Annabel Richter in her FIT dorm room. Authorities say he then took photos of her that he sent to friends.
He waited 45 minutes before seeking help from campus security, to whom he claimed the two undergraduates had simply consumed too much alcohol.
Campus security responded and administered emergency aid, including Narcan. Both victims were transported to hospitals in Manhattan.
Toxicology results later confirmed that both women had ingested fentanyl and no cocaine.
The second victim regained consciousness after life‑saving treatment.
Richter remained in critical condition and eventually died from complications of acute fentanyl intoxication.
"This case alleges not only the deadly distribution of fentanyl to two young women but also the sexual assault of a victim rendered defenseless by that poisoning," said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. "We will work tirelessly to hold accountable those who endanger young people living and learning on our campuses."
Christopher Roberts, the head of the Drug Enforcement Administration New York Task Force Division, said the allegations were "beyond disturbing and include a cruel deception and unimaginable assault."
"College should be a place where young people can learn, grow, and pursue their dreams, not a place where predators exploit their vulnerability," Roberts said. "Every student deserves to feel safe, whether walking across campus, sitting in a classroom, or inside their own dorm room."
Freire and Peralta, both from Queens, are charged with conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance resulting in death. They face at least 20 years in prison if convicted. Freire is also charged with distributing a controlled substance with the intent to commit rape.
(The Associated Press and ABC News contributed to this report.)

articles.title_orig: Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May
articles.title_zh: Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants fired missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
Brent futures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to close at $109.86, a gain of 3.7%.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% this week while Brent advanced nearly 5%.
Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, a military spokesman said. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said.
Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia this week. Oil giant Aramco came under attack when one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran was hit Tuesday, the kingdom's energy ministry said .
The Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport on Oct. 10, killing 12 and injuring more than 300.
In the Strait of Hormuz, at least nine tankers and cargo ships have come under attack since Sunday as Iran tries to choke off oil exports through the waterway. Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday, U.S. Central Command said. The crew of the Singapore-registered ship was safely evacuated, according to Singapore's maritime authority.
The attacks have left three seafarers injured and two missing this week, according to the International Maritime Organization .
Crude exports through Hormuz have pulled back after touching prewar levels in September. Shipments  stood at 9.4 million barrels per day for the week ended Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war, according to data provided by the energy researcher Kpler.
Meanwhile, the " energy ceasefire " that President Donald Trump tried to broker between Ukraine and Russia has quickly unraveled. The Kremlin continued attacking Ukrainian infrastructure despite the supposed truce. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation.
Diesel prices have surged this year due to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and Iranian strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East. The fuel cost an average of $6.33 a gallon in the U.S. Friday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA data.
U.S. crude oil prices were also driven higher by a big decline of more than 8 million barrels for the week ended Oct. 9 in commercial inventories due to production shut-ins on the Gulf Coast from Hurricane Isaias, according to the Energy Information Administration.

articles.title_orig: Airline High School students run their own store to build real-world business skills
articles.title_zh: Airline High School students run their own store to build real-world business skills
articles.content_orig:
BOSSIER PARISH, La. (KSLA) - Airline High School students are getting a hands-on lesson in business through the Viking Exchange, a student-run store designed to help prepare them for the workforce and life after graduation.
The store sells concessions, school supplies, and Airline spirit gear to the school’s approximately 1,700 students. But the program goes beyond selling products. Students manage inventory, place orders, provide customer service, maintain the store and handle the daily responsibilities of running a business.
Brad Winstead, an Airline teacher and coach, serves as the school advisor and sponsor. He says the program was created to give students practical experience they can use on a resume and in future careers.
“It’s practical education and instruction,” Winstead said. “What’s taught in the abstract and the principles of business classes—inventory, receiving, the inventory accounting process, workplace safety—those things, which in a traditional classroom setting are taught in the abstract, this allows us to teach it in three dimensions.”
The Viking Exchange proposal is aligned with customer service and business-of-retail credentials from the National Retail Federation. Students can earn experience with customer interaction, inventory control, workplace safety and business operations.
Winstead said students also learn the small details that matter in a professional setting, including how to present themselves while serving customers.
The store is managed by students, with school staff providing guidance. Maxwell Moore serves as the Viking Exchange store manager. He said the experience can give students an advantage when they begin looking for jobs.
“This is a great opportunity for everybody to gain business experience,” Moore said. “Whenever they want to get in the workforce, they can join the business industry.”
Moore said he earned the manager position by working consistently, showing leadership, helping with inventory and making sure the store is clean and organized—even coming in on weekends when needed.
He plans to study kinesiology and hopes to eventually open his own physical therapy business. Moore said the program is helping him develop skills he can use as a future business owner.
“My path right now is kinesiology and hopefully starting my own business in kinesiology one day and helping my own physical therapy business because I want to help people,” Moore said.
Winstead believes more schools could benefit from similar programs. He said students who gain hands-on experience at a younger age may be better prepared for employment, college, trade school or entrepreneurship.
The Viking Exchange was supported by Red River Credit Union. Winstead said the partnership helped make the program possible and aligned with the credit union’s interest in supporting student education.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street ends down sharply, worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
articles.title_zh: Wall Street ends down sharply, worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slid on Friday as traders notched a mostly losing week amid a shift away from tech and artificial intelligence-related names as well as a rise in oil prices.
The S&P 500 lost 1.09% and ended at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 2.14% to close at 26,140.03. Both indexes ended the session below their 50-day moving averages. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41. The sell-off sent the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months .
Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 3%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH slid 10% week to date for its biggest weekly decline since April 2025.
Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, dragged the S&P 500 to a losing week. The benchmark index fell about 2% this week, while the Nasdaq shed more than 4% for its worst week since June. The Dow, on the other hand, advanced 0.7% on the week.
Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down nearly 12%, bringing the stock's week-to-date losses to 25%.
"The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now."
Other areas of the market such as energy saw gains Friday, with stocks like Chevron helping to keep the Dow's losses in check. Oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions between the U.S. and Iran as well as between Russian and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate crude futures increased 3.51% to settle at $101.41 per barrel, while Brent crude futures advanced 3.72% to $109.86.
Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 82% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
The three leading U.S. indexes ended Friday's session with losses.
The S&P 500 dropped 1.09% to finish at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41.
As the market sell-off intensified Friday afternoon, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) rose to levels it last closed at four months ago.
The VIX rose to 21.32, as of 3:10 p.m., rising more than 4.8 points on the session. It's on pace for its highest close since June 10, when it closed at 22.22.
Typically, when the VIX is above 20 that indicates greater fear in the market. The index last closed above that level on July 29 , when markets fell after the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its meeting that month. The next day , stocks rose, and the day marked a bottom in a market where many AI-related stocks had been selling off in the previous month .
The Nasdaq Composite was down about 2.5% in afternoon trading on Friday, bringing its loss on the week to almost 5%.
With that move, the tech-heavy index on pace for its worst weekly performance since the week ended April 4, 2025, when the index recorded a roughly 10% drop.
Communication services and information technology led the S&P 500 lower on Friday.
The two sectors were down 2.7% and 2.4%, respectively, becoming the two biggest laggards among the 11 S&P 500 sectors. Consumer discretionary followed behind them, falling 1.5%.
However, a look beneath the surface showed that the S&P 500 — which was last down 1.3% — was more evenly split despite the losses at the index level. There were about 280 losers in the index and 222 gainers.
In total, five out of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were in positive territory, led by energy with its 2.1% gain and utilities with its rise of 1.2%.
— Sean Conlon and Sarah Min

U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 2.9% to $100.78 per barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was 3.3% higher at $109.37 per barrel. Read more .
Here are the stocks making moves in midday trading:
Early in the "SaaSpocalypse" that roiled software companies this year, Manish Gupta, a portfolio manager at First Eagle Investments, added to Workday as he parsed through the wreckage for some bargains.
In recent months, that bet has paid off for the value investor. After falling about 40% in the first quarter of 2026, during which the enterprise software stock at various points was trading at not even three times revenue, the stock went on to surge more than 55% in the third.
